Argo Project — Complete CAPA Learning Guide

GitOps · Continuous Delivery · Workflows · Progressive Rollouts · Event-Driven Automation

A comprehensive beginner-to-certification learning resource using anihpj/jobpost (Django project) as your real-world example. Covers all four Argo projects and prepares you for the Certified Argo Project Associate (CAPA) exam.

🟢 Beginner-Friendly 📦 Argo CD 34% 🔄 Argo Workflows 36% 🚀 Argo Rollouts 18% 🔔 Argo Events 12% 🎯 CAPA Certified

Welcome to the Argo Project Complete Learning Guide! Whether you're a Kubernetes novice or an experienced DevOps engineer, this guide takes you from zero to CAPA-certified. We'll use the anihpj Django project with its jobpost application (models: Skills, User, Author, Location, JobPost) as our hands-on example throughout every chapter.

📖 Argo CD Core Concepts — Official Terminology

From the official Argo CD documentation. These terms appear throughout the CAPA exam — understanding them precisely is essential.

ConceptDefinitionCAPA Context
ApplicationA group of K8s resources defined by a manifest. This is a Custom Resource Definition (CRD) — the core object in Argo CD.The most-tested CRD on CAPA. Know: source, destination, project, syncPolicy fields.
Target StateThe desired state of an application, as represented by files in a Git repository. The "source of truth."Git = target state. Argo CD continuously reconciles to this. Key GitOps principle.
Live StateThe actual state of the application in the cluster. What pods, services, etc. are running RIGHT NOW.Argo CD compares live vs target every 3 minutes (default). Drift = live ≠ target.
Sync StatusWhether the live state matches the target state. Synced = matches; OutOfSync = differs.Independent from Health. An app can be Synced but Degraded.
SyncThe PROCESS of making an application's live state match its target state. Applying Git changes to the cluster.Can be manual (click "Sync") or automated (auto-sync policy).
RefreshCompare the latest code in Git with the live state. Also called "hard refresh" — forces a fresh Git fetch.Normal refresh = 3min poll. Hard refresh = immediate Git fetch + comparison.
HealthWhether the application is running correctly. Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, Suspended, Missing.Determined by K8s resource status. Deployment = availableReplicas; Pod = Ready condition.
Sync Operation StatusWhether a sync attempt succeeded or failed. Independent from the ongoing Sync Status.Tracks the LAST sync attempt. Used for CI/CD pipeline verification.
Tool / Source TypeThe tool used to build manifests: Directory (plain YAML), Helm, Kustomize, Jsonnet, Plugin.Argo CD auto-detects. Override with explicit source.type if detection fails.
Config Management PluginA custom tool for generating manifests. Extends Argo CD beyond built-in source types (v2.8+ uses sidecar plugins).Advanced topic. CAPA mentions CMPs but focuses on built-in types.
Tracking StrategyHow an Application follows Git: branch (HEAD), tag (immutable), or commit SHA (pinned).Use branch for dev, tag for production. Defines WHEN Argo CD detects changes.

📖 Argo ecosystem overview and GitOps principles are covered in detail in Part 1: Foundation (Chapters 1-3).

🚀 anihpj/jobpost — Your Hands-On Project Overview

Throughout this guide, we use the anihpj Django project with its jobpost application as a real-world example. This is not a toy — it's a production-style Django app with 5 data models that you'll containerize, GitOps-deploy, CI/CD-automate, canary-release, and event-trigger.

ComponentDetails
Projectanihpj — Django 4.x Job Board Application
Appjobpost — Job listing, search, and filtering application
ModelsSkills, User, Author, Location, JobPost (with M2M/FK relationships)
Docker Imageregistry.example.com/anihpj:v1.0 — multi-stage build, python:3.12-slim
GitOps Repogithub.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s — Kustomize base+overlays
Namespacesanihpj-dev, anihpj-staging, anihpj-prod
💡 How Each Argo Tool Serves anihpj
Argo Toolanihpj Use Case
Argo CDDeploy anihpj to dev/staging/prod via GitOps. Git = source of truth.
Argo WorkflowsCI pipeline: test→build→push. DB migration: backup→migrate→verify. Nightly backup via CronWorkflow.
Argo RolloutsCanary deploy new jobpost search: 10%→25%→50%→100%. Auto-rollback if error > 5%.
Argo EventsGitHub push → auto-deploy to dev. S3 CSV upload → import jobs. Calendar → nightly maintenance.

📜 Argo History, Timeline & Industry Adopters Reference

2017 — Argo Created at Intuit

Applatix acquisition. Argo Workflows v1.0 released as the first Argo project.

2018 — Argo CD + Rollouts

Argo CD first release (GitOps delivery). Argo Rollouts first release (progressive delivery).

2019 — Argo Events

Argo Events first release. All four projects now under the Argo umbrella.

2020 — Donated to CNCF

ALL FOUR projects donated to CNCF. Argo CD joins CNCF Sandbox.

2021 — Argo CD Incubating

Argo CD moves to Incubating. Workflows, Events, Rollouts join Sandbox.

2022 — Argo CD Graduates! 🎓

First GitOps tool to reach CNCF graduation. CAPA Certification announced.

2023-2024 — All Projects Mature

CAPA goes live. Argo Workflows approaches graduation. 50,000+ GitHub stars across all projects.

📦
Argo CD (GitOps Delivery)

What it does: Watches Git repos and continuously reconciles cluster state to match. Setup: Install in argocd namespace → Create Application CRDs pointing to GitOps repo → Configure sync policy (auto/manual). anihpj example: 3 Applications (dev/staging/prod) pointing to overlays/ directories. Auto-sync for dev/staging; manual approval for prod.

🔄
Argo Workflows (CI Engine)

What it does: Orchestrates containerized pipeline steps as DAG/Steps. Setup: Install in argo namespace → Create WorkflowTemplates for CI/migration/backup → Submit via CLI or trigger from Events. anihpj example: CI WorkflowTemplate: clone→test→build→push→update-gitops. DB migration: backup→migrate→verify. Nightly backup via CronWorkflow.

🚀
Argo Rollouts (Progressive Delivery)

What it does: Replaces K8s Deployment with canary/blue-green strategies + metric-driven analysis. Setup: Install in argo-rollouts namespace → Convert Deployments to Rollouts → Define canary/blue-green strategy with AnalysisTemplate. anihpj example: Rollout with canary 10%→50%→100%. AnalysisTemplate checks error rate and p95 latency via Prometheus. Auto-rollback on failure.

🔔
Argo Events (Trigger Automation)

What it does: Listens for external events and triggers workflows/actions. Setup: Install in argo-events namespace → Deploy EventBus (NATS) → Create EventSources (webhook, GitHub, S3, calendar) → Create Sensors with triggers. anihpj example: GitHub EventSource detects push → Sensor filters main branch → Triggers CI WorkflowTemplate with commit SHA parameter.

🧠 Key Architecture Decisions for Your Implementation
DecisionOption AOption BRecommendation
Git strategyMonorepo (code + config)Separate repos (config = GitOps repo)Separate repos — cleaner audit, independent CI triggers
Config toolHelm ChartsKustomize OverlaysKustomize — pure YAML, easier Git diffs, GitOps-native
Sync policyManual sync (prod)Auto-sync (all envs)Auto-sync dev/staging; Manual or sync-window-gated for prod
SecretsSealed SecretsExternal Secrets OperatorStart with Sealed Secrets (simple); graduate to ESO for cloud
Traffic MgmtPod count ratioIngress/Mesh (Istio/NGINX)Pod count for simplicity; Traffic manager for precision

🔄 Before & After — Manual Deploy vs Argo GitOps

❌ BEFORE: Manual Deployment (No Argo)
  • SSH into server → run deploy script → hope it works
  • "Which version is running?" → nobody knows
  • Rollback = SSH in again, manually revert
  • Secrets in .env files, shared over Slack
  • No audit trail — who deployed what, when?
  • "It worked in staging!" → production is different
  • CI/CD server holds cluster credentials (security risk)
✅ AFTER: Argo GitOps (This Guide)
  • git push → automated pipeline → deployed
  • Argo CD shows exact version: commit SHA + timestamp
  • Rollback = git revert → Argo CD auto-syncs
  • Secrets encrypted (Sealed Secrets/SOPS), safe in Git
  • Git history = complete audit trail, SOC2 compliant
  • Identical dev/staging/prod (same Kustomize base)
  • Argo CD agent lives INSIDE cluster (no external creds)
📚
Learn the Theory

Ch 1-3: GitOps principles, K8s refresh, Argo CD installation. ~6 hours. Build mental models through shipping port analogy, push-vs-pull diagrams, and CRD concept maps.

🛠️
Master the Tools

Ch 4-19: Argo CD (5 ch), Workflows (5 ch), Rollouts (3 ch), Events (3 ch). ~31 hours. Hands-on YAML, CLI practice, diagrams, and 170 practice questions across all four domains.

🎯
Pass the Exam

Ch 20-25: Full integration, production hardening, exam strategy, 22 domain Qs, 5 hands-on labs, full CAPA simulation. ~18 hours. Proven study plan, aliases, and test-taking strategies.

📋 Step-by-Step Implementation Plan

1
Prepare Infrastructure (Ch1-3): Set up K8s cluster (minikube/kind/k3s). Install all 4 Argo CLIs. Create argocd, argo, argo-rollouts, argo-events namespaces. Install all 4 controllers.
2
Containerize anihpj (Ch2): Write multi-stage Dockerfile. Build image: docker build -t registry.io/anihpj:v1 .. Push to registry. Test locally: docker run -p 8000:8000 registry.io/anihpj:v1.
3
Set Up GitOps Repo (Ch7): Create anihpj-gitops repo. Structure with Kustomize base + overlays (dev/staging/prod). Write Deployment, Service, ConfigMap. Commit and push.
4
Configure Argo CD (Ch4-8): Create AppProjects for dev/staging/prod with source/destination restrictions. Create 3 Application YAMLs (or App-of-Apps pattern). Sync to deploy anihpj to all environments.
5
Create CI Pipeline (Ch9-13): Write CI WorkflowTemplate: clone→test(pytest+flake8)→build(docker)→push(registry)→update(gitops). Test with argo submit --from wftmpl/ci-pipeline -p image-tag=v2.
6
Set Up Events (Ch17-19): Deploy EventBus (NATS). Create GitHub EventSource with webhook. Create Sensor: filter main branch → trigger CI WorkflowTemplate. Test with curl to webhook endpoint.
7
Configure Rollouts (Ch14-16): Convert Deployment to Rollout in GitOps repo. Define canary strategy with steps and AnalysisTemplate (Prometheus). Argo CD syncs the Rollout. Test with argo rollouts promote.
8
Wire Everything Together (Ch20-22): End-to-end test: git push → Events detects → Workflow runs CI → Updates GitOps repo → Argo CD syncs → Rollout canary deploys → Analysis validates → Full promotion. Add monitoring alerts at each stage.

# 2. Argo Workflows (CI Engine)

# 3. Argo Rollouts (Progressive Delivery)

kubectl apply -n argo-rollouts -f https://github.com/argoproj/argo-rollouts/releases/latest/download/install.yaml

# 4. Argo Events (Trigger Automation)

kubectl apply -n argo-events -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-events/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Verify all controllers are running:
kubectl get pods -n argocd && kubectl get pods -n argo && kubectl get pods -n argo-rollouts && kubectl get pods -n argo-events

📚 Part 1: Foundation — GitOps, K8s & Argo CD Chapters 1-3

Chapter 1: What is GitOps? (The Philosophy Behind Argo)

Before installing any Argo tools, let's understand why GitOps exists, what problems it solves, and how it transforms the way we deploy software. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost Django app to make every concept concrete.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 📖 Conceptual 🎯 CAPA Foundation

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why traditional deployment methods fail at scale
  • ✅ The 4 core principles of GitOps
  • ✅ Push vs Pull deployment models — and why GitOps pulls
  • ✅ What the Argo project family is and how all 4 tools fit together
  • ✅ How anihpj/jobpost maps to each Argo tool
  • ✅ GitOps vs Traditional CI/CD — a clear comparison
  • ✅ The history of Argo from Intuit to CNCF graduation

1.1 The Problem Before GitOps

Imagine you've built anihpj — a Django job board with the jobpost app. It works perfectly on your laptop. Now you need to deploy it to production. How do you do it?

😰 Deploying anihpj WITHOUT GitOps
  • Developer: "I SSH'd into the server and ran the deploy script at 2 AM"
  • Ops: "The script failed halfway — database migrated but new code didn't deploy"
  • Manager: "Which version of anihpj is running in production RIGHT NOW?"
  • Everyone: "Let me check the server... oh wait, I don't have SSH access"
  • RESULT: 45 minutes of downtime, unknown production state, 3 people woken up at 2 AM

The core problems with traditional deployment:

🔧
Manual Processes

SSH + scripts = human error. Every manual step is a potential failure point. No two deployments are exactly the same.

📋
Configuration Drift

"It worked in staging!" — but staging was configured differently from production. No one knows what changed.

🔍
No Audit Trail

Who changed the nginx config? When? Why? Without Git history, every investigation starts from zero.

🚫
Credentials Everywhere

CI/CD servers hold cluster credentials. If compromised, attacker has full cluster access. Security nightmare.

🚢 The Shipping Port Analogy — Understanding Containers & Orchestration

One of the best ways to understand containers and Kubernetes (and by extension, Argo) is through the shipping port analogy. This analogy is used by Docker's own documentation and helps explain why containers revolutionized software deployment:

📖 Why This Analogy Matters for CAPA

Understanding the physical world equivalent of containers and orchestration helps you reason about Kubernetes and Argo from first principles. When you encounter a new concept, ask: "What's the shipping port equivalent?" This mental model is especially useful for the CAPA exam where you need to troubleshoot unfamiliar scenarios.

1.2 GitOps Defined — The 4 Principles

GitOps is a way of managing infrastructure and application deployments where Git is the single source of truth. Instead of running scripts or clicking buttons, you describe your desired state in Git, and software agents make reality match.

📖 GitOps Definition (Official)

GitOps is a set of practices that use Git pull requests to manage infrastructure and application configurations. Git becomes the single source of truth, and the system is continuously reconciled to match the desired state declared in Git.

📋
1. Declarative

Everything described as code (YAML). You declare what you want, not how to get there.

📚
2. Versioned

Git is the single source of truth. Every change is a commit. Full audit history.

⬇️
3. Pull-Based

Agents pull desired state from Git. No external credentials pushed into your cluster.

🔄
4. Reconciled

Software agents continuously ensure actual state = desired state. Self-healing built in.

💡 The "Aha!" Moment

GitOps flips the deployment model inside out. Instead of your CI system pushing changes to your cluster (requiring credentials), a GitOps agent inside your cluster pulls from Git. Your cluster is never exposed to external credentials. And because Git is the source of truth, git revert becomes your rollback mechanism!

Each Principle Explained — With anihpj Examples

Principle 1: DECLARATIVE — "Describe what you want, not how to get it"

In traditional deployment, you write a script: "SSH into server A, copy files, restart nginx, run migrations." That's imperative — you specify exact steps. In GitOps, you write a YAML file that says "I want 3 replicas of anihpj:v2.1 running on namespace anihpj-prod." That's declarative — you specify the desired end state.
anihpj example: Your deployment.yaml declares replicas: 3 and image: anihpj:v2.1. You never write "start 3 containers" — Kubernetes does that for you.

Principle 2: VERSIONED & IMMUTABLE — "Git is the single source of truth"

Every change to your infrastructure is a Git commit. You can see who changed what, when, and why. If production breaks, you don't guess — you look at the Git log.
anihpj example: git log --oneline shows: a1b2c3d Bump anihpj to v2.1, e4f5g6h Increase prod replicas to 5. Full audit trail, instantly accessible.

Principle 3: PULL-BASED — "Agents pull. Nothing pushes from outside."

Argo CD runs INSIDE your cluster. It reaches OUT to your Git repo, pulls the desired state, and applies it. No external system needs your cluster credentials. If your CI server is compromised, the attacker can't reach your cluster because there's no connection from CI to cluster.
anihpj example: Argo CD polls github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s every 3 minutes. It pulls changes — GitHub never pushes to your cluster.

Principle 4: CONTINUOUSLY RECONCILED — "Actual state always converges to desired state"

Argo CD doesn't just deploy once and forget. It checks every 3 minutes: "Does the cluster match Git?" If someone manually deletes a pod, Argo CD recreates it. If someone edits a ConfigMap directly, Argo CD reverts it. This is self-healing.
anihpj example: A curious developer runs kubectl delete pod anihpj-xxx in production. Within 3 minutes, Argo CD detects the missing pod and recreates it. The developer gets a Slack notification: "⚠️ Drift detected and auto-corrected."

1.3 Push vs. Pull Deployment Models

This is the single most important concept in GitOps. Once you understand push vs pull, everything about Argo CD makes sense.

📦
Argo CD (Graduated 🎓)

Declarative, GitOps continuous delivery. Watches your Git repo and automatically syncs your cluster to match. The first GitOps tool to reach CNCF graduation (2022).

🔄
Argo Workflows (Incubating)

Container-native workflow engine. Each step runs in its own container. Supports DAGs, parallel execution, artifact passing. Used for CI/CD, ML pipelines, data processing.

🚀
Argo Rollouts (Incubating)

Progressive delivery controller. Replaces Kubernetes Deployment with blue-green and canary strategies. Metric-driven auto-promotion and rollback.

🔔
Argo Events (Incubating)

Event-driven workflow automation. 20+ event sources (webhook, S3, Kafka, GitHub, calendar). Triggers workflows when events happen.

The "Push vs Pull" Question WILL Be on the CAPA Exam

This is one of the most fundamental concepts tested. Be prepared to:

  • Explain why pull-based GitOps is more secure (no external credentials in your cluster)
  • Identify the 3 key differences: credentials, rollback mechanism, drift detection
  • Know when push is appropriate (simple deployments, non-K8s targets) vs pull (production K8s, compliance, multi-cluster)
  • Memorize: git revert = rollback in GitOps. This is a one-word answer that demonstrates understanding.

📝 Chapter 1 — CAPA Practice Questions

Q1
What are the 4 principles of GitOps?
Show Answer
Answer

Declarative (everything as code), Versioned & Immutable (Git = source of truth), Pull Automatically (agents pull, not push), Continuously Reconciled (actual state constantly matched to desired).

Explanation

These four principles form the foundation that every Argo tool builds upon. Declarative means you describe WHAT you want (YAML), not HOW to achieve it (scripts). Versioned & Immutable means Git history IS your audit trail — every change has a commit SHA, author, and timestamp. Pull Automatically is why Argo CD agents live INSIDE the cluster — no external system ever needs cluster credentials. Continuously Reconciled means the agent never stops watching; if drift occurs (manual kubectl edit), it auto-corrects within minutes. CAPA tip: These 4 principles are the answer to ANY 'Why GitOps?' question on the exam.

🔍 GITOPS PRINCIPLES
┌──────────┐   watch   ┌──────────┐   sync   ┌──────────┐
│ Git Repo │─────────▶│ Argo CD  │─────────▶│ Cluster  │
│ (Truth)  │          │ (Agent)  │          │ (Actual) │
└──────────┘          └──────────┘          └──────────┘
     ▲                                           │
     └──────── git revert = rollback ────────────┘
Q2
Why is pull-based deployment more secure than push-based?
Show Answer
Answer

In pull-based, the agent lives INSIDE the cluster — no external CI system needs cluster credentials. Push-based requires exposing cluster access to external CI servers, creating a security risk.

Explanation

In push-based CI/CD, your Jenkins/GitHub Actions server holds kubeconfig or a ServiceAccount token — if that server is compromised, the attacker gets full cluster access. In pull-based GitOps, the Argo CD agent authenticates TO Git (read-only usually), and the cluster has NO inbound CI connections. This means: (a) the attack surface is smaller — no CI server port open to the cluster, (b) even if CI credentials leak, the attacker can only push to Git (not deploy directly), and (c) SOC2/PCI compliance auditors love this because access control is centralized in Git. CAPA tip: The exam will ask you to identify the security advantage of pull-based over push-based — the one-word answer is 'credentials.'

🔍 PUSH vs PULL
PUSH:  CI Server ──kubectl──▶ Cluster  ⚠️ external creds
PULL:  Git ◀── CI ──▶ Git ──▶ ArgoCD ──▶ Cluster ✅ safe
Q3
How do you roll back in GitOps?
Show Answer
Answer

git revert the commit that introduced the bad change. The GitOps agent detects the Git change and syncs the cluster back to the previous state. This is an audit-friendly, version-controlled rollback.

Explanation

Unlike kubectl rollout undo (which only works for Deployments and doesn't track who did it), git revert creates a documented, reviewable, version-controlled rollback. The revert itself goes through the same PR process as any other change — a senior engineer must approve before it reaches production. This means: (1) you know WHO rolled back, (2) you know WHEN, (3) you can see exactly WHAT changed, and (4) the rollback is tested through CI before reaching production. CAPA tip: If the exam asks 'How do you rollback in GitOps?', the answer is always git revert — not argocd app rollback or kubectl rollout undo.

🔍 GITOPS PRINCIPLES
┌──────────┐   watch   ┌──────────┐   sync   ┌──────────┐
│ Git Repo │─────────▶│ Argo CD  │─────────▶│ Cluster  │
│ (Truth)  │          │ (Agent)  │          │ (Actual) │
└──────────┘          └──────────┘          └──────────┘
     ▲                                           │
     └──────── git revert = rollback ────────────┘
Q4
Which Argo tool implements GitOps continuous delivery?
Show Answer
Answer

Argo CD. It watches Git repositories and continuously reconciles the cluster state to match the desired state defined in Git.

Explanation

Argo CD is purpose-built for GitOps continuous delivery. Unlike traditional CD tools (Spinnaker, Octopus Deploy) that push changes, Argo CD watches Git and PULLS. It compares the desired state (Git) with the actual state (cluster) every 3 minutes by default, and can auto-sync or alert on drift. Argo CD's architecture (API Server + Application Controller + Repo Server) is designed to be Git-native — every operation is triggered by Git changes. The other Argo tools solve different problems: Workflows = CI pipelines, Rollouts = progressive delivery, Events = triggers.

🔍 GITOPS PRINCIPLES
┌──────────┐   watch   ┌──────────┐   sync   ┌──────────┐
│ Git Repo │─────────▶│ Argo CD  │─────────▶│ Cluster  │
│ (Truth)  │          │ (Agent)  │          │ (Actual) │
└──────────┘          └──────────┘          └──────────┘
     ▲                                           │
     └──────── git revert = rollback ────────────┘
Q5
What CNCF maturity level has Argo CD achieved?
Show Answer
Answer

Graduated (2022) — the first GitOps tool to reach CNCF graduation. Workflows, Rollouts, and Events are at Incubating level.

Explanation

CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation) has three maturity levels representing a project's adoption and governance maturity: Sandbox (experimental, early-stage), Incubating (growing adoption, maturing governance, passing security audits), and Graduated (production-ready, widely adopted, diverse maintainers, passed rigorous security review). Argo CD reached Graduated in December 2022 — the FIRST GitOps tool to achieve this. Argo Workflows, Rollouts, and Events remain at Incubating. CAPA tip: 'Graduated' status means enterprise trust — this is often a one-word answer on the exam.

Scenario: Choosing the Right Deployment Model

For each scenario below, determine whether Push-based CI/CD or Pull-based GitOps (Argo CD) is the better choice and explain why:

  1. A startup with 3 developers deploying a simple web app to a single server
  2. A financial services company with 50 microservices requiring SOC2 compliance and full audit trails
  3. A team that wants instant rollback capability — reverting a bad deploy in under 60 seconds
  4. A platform team managing 8 Kubernetes clusters across 3 regions that must stay in sync
📝 Click to reveal answers
# 1. Push-based CI/CD — Simple, low overhead. GitOps (Argo CD) is overkill for a single server.
# 2. Pull-based GitOps — SOC2 requires audit trails. Git history = immutable audit log.
# 3. Pull-based GitOps — git revert + Argo CD auto-sync = instant rollback.
# 4. Pull-based GitOps — Argo CD's multi-cluster management is built in.

# CAPA Insight: The exam tests WHEN to use GitOps vs traditional CI/CD,
# not just HOW to use Argo CD.

CAPA Exam: K8s Prerequisites Are Implicitly Tested

While CAPA doesn't directly ask "What is a Pod?", it assumes you can read and write YAML for K8s objects. You'll encounter Pod specs inside Workflow templates, Service definitions in Rollout configs, and ConfigMaps/Secrets everywhere. Key areas to be fluent in: labels & selectors (how Services find Pods), namespaces (Argo CD deploys to specific namespaces), and CRDs (Argo IS a set of CRDs). If you can't read a Deployment YAML at a glance, practice with kubectl explain before exam day.

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 2
  • YAML indentation errors: Argo is STRICT about YAML. One tab character or wrong indentation level causes silent failures. Always use spaces (2 per level), never tabs. Use yamllint or your IDE's YAML validator.
  • Confusing labels vs annotations: Labels are for K8s selectors (used by Services, Deployments). Annotations are for tool metadata (Argo CD uses annotations like argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options). They're NOT interchangeable — selectors use labels only.
  • Forgetting CRDs extend the API: When Argo is installed, it teaches K8s new resource types. kubectl api-resources | grep argo shows them all. A Workflow is as real as a Pod to the API server.

2.1 Quick Kubernetes Concepts Review (for Argo)

Here are the K8s objects you absolutely need to know before using Argo. Every Argo tool ultimately manages these resources:

❌ Running anihpj WITHOUT K8s
  • Manual ssh into each server
  • python manage.py runserver (single process)
  • If server crashes, app is DOWN until manual restart
  • Scaling = buy new servers, configure from scratch
  • "Which server runs which version?" — nobody knows
✅ Running anihpj WITH K8s + Argo
  • kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml — done
  • 3 Pods running gunicorn with auto-restart
  • Pod crashes → K8s auto-recreates in seconds
  • Scaling = kubectl scale --replicas=10
  • Argo CD shows exactly what's deployed where
K8s ObjectWhat It DoesArgo Relevance
PodSmallest deployable unit (1+ containers)Argo Workflows create pods for each step. Argo CD deploys pods via Deployments.
DeploymentManages replica pods, rolling updatesArgo CD syncs Deployments. Argo Rollouts REPLACES Deployment with Rollout CRD.
ServiceStable network endpoint for podsArgo CD deploys Services. Rollouts needs activeService + previewService.
ConfigMapNon-sensitive configurationStore Django settings for anihpj. Synced by Argo CD.
SecretSensitive data (passwords, keys)DB password, Django SECRET_KEY. Use Sealed Secrets with Argo CD!
NamespaceLogical isolation boundaryanihpj-dev, anihpj-staging, anihpj-prod. Argo CD deploys to specific namespaces.

During the CAPA exam, you can generate YAML skeletons instantly instead of typing from scratch:

kubectl create deploy anihpj --image=registry.io/anihpj:v1 --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml

This saves 2-3 minutes per YAML file. Never write Kubernetes YAML from scratch during the exam!

💡 Pro Tip

If you're rusty on K8s, spend 30 minutes with kubectl explain pod.spec, kubectl explain deployment.spec, and kubectl explain service.spec — these are your in-terminal documentation during the CAPA exam!

Labels & Selectors — The Glue That Binds Everything

Labels are the most important Kubernetes concept for Argo CD. Think of labels as tags you attach to resources, and selectors as filters that find resources with specific tags. Argo CD uses labels and selectors extensively:

How Labels Connect Resources
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LABELS & SELECTORS in Argo CD                              │
│                                                             │
│  Pod:                                                       │
│    labels:                                                  │
│      app: anihpj          ← Label (the "tag")               │
│      version: v2.1                                         │
│      environment: prod                                       │
│                                                             │
│  Service:                                                   │
│    selector:                                                │
│      app: anihpj          ← Selector (the "filter")         │
│                                                             │
│  Service finds Pods with app=anihpj → routes traffic to them│
│                                                             │
│  Argo CD Application:                                       │
│    spec.destination.namespace: anihpj-prod                  │
│    → Only deploys to namespace labeled "anihpj-prod"        │
│                                                             │
│  Argo Workflows:                                            │
│    templates can select nodes by label:                     │
│      nodeSelector:                                          │
│        disktype: ssd    ← Only run on SSD nodes             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

2.2 CRDs (Custom Resource Definitions) — How Argo Extends Kubernetes

A CRD lets you teach Kubernetes new tricks. Instead of only knowing about Pods, Deployments, and Services, you can define your own resource types. Argo installs CRDs so you can create Application, Workflow, Rollout, and EventSource objects just like you create Pods.

│  │  Deployment      │  │  Workflow        WorkflowTmpl   ││
│  │  Service         │  │  CronWorkflow    Rollout        ││
│  │  ConfigMap       │  │  AnalysisTmpl    AnalysisRun    ││
│  │  Secret          │  │  EventSource     Sensor         ││

2.3 Git Refresher for GitOps

GitOps means Git is the source of truth. Here's what you need to know:

GitOps Repo Structure for anihpj
anihpj-k8s/                        ← GitOps repository
├── base/                          ← Common K8s manifests
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   ├── configmap.yaml
│   └── kustomization.yaml
├── overlays/                      ← Environment variations
│   ├── dev/    (1 replica)
│   ├── staging/(2 replicas)
│   └── prod/   (5 replicas)
└── argo-apps/                     ← Argo CD Application YAMLs
    ├── anihpj-dev.yaml
    ├── anihpj-staging.yaml
    └── anihpj-prod.yaml

HOW ARGO CD USES IT:
Application → source.path = "overlays/dev"
Argo CD clones repo → runs kustomize build → applies to cluster
FOR VERSIONING: Git tags like "v1.2.3" for targetRevision
📌 Key Concept

git revert = rollback. git log = audit trail. git diff = preview changes. Everything you know about Git becomes your deployment management tool!

2.4 YAML Mastery for Argo

Argo is VERY strict about YAML indentation. One wrong space and your Application won't sync. Here are the top mistakes to avoid:

⚠️ TOP 5 YAML MISTAKES IN ARGO
  • 1. Wrong namespace: Applications MUST be in argocd namespace
  • 2. Indentation errors: spec: → 2 spaces → source: → 2 spaces → repoURL:
  • 3. Wrong API version: Always argoproj.io/v1alpha1 (NOT v1!)
  • 4. Missing --- separator: Multi-doc YAML needs --- between documents
  • 5. Trailing slash in cluster URL: https://kubernetes.default.svc (no trailing /)
💡 CAPA Speed Tip

Use kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate YAML skeletons quickly during the exam. Never write YAML from scratch when kubectl can do it for you!

2.5 Your Lab Environment Setup

You need a running Kubernetes cluster. Choose one:

Terminal — Lab Setup
# Option A: KIND (lightweight, Docker-based — RECOMMENDED)
kind create cluster --name argo-lab

# Option B: Minikube
minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=8192 --driver=docker

# Option C: k3s (Rancher, very lightweight)
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -

# Verify cluster:
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes  # Should show: Ready

# Install Argo CD CLI (macOS):
brew install argocd
# Linux: curl -sSL https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/releases/latest/download/argocd-linux-amd64 -o /usr/local/bin/argocd && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/argocd

# Install Argo Workflows CLI:
curl -sLO https://github.com/argoproj/argo-workflows/releases/latest/download/argo-linux-amd64.gz
gunzip argo-linux-amd64.gz && chmod +x argo-linux-amd64 && sudo mv argo-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/argo

# Verify tools:
kubectl version --client && argocd version --client && argo version

2.6 Docker Image for anihpj — Preparing Your App

Before Argo CD can deploy anihpj, we need a container image. Here's a production-ready multi-stage Dockerfile:

Dockerfile — anihpj/jobpost
# STAGE 1: Build dependencies
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# STAGE 2: Runtime (minimal)
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
RUN useradd -m -u 1000 django && chown -R django:django /app
USER django
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health/')"
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]

# Build & push:
# docker build -t registry.example.com/anihpj:v1.0 .
# docker push registry.example.com/anihpj:v1.0
💡 .dockerignore (keep image small!)

__pycache__/ *.pyc .git/ .env .venv/ db.sqlite3 static/ media/

📝 Chapter 2 — CAPA Practice Questions

Q1
What is a CRD and how does Argo use them?
Show Answer
Answer

A Custom Resource Definition extends the K8s API with new resource types. Argo installs CRDs for Application, Workflow, Rollout, EventSource etc. Check: kubectl api-resources | grep argoproj.

Explanation

A CRD extends the Kubernetes API by teaching it a NEW resource type. When you install Argo CD, it creates CRDs for Application, AppProject, etc. After that, kubectl get applications works just like kubectl get pods. The CRD defines the SCHEMA (what fields are valid), and a CONTROLLER watches for instances of that CRD and takes action. This is key: CRD = the definition (like a class), Custom Resource (CR) = an instance (like an object). All 4 Argo projects are implemented as CRDs + controllers.

🔍 CRDs EXTEND K8s
K8s Built-in: Pod | Service | Deployment | ConfigMap
    +
Argo CRDs: Application | Workflow | Rollout | Sensor
    =
K8s now understands GitOps resources!

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 3
  • Wrong namespace: Argo CD components MUST be in argocd namespace (unless explicitly configured otherwise). Installing elsewhere breaks default RBAC and network configurations.
  • Forgetting to change the admin password: The initial password is in a K8s Secret. The exam may test: kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d.
  • Port-forward gotcha: argocd-server serves on port 443 (HTTPS), not 80. kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443 — notice the 443.
  • Non-HA vs HA install: The quick-start manifest is a single YAML for development/testing. HA/production requires separate manifests with replicas > 1 and external Redis/Postgres.
🎓 CAPA Exam Relevance — Argo CD (34% of exam)

Chapters 3-8 cover the Argo CD domain (34%) of the CAPA exam. This chapter specifically maps to the official competency "Understand Argo CD Fundamentals." You'll need to know how to install Argo CD, access its UI, and understand its architecture. The Application CRD and sync policies you learn here are tested in virtually every Argo CD exam question.

3.1 What is Argo CD? — The Heart of GitOps

Argo CD is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. Its job is simple: watch your Git repository and make your cluster match it. If someone manually changes something in the cluster, Argo CD detects the drift and corrects it (if self-heal is enabled).

Argo CD Architecture

┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
│  Git Repo    │    │ Argo CD API  │    │  Kubernetes  │
│ (anihpj-k8s) │◀──▶│   Server     │───▶│   Cluster    │
└──────────────┘    └──────┬───────┘    └──────────────┘
                           │
                  ┌────────┴─────────┐
                  │  Application     │
                  │  Controller      │  ← Reconciliation Loop
                  │  (every 3 min)   │
                  └──────────────────┘
                           │
                  ┌────────┴─────────┐
                  │  Repo Server     │  ← Clones Git, runs Helm/Kustomize
                  └──────────────────┘

The Reconciliation Loop — How Argo CD Thinks

Argo CD's core innovation is the reconciliation loop — an infinite cycle that constantly compares desired state (what's in Git) with actual state (what's in the cluster) and takes action when they differ.

1
OBSERVE

Get desired state from Git + actual state from cluster

2
DIFF

Compute the difference: what needs to be created, updated, or deleted?

3
ACT

Apply kubectl commands to make actual match desired

4
REPEAT

Wait 3 minutes (configurable), then go to Step 1

📖 Key Insight: Level-Triggered, Not Edge-Triggered

Argo CD doesn't care how the drift happened. It just checks: "Does the cluster match Git? No? Then fix it." This is called level-triggered (checking the current level/state) vs edge-triggered (reacting to a specific event). This is why kubectl apply is idempotent — running it 100 times produces the same result as running it once.

3.2 Installing Argo CD on Your Cluster

The installation process deploys 7 microservices into the argocd namespace. Understanding what happens at each step is crucial for the CAPA exam — you may need to troubleshoot a failed installation.

📦
Step 1: Namespace Creation

kubectl create namespace argocd — Creates a logical isolation boundary. All Argo CD components live here. This keeps Argo CD separate from your application workloads. The namespace name must be argocd — Argo CD will not work in any other namespace.

📥
Step 2: Apply the Install Manifest

kubectl apply -f install.yaml — This single YAML file contains ~20 Kubernetes resources: Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, ServiceAccounts, ClusterRoles, and CRDs. It's fetched directly from the official Argo CD GitHub repository. Always use the stable tag for production, not master.

⏳
Step 3: Wait for Readiness

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready — Blocks until all pods are running. The --timeout=300s gives 5 minutes for image pulls and startup. If pods don't become ready, check: kubectl describe pod -n argocd to see if it's an image pull issue, resource constraint, or configuration error.

🔑
Step 4: Retrieve Admin Password

The initial admin password is stored in a Kubernetes Secret named argocd-initial-admin-secret. The jsonpath extraction gets the base64-encoded password and pipes it through base64 -d to decode it. CAPA exam tip: memorize this exact command — you'll need it.

🌐
Step 5: Access the UI

kubectl port-forward creates a temporary tunnel from your local machine to the Argo CD API server. This is the simplest way to access the UI in a lab environment. For production, you'd configure an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service instead. The UI runs on HTTPS (port 443) with a self-signed certificate — accept the warning in your browser.

⌨️
Step 6: CLI Login

argocd login authenticates your CLI to the Argo CD API server. The --insecure flag skips TLS verification (OK for localhost, never for production). After login, your session token is stored in ~/.argocd/config and persists across terminal sessions.

🔐
Step 7: Change the Password!

argocd account update-password — The default admin password is publicly known (it's in the documentation!). Change it immediately. For production, also disable the admin account entirely after configuring SSO/OIDC: set admin.enabled: "false" in the argocd-cm ConfigMap.

Terminal — Argo CD Install
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace argocd

# Step 2: Install Argo CD
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Step 3: Wait for pods
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n argocd --timeout=300s

# Step 4: Get admin password
kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d; echo

# Step 5: Access UI
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443
# Open https://localhost:8080 — Username: admin

# Step 6: CLI login
argocd login localhost:8080 --username admin --password $(kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d) --insecure

# Step 7: CHANGE THE PASSWORD!
argocd account update-password

3.3 Argo CD Core Components Walkthrough

ComponentWhat It DoesCAPA Note
argocd-serverAPI server + Web UI. Handles all user interactions.Port-forward to access during exam
argocd-repo-serverClones Git repos, runs Helm/Kustomize/Plugin, returns rendered YAML.Caches clones in Redis
argocd-application-controllerTHE reconciliation engine. Compares desired (Git) vs actual (cluster) every 3 min.Core of GitOps — know this!
argocd-applicationset-controllerGenerates multiple Applications from templates (List, Git, Cluster generators).Exam topic: ApplicationSets
argocd-redisCache layer. Stores Git repo clones to avoid re-cloning.If sync is stale, check Redis
argocd-dex-serverOIDC/SSO authentication (Okta, Google, GitHub, Azure AD).Production requirement
argocd-notifications-controllerSends alerts to Slack, Email, Teams, Webhook on sync events.Optional but recommended

3.4 First Argo CD Application — Deploy anihpj

Let's deploy anihpj using Argo CD! But first, let's plan our namespaces. Good namespace design is critical for GitOps:

📦 anihpj-dev — Development environment. Auto-sync ON, prune ON. 1 replica. Fast iteration.
📦 anihpj-staging — Staging environment. Auto-sync ON after tests pass. 2 replicas. Integration testing.
📦 anihpj-prod — Production environment. Manual sync preferred. 5 replicas. Canary deployments via Rollouts.

Create this Application manifest for the dev environment:

anihpj-dev-app.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj-dev
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/YOUR-USER/anihpj-k8s
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/dev
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: anihpj-dev
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
1
Apply

kubectl apply -f

2
Clone

Repo-server clones Git

3
Render

kustomize build

4
Apply

Resources to cluster

5
Health

Check → Healthy ✓

💡 Watch the Magic

argocd app get anihpj-dev — Watch status go: OutOfSync → Syncing → Synced → Healthy. Your Django app is now deployed via GitOps!

3.5 Argo CD Sync Strategies and Policies

ScenarioAuto-Sync?Prune?Self-Heal?
DEV (fast feedback)✅ YES✅ YES✅ YES
STAGING (after tests)✅ YES✅ YES✅ YES
PRODUCTION⚠️ Manual⚠️ Careful✅ YES
DB MIGRATIONS❌ Manual❌ Manual❌ Manual
⚠️ CRITICAL

In production, prune: true means "delete anything not in Git" — if you accidentally delete a YAML file from Git, Argo CD WILL delete that resource from production! Start with manual sync, build trust, then enable automation progressively.

  • Gotcha 1: Applications MUST be created in the argocd namespace. If you create them in default or any other namespace, Argo CD won't recognize them! Always: kubectl apply -f app.yaml -n argocd
  • Gotcha 2: The destination.server field for the local cluster is https://kubernetes.default.svc — NOT localhost, NOT the external IP. Copy-paste exactly.
  • Gotcha 3: If sync fails with "namespace not found", you forgot syncOptions: - CreateNamespace=true. Argo CD does NOT auto-create namespaces by default!
  • Gotcha 4: After changing the admin password, the old password stored in argocd-initial-admin-secret is no longer valid. Use argocd account update-password instead.
  • argocd app get anihpj-dev — Confirm status is "Healthy" and "Synced"
  • kubectl get pods -n anihpj-dev — Verify pods are Running
  • kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj -n anihpj-dev 8000:80 — Test the app responds
  • argocd app diff anihpj-dev — Confirm no unexpected differences

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 4
  • Confusing sync status with health status: An app can be "Synced" (cluster matches Git) but "Degraded" (pod is crashing). Sync is about configuration; health is about runtime behavior. These are independent dimensions.
  • Auto-sync without pruning: If you enable automated sync but NOT pruning, deleted resources in Git remain in the cluster. Always pair auto-sync with prune: true for true GitOps.
  • Source type detection: Argo CD auto-detects source type (Helm, Kustomize, directory) based on files present. If detection fails, explicitly set source.type.
  • Multiple sources order matters: When using multiple sources, the first source is the "main" one for parameter resolution.
🎓 CAPA Relevance — "Use Argo CD Application"

This chapter directly maps to the official competency "Use Argo CD Application" (34% domain). The Application CRD is the most-tested object on the exam — you'll create, modify, and troubleshoot Applications in nearly every hands-on task.

4.1 The Application CRD — Deep Dive

🔍 Anatomy of an Argo CD Application

📋 Kind/VersionapiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 — kind: Application. This tells Kubernetes this is an Argo CD resource. The apiVersion MUST be v1alpha1 — v1 does not exist!
🏷️ Metadataname: anihpj-prod must be unique within the namespace: argocd. Applications MUST live in the argocd namespace — Argo CD ignores them elsewhere.
📂 SourcerepoURL: Git repository URL. targetRevision: branch, tag, or commit SHA. path: folder within the repo containing manifests. Argo CD clones this repo and renders YAML from this path.
🎯 Destinationserver: Cluster API URL (for local: https://kubernetes.default.svc). namespace: Target namespace. Argo CD deploys rendered YAML to this cluster+namespace.
📦 Projectproject: default — which AppProject this belongs to. AppProjects restrict what sources and destinations are allowed (Chapter 5).
🔄 SyncPolicyautomated.prune: delete resources not in Git. automated.selfHeal: auto-correct drift. syncOptions: e.g., CreateNamespace=true.
anihpj-prod Application
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

4.2 Source Types — Choosing the Right One

Argo CD supports multiple ways to define your Kubernetes manifests. The source type determines how Argo CD reads your Git repository:

Source TypeHow It WorksBest Foranihpj?
DirectoryPlain YAML/JSON files in a folder. Simplest option.Simple apps, quick prototypes⚠️ Works but limited
HelmHelm chart + values.yaml. Supports Go templates.Packaged apps, complex templatingMaybe later
KustomizeBase + overlay patching. Built into kubectl.Multi-environment apps✅ RECOMMENDED
PluginCustom config management (CUE, Jsonnet, etc.)Legacy/non-standard tools❌ Overkill
❌ Directory Source (Flat YAML)

Every environment has its own complete set of YAML files. Duplication everywhere.

envs/dev/ → deployment.yaml (1 replica)
envs/staging/ → deployment.yaml (2 replicas)
envs/prod/ → deployment.yaml (5 replicas)
✅ Kustomize Source (Base + Overlay)

One base, environment-specific patches. DRY principle.

base/deployment.yaml (template)
overlays/dev/ → patch: replicas=1
overlays/staging/ → patch: replicas=2
overlays/prod/ → patch: replicas=5
Directory Source

Plain YAML files in a folder. Argo CD reads all .yaml/.json files and applies them. No templating, no patching. Simplest option but requires duplicating YAML across environments.

Helm Source

Helm chart with values.yaml. Supports Go templates with {{ .Values.image.tag }} syntax. Best for packaged applications distributed via Artifact Hub. More complex but more flexible.

Kustomize Source

Base + overlay patching. Built into kubectl. No external tools needed. Write one base manifest, then patch differences per environment. Recommended for anihpj.

Plugin Source

Custom config management via sidecar container. Use for non-standard tools like CUE, Jsonnet, or proprietary templating engines. Requires custom plugin setup in Argo CD.

4.3 Multiple Sources (Argo CD 2.6+)

Need to combine a Helm chart from one repo with environment values from another? Multiple sources let you do exactly that — without merging repos.

MULTIPLE SOURCES — One Application, Two Repos
┌─────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────┐
│ REPO A: App Chart    │    │ REPO B: Env Values   │
│ anihpj-helm-chart    │    │ anihpj-env-values    │
│  Chart.yaml          │    │  dev-values.yaml     │
│  templates/          │    │  prod-values.yaml    │
└──────────┬──────────┘    └──────────┬──────────┘
           └──────────┬───────────────┘
                      ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │  ARGO CD APPLICATION     │
        │  sources:               │
        │    - repo: .../chart    │
        │    - repo: .../values   │
        │  RESULT: Merged YAML    │
        └─────────────────────────┘

4.4 Sync Waves — Ordered Deployment

🌊
Wave -1
Namespaces
🔐
Wave 0
Secrets
📦
Wave 1
Deployments
🌐
Wave 2
Services
🚪
Wave 3
Ingress
📖 How to Set a Sync Wave

Add annotation: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "2" to any resource. All wave N resources sync before wave N+1 starts. Within the same wave, resources sync in parallel.

Wave -1 (Namespaces): Create namespaces first. Use CreateNamespace=true or create namespace YAML with wave -1 annotation. Everything else depends on namespaces existing.

Wave 0 (Secrets/ConfigMaps): Deploy secrets and configs before apps. Pods can't start without them. anihpj needs DB_PASSWORD Secret and Django settings ConfigMap.

Wave 1 (Deployments/PVCs): The actual application workloads. anihpj Deployment with 3 replicas. PVCs for persistent storage.

Wave 2 (Services): Network endpoints that route traffic to pods. Must be created AFTER deployments are ready. Otherwise, Service points to nothing.

Wave 3+ (Ingress/Hooks): External access and post-deployment operations. Ingress exposes anihpj to the internet. PostSync hooks run smoke tests.

4.5 Sync Options — Fine-Tuning

OptionEffectWhen to Use
Replace=trueDelete + recreate (not patch)Immutable fields (Job specs)
ServerSideApply=trueUse K8s server-side applyK8s 1.22+, handles field conflicts
PruneLast=trueDelete old AFTER creating newZero-downtime resource replacement
RespectIgnoreDifferences=trueSkip fields that drift intentionallyHPA replicas, lifecycle fields

4.6 Health Checks & Status

Healthy
All good ✅
Progressing
Deploying...
Degraded
Failed ❌
Suspended
Paused ⏸️

Argo CD checks Deployment → readyReplicas == replicas. For anihpj, that means all 3 gunicorn pods are running and passing readiness probes. Custom health checks can be added via Lua scripts in argocd-cm ConfigMap.

4.8 Sync Options — Fine-Tuned Control (CAPA Critical!)

Argo CD provides 15+ sync options that give you surgical control over how resources are applied, pruned, and validated. These are configured as annotations on individual resources OR as application-level syncOptions.

SYNC OPTIONS — QUICK REFERENCE
ANNOTATION-BASED (per resource):
  argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false
  argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Delete=false
  argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: PruneLast=true

APPLICATION-LEVEL (spec.syncPolicy.syncOptions):
  Prune=false          → Never auto-delete this resource
  Delete=false         → Keep resource when app is deleted
  CreateNamespace=true → Auto-create target namespace
  PruneLast=true       → Delete old AFTER new is healthy (zero-downtime!)
  ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true → Only sync changed resources (perf boost)
  Replace=true         → Use kubectl replace (bypasses annotation limit)
  Force=true           → Delete + recreate (destructive! use with Replace)
  ServerSideApply=true → Use SSA for large resources > 262KB
  Validate=false       → Skip kubectl schema validation
  FailOnSharedResource=true → Error if resource owned by another app
  RespectIgnoreDifferences=true → Honor ignoreDifferences during sync
CAPA Must-Know Sync Options

PruneLast=true — Zero-downtime deployment pattern. Deletes old resources only AFTER new ones are healthy. Essential for stateful apps. ServerSideApply=true — Required for manifests > 262KB (annotation size limit). CreateNamespace=true — Auto-creates namespace if missing. Force=true + Replace=true — Destructive recreate. Needed for Job resources that must re-run.

📝 Chapter 4 — CAPA Practice Questions

Q1
What are the 6 key fields of an Argo CD Application CRD?
Show Answer
Answer

apiVersion/kind, metadata (name + namespace=argocd), spec.source (repoURL, path, targetRevision), spec.destination (server, namespace), spec.project, spec.syncPolicy.

Explanation

A CRD extends the Kubernetes API by teaching it a NEW resource type. When you install Argo CD, it creates CRDs for Application, AppProject, etc. After that, kubectl get applications works just like kubectl get pods. The CRD defines the SCHEMA (what fields are valid), and a CONTROLLER watches for instances of that CRD and takes action. This is key: CRD = the definition (like a class), Custom Resource (CR) = an instance (like an object). All 4 Argo projects are implemented as CRDs + controllers.

Q6
What is the difference between "Synced" and "Healthy"?
Show Answer
Answer

Synced = cluster state matches Git (no drift). Healthy = the application is running correctly (pods are up, passing health checks). A resource can be Synced but not Healthy (e.g., a CrashLoopBackOff pod whose YAML matches Git).

Chapter 5: AppProjects — Organizing & Securing Applications

AppProjects are the security boundary of Argo CD. They control WHO can deploy WHAT to WHERE. Without AppProjects, any Application can deploy to any cluster and namespace — a security nightmare in production.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔐 Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Create AppProjects as security boundaries
  • ✅ Restrict source repos, destinations, and resource types
  • ✅ Set up RBAC with project roles
  • ✅ Follow production best practices
APPPROJECT — SECURITY BOUNDARY
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    AppProject                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  ALLOW LISTS (everything else is DENIED!)        │   │
│  │                                                  │   │
│  │  ✅ Source Repos: github.com/org/anihpj-*       │   │
│  │  ✅ Destinations: *.anihpj-dev, *.anihpj-staging │   │
│  │  ✅ Resources: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap    │   │
│  │  ❌ Blocked:     LoadBalancer, Ingress, CRDs    │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                         │
│  Application "dev-api" → Project "anihpj-dev" ✓         │
│  Application "dev-api" → Default Project ✓ (unrestricted)│
│  Application "prod-api" → Wrong Project ✗ (BLOCKED!)    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 5
  • Default project is wide open: Every new Application is in the "default" project unless specified otherwise. The default project has NO restrictions — any repo, any cluster, any namespace. For production, always create dedicated AppProjects.
  • Allow-list mentality: AppProjects use ALLOW lists for source repos, destinations, and cluster resources. If you don't whitelist it, it's blocked. An empty whitelist blocks everything — including valid resources.
  • Orphaned resources: Deleting an AppProject does NOT delete its Applications — they become orphaned. Migrate Applications to a new project before deleting the old one.

5.1 What is an AppProject?

AppProject as a Security Boundary

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AppProject: anihpj-prod                     │
│                                              │
│  ✅ ALLOWED sources:                          │
│     github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s        │
│  ❌ BLOCKED sources:                          │
│     github.com/random-user/*                 │
│                                              │
│  ✅ ALLOWED destinations:                      │
│     namespace: anihpj-prod                   │
│  ❌ BLOCKED destinations:                      │
│     namespace: kube-system                   │
│     namespace: * (wildcard)                  │
│                                              │
│  ❌ BLACKLISTED resources (can NEVER deploy):  │
│     ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding           │
│     ResourceQuota, LimitRange                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

5.2 AppProjects for anihpj

anihpj-prod AppProject
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  sourceRepos:
    - https://github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s
  destinations:
    - namespace: anihpj-prod
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
  namespaceResourceBlacklist:
    - group: 'rbac.authorization.k8s.io'
      kind: ClusterRole
    - group: 'rbac.authorization.k8s.io'
      kind: ClusterRoleBinding
  roles:
    - name: prod-deployer
      policies:
        - p, proj:anihpj-prod:prod-deployer, *, sync, *, allow
    - name: prod-readonly
      policies:
        - p, proj:anihpj-prod:prod-readonly, *, get, *, allow

5.3 RBAC & Security

AppProject roles let you define fine-grained permissions. The policy format is: p, <subject>, <resource>, <action>, <object>, <effect>

⚠️ Production Rule

NEVER use destinations: - namespace: "*" in a production AppProject. This allows Applications in that project to deploy to ANY namespace — including kube-system. Always use explicit namespace lists.

5.4 Best Practices

🎯
One Project Per Team/Environment

anihpj-dev, anihpj-staging, anihpj-prod — each gets its own AppProject with appropriate restrictions.

🔒
Allow-List, Not Block-List

Specify which repos and destinations ARE allowed. Don't try to list everything that's blocked — you'll miss something.

🚫
Blacklist Dangerous Resources in Prod

ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, NetworkPolicy — block these from ever being deployed by an Application.

👥
Least Privilege Roles

Most users only need get + sync. Admin-level * access should be rare and audited.

Q4
What are the built-in Argo CD RBAC roles?
Show Answer
Answer

role:readonly (view only), role:admin (create/update/delete apps within assigned projects). Custom roles can be defined in argocd-cm.

Explanation

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) in Kubernetes has 4 components: Role/ClusterRole (defines permissions — 'CAN get pods'), RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding (assigns role to users/groups — 'Alice GETS pod-reader role'), Subject (User, Group, or ServiceAccount), and Verbs (get, list, create, update, delete, watch). Argo uses ServiceAccounts: the Application Controller, Repo Server, and API Server each have ServiceAccounts with specific permissions. On CAPA, you need to know which ServiceAccount needs which permissions.

🔍 RBAC CHAIN
Subject ──▶ Role ──▶ RoleBinding
(User/SA)   (verbs)  (assignment)
'Alice CAN get pods in namespace anihpj'

Q7
Where is Argo CD RBAC policy configured?
Show Answer
Answer

In the argocd-rbac-cm ConfigMap. Format: p, <role>, <resource>, <action>, <object>. Example: p, admin, applications, sync, */*.

Explanation

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) in Kubernetes has 4 components: Role/ClusterRole (defines permissions — 'CAN get pods'), RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding (assigns role to users/groups — 'Alice GETS pod-reader role'), Subject (User, Group, or ServiceAccount), and Verbs (get, list, create, update, delete, watch). Argo uses ServiceAccounts: the Application Controller, Repo Server, and API Server each have ServiceAccounts with specific permissions. On CAPA, you need to know which ServiceAccount needs which permissions.

🔍 RBAC CHAIN
Subject ──▶ Role ──▶ RoleBinding
(User/SA)   (verbs)  (assignment)
'Alice CAN get pods in namespace anihpj'

Go beyond basic Applications. Learn ApplicationSets for scale, notifications for visibility, and resource hooks for safe database migrations.

6.1 ApplicationSets — Scale Your Deployments

ApplicationSet Generators

🔧 Generators
📋
List

Fixed list: [dev, staging, prod]

🌐
Cluster

One app per managed cluster

📂
Git

One app per folder/branch

🔀
Matrix

Combine 2 generators

🔗
Merge

Merge multiple generators

🔀
Pull Request

Preview env per PR

List Generator: Fixed list of values: [dev, staging, prod]. Generates one Application per item. Simplest generator — perfect for environment-based deployments.

Cluster Generator: One Application per cluster that Argo CD manages. Fleet management — deploy to every cluster automatically.

Git Generator: One Application per folder or file in a Git repo. Monorepo pattern — add a folder, Application auto-generated.

Matrix Generator: Cartesian product of TWO generators. Example: env × region = [dev-us, dev-eu, staging-us, staging-eu, prod-us, prod-eu].

Merge Generator: Combine multiple generators where one provides base params and another provides overrides.

Pull Request Generator: Auto-creates ephemeral preview environments for GitHub/GitLab PRs. Auto-cleanup when PR is closed. Great for testing features before merge!

SCM Provider Generator: Scans GitHub/GitLab org and creates one Application per repository. Platform engineering pattern — every repo gets auto-deployed.

🧠 Deep Dive: Why ApplicationSets Matter

Without ApplicationSets, you'd need to manually create one Application YAML per environment × per cluster. With 3 environments and 4 clusters, that's 12 separate YAML files — each nearly identical but with different namespace and path values. ApplicationSets solve this with templating: write ONE template, let the generator produce all 12 Applications automatically.

The real power comes when you add a new cluster or environment — instead of writing new YAML, the ApplicationSet detects the change and auto-generates the new Application. This is GitOps at scale: your ApplicationSet YAML in Git describes the pattern, and Argo CD materializes it into real Applications.

💡 CAPA Insight — Which Generator to Use?
  • List Generator: Use when you have a KNOWN, FIXED set (dev, staging, prod). Simplest, most predictable.
  • Cluster Generator: Use for FLEET management — automatically deploy to every cluster Argo CD manages. New cluster = auto-deployed.
  • Git Generator: Use with MONOREPOS — each team folder auto-generates its own Application. Add a folder → Argo CD auto-discovers it.
  • Matrix Generator: Use when you need CARTESIAN combinations — e.g., every environment in every region.
  • Pull Request Generator: Use for EPHEMERAL PREVIEW environments — test a PR in a live K8s namespace before merging.

6.2 Progressive Sync — Staged Rollouts

Progressive Sync is Argo CD's way of deploying applications through a pipeline of environments — dev → staging → prod — with automatic promotion when each stage succeeds. Unlike traditional CI/CD where promotion is handled by external scripts, Argo CD keeps it Git-native.

PROGRESSIVE SYNC
┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────┐
│   DEV    │────▶│   STAGING    │────▶│   PROD   │
│  🟢 Auto │     │   🟡 Auto    │     │  🔴 Manual│
│  on push│     │ after tests  │     │ approve  │
└──────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────┘
     │                  │                   │
  Immediate        10 min delay        Canary 10→100%
🧠 How Progressive Sync Actually Works

Progressive sync is implemented through ApplicationSets with rolling sync or sequential sync waves. Here's the mechanism:

Step 1 — Dev Auto-Deploy: Git push to the dev branch → Argo CD detects change → auto-syncs dev Application → dev environment updated immediately. No approval needed — dev is for experimentation.

Step 2 — Staging Promotion: When dev is Healthy + Synced, the CI pipeline (Argo Workflows) automatically merges the dev branch into staging. Argo CD detects the staging branch change → auto-syncs staging. Optional: wait 10 minutes for automated tests to pass.

Step 3 — Production Gate: When staging is verified, a PR is created from staging to main. A SENIOR ENGINEER must approve. This PR approval is the production gate. After merge, Argo CD detects the main branch change. Production sync may require manual approval (sync window, manual sync policy).

Key insight: The promotion mechanism IS Git. There's no separate "promotion tool." Merging branches = promoting. This means every promotion has a Git audit trail — who approved, when, and what changed.

6.3 Notifications — Stay Informed

📦Sync Succeeds
→
💬Slack#deployments
→
📧Email
→
🔗Webhook

Supported services: Slack, Email, Teams, Discord, Telegram, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Grafana, Pushover, Webhook. Configured via argocd-notifications-cm ConfigMap.

🧠 Deep Dive: How Argo CD Notifications Work

Notifications are powered by the argocd-notifications controller, which watches Application events and matches them against configured triggers. Each notification has three parts: (1) Trigger — WHEN to send (on-sync-succeeded, on-health-degraded, etc.). (2) Template — WHAT to say (subject, body, formatting). (3) Service — WHERE to send (Slack webhook, email SMTP, Teams, etc.).

Triggers use Go templates to access Application metadata: {{.app.metadata.name}} for app name, {{.app.status.sync.status}} for sync status, {{.app.status.health.status}} for health status. You can build rich messages like: "App {{.app.metadata.name}} sync {{.app.status.sync.status}} at {{.app.status.operationState.finishedAt}}."

6.4 Resource Hooks — Safe Operations

Resource hooks let you run operations BEFORE, DURING, and AFTER a sync. Unlike sync waves (which control ORDER of resource creation), hooks control ACTIONS at specific lifecycle points. Hooks can be any K8s resource — Job, Pod, Workflow — annotated with argocd.argoproj.io/hook.

🔧
PreSync
DB backup
📦
Sync
Deploy app
✅
PostSync
Smoke tests
❌
SyncFail
Cleanup
🧠 Deep Dive: Hooks vs Sync Waves — Don't Confuse Them!

This is a common CAPA confusion point. Sync Waves (annotation: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave) control the ORDER in which resources are applied — lower numbers go first. Waves run within the Sync phase. Hooks (annotation: argocd.argoproj.io/hook) run at specific LIFECYCLE POINTS — before sync, after sync, or on sync failure.

Example: A PreSync Job runs a database backup BEFORE any manifests are applied. A sync-wave-1 ConfigMap is applied during Sync, but before sync-wave-2 Deployment. Both can coexist — a ConfigMap could be wave -1 AND have a PreSync hook annotation.

Hook deletion policies: BeforeHookCreation (delete old hook before running new one — default), HookSucceeded (delete after success), HookFailed (delete after failure). For anihpj DB migrations: use PreSync hook with HookSucceeded policy — the migration Job is cleaned up automatically after it succeeds.

6.5 Orphaned Resources — Safe Cleanup

When you delete a YAML file from Git, Argo CD can either prune (delete) the orphaned resource or warn you.

⚠️ The Prune Danger

If prune: true and you delete a file from Git, Argo CD WILL delete that resource from your cluster. For databases, PVCs, and critical infrastructure, this is catastrophic. In production, use orphanedResources.warn: true to get warnings without auto-deletion, or PruneLast=true to delete old resources AFTER creating new ones (zero-downtime).

6.6 Sync Windows — Time-Based Access Control

Sync Windows let you define time periods where syncs are ALLOWED or DENIED. Configured in the AppProject, they prevent deployments during production freeze, business hours, or holidays.

SYNC WINDOWS
AppProject syncWindows:
- kind: deny              # BLOCK syncs
  schedule: '0 9 * * 1-5' # Mon-Fri 9 AM
  duration: 8h            # 8 hours
  applications: ['*-prod']# Only prod apps
  manualSync: false       # No override

- kind: allow             # ALLOW syncs
  schedule: '0 22 * * *'  # Daily 10 PM
  duration: 2h            # 2 hour window
  manualSync: true        # Can override manually

RULES: No windows=all allowed | Active ALLOW=only window |
Active DENY=all blocked | ALLOW+DENY=DENY wins
CLI: argocd proj windows list/add/update/delete PROJECT

Chapter 7: anihpj — Complete GitOps Setup

Now we put everything together. This chapter walks through the complete GitOps repository structure for anihpj, from Kustomize layouts to Argo CD Applications and secrets management.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🛠️ Hands-On

7.1 GitOps Repository Structure

anihpj-k8s Repo Structure
anihpj-k8s/
├── base/                    # Common manifests (DRY)
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   ├── configmap.yaml
│   └── kustomization.yaml
├── overlays/                # Environment variations
│   ├── dev/                 # 1 replica, dev config
│   ├── staging/             # 2 replicas, staging config
│   └── prod/                # 5 replicas, prod config, resource limits
└── argo-apps/               # Argo CD Application definitions
    ├── anihpj-dev.yaml
    ├── anihpj-staging.yaml
    ├── anihpj-prod.yaml
    └── app-of-apps.yaml     # Bootstrap!

7.2 Kustomize vs Helm for anihpj

Both Kustomize and Helm solve the same problem — managing multiple environment configurations — but with fundamentally different philosophies. Understanding when to use each is critical for both the CAPA exam and real-world GitOps.

FeatureKustomize ✅Helm
Learning CurveEasy (YAML patching)Moderate (Go templates)
Built-in to kubectlYes (-k flag)Needs Helm CLI
Environment MgmtBase + Overlaysvalues.yaml per env
Sharing/PackagingNot designed for itChart repos, Artifact Hub
GitOps FriendlinessPure YAML, easy diffTemplates harder to read
ParameterizationLimited (patch-based)Full Go templating
🧠 The Philosophical Difference

Kustomize takes a BASE set of YAML files and applies OVERLAYS (patches) to customize them per environment. The base + patches are ALL plain YAML — no templating language. This makes Kustomize ideal for GitOps because you can see exactly what changes at a glance: git diff shows real YAML changes.

Helm uses Go templates with {{.Values.image}} placeholders that get filled in at render time. The templates themselves aren't valid YAML — you need Helm to render them first. This makes Git diffs harder to read (you see template changes, not final YAML changes). However, Helm excels at packaging and distribution — if you're sharing an app with the community, Helm charts on Artifact Hub are the standard.

CAPA Recommendation: For GitOps with Argo CD, Kustomize is preferred because Argo CD can natively render it and show diffs in pure YAML. For the exam, know BOTH — Helm is still widely used, and Argo CD supports it as a first-class source type.

7.3 Argo CD Applications for anihpj

Create three Application YAMLs in argo-apps/, one per environment:

FileSource PathDestination NSSync Policy
anihpj-dev.yamloverlays/devanihpj-devAuto + Prune + SelfHeal
anihpj-staging.yamloverlays/staginganihpj-stagingAuto + Prune + SelfHeal
anihpj-prod.yamloverlays/prodanihpj-prodManual + Warn (no auto-prune)

Generate Application YAMLs fast: argocd app create anihpj-dev --repo <URL> --path overlays/dev --dest-server https://kubernetes.default.svc --dest-namespace anihpj-dev --sync-policy automated --auto-prune --dry-run -o yaml > anihpj-dev.yaml

7.4 The App-of-Apps Pattern

✅ BOOTSTRAP YOUR ENTIRE CLUSTER WITH ONE COMMAND
  • Root Application: Points to argo-apps/ folder
  • Effect: Argo CD sees 4 Application YAMLs in that folder
  • Result: All 4 Applications are created, which deploy anihpj to all environments
  • Disaster Recovery: kubectl apply -f app-of-apps.yaml on a fresh cluster — everything is back!

7.5 Secrets Management in GitOps

❌ NEVER: Plaintext Secrets in Git

db-password: supersecret123 committed to Git = security incident. Everyone with repo access can read it. Git history is forever.

✅ USE: Sealed Secrets

Encrypt secrets with a cluster-specific key. Safe to commit. Only your cluster can decrypt. kubeseal < secret.yaml > sealed-secret.yaml

Option A: Sealed Secrets (Recommended for anihpj)

Encrypt secrets with a cluster-specific key. Safe to commit to Git. Only your cluster can decrypt. Simple setup: kubeseal < secret.yaml > sealed-secret.yaml. The Sealed Secrets controller in your cluster automatically decrypts and creates the actual K8s Secret.

Option B: External Secrets Operator (ESO)

Syncs secrets from external providers (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault) into Kubernetes Secrets. Git stores an ExternalSecret CRD that references the external secret — no actual secret data in Git. Best for cloud-native environments.

Option C: HashiCorp Vault (Enterprise)

Most secure option. Argo CD uses a Vault plugin to inject secrets at sync time. Secrets never touch Git or Kubernetes Secrets — they're injected directly into pods. Requires Vault infrastructure and plugin configuration. Overkill for anihpj but standard in financial/healthcare sectors.

Q2
Why use Kustomize over plain Directory for multi-environment deployments?
Show Answer
Answer

Kustomize eliminates YAML duplication. Base has common config; overlays only contain differences. Change the base once → all environments inherit it.

What is the App-of-Apps pattern?
Show Answer
Answer

A single "parent" Application whose Git path contains child Application YAMLs. Syncing the parent → syncs ALL children. One kubectl apply deploys the entire platform.

What is Sealed Secrets and why use it for anihpj?
Show Answer
Answer

Encrypts K8s Secrets with a cluster-specific key. Safe to commit to Git — only your cluster can decrypt. Simple: kubeseal < secret.yaml > sealed-secret.yaml.

Safe to commit to Git — only your cluster can decrypt. Simple: kubeseal < secret.yaml > sealed-secret.yaml. Chapter 8: Argo CD CLI & UI Mastery

Master the command-line interface and web UI that you'll use daily as an Argo CD operator. The CLI is especially critical for the CAPA exam — speed matters.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours⚡ Speed Critical

8.1 CLI Commands — Essential Reference

CommandWhat It Does
argocd login <server>Authenticate CLI to Argo CD server
argocd app listList all Applications and their status
argocd app get <name>Detailed view of one Application
argocd app sync <name>Trigger manual sync (exam most-used!)
argocd app diff <name>Preview what would change BEFORE syncing
argocd app history <name>Show deployment history (for rollback)
argocd app rollback <name> <ID>Rollback to a previous deployment
argocd proj listList all AppProjects
argocd repo listList registered Git repositories
🧠 Deep Dive: CLI Design Philosophy

The Argo CD CLI follows a consistent pattern: argocd <resource> <action> [flags]. Resources are: app, proj, repo, cluster, account, cert. Actions are: list, get, create, delete, sync, diff. Once you learn this pattern, you can guess commands for resources you haven't used before — it's the same design as kubectl and git.

The CLI communicates with the Argo CD API server via gRPC (not REST!), which is faster and supports streaming. This is why argocd app sync shows real-time progress — it's streaming gRPC responses. The --grpc-web flag is needed when the client is behind a proxy that doesn't support HTTP/2 (required for gRPC).

8.2 Web UI Walkthrough

The Argo CD Web UI provides a visual overview of all Applications. Access via kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443 then open https://localhost:8080.

📊
Dashboard

All Applications with sync/health status. Color-coded: green=healthy, yellow=progressing, red=degraded.

🌳
Tree View

Hierarchical view of all K8s resources in an Application. Click any node for details and logs.

🔗
Network Graph

Visualizes Service→Pod connections. See traffic flow and identify misconfigurations.

📜
Logs

Stream pod logs directly in the UI. Filter by container. No kubectl needed.

🧠 UI vs CLI — When to Use Each

UI is best for: Visualizing complex Application dependencies (Tree View), seeing overall cluster health at a glance (Dashboard), explaining deployments to non-CLI users, and exploring unfamiliar Applications. CLI is best for: Automation (scripts, CI/CD), speed (typing is faster than clicking), troubleshooting (grep through logs), and the CAPA exam (CLI fluency is tested). In production, operators typically use the UI for monitoring and the CLI for operations — both are essential skills.

8.3 Debugging Sync Failures

  • Error: "repo not found" → Check repoURL is correct and accessible from cluster
  • Error: "path does not exist" → Verify the path exists on the specified targetRevision
  • Error: "permission denied" → Check AppProject sourceRepos and destinations
  • Sync stuck at "Unknown" → Check controller logs: kubectl logs -n argocd deploy/argocd-application-controller

8.4 Multi-Cluster Management

One Argo CD instance can manage multiple Kubernetes clusters. Add external clusters with argocd cluster add <context-name>. Applications can then target any registered cluster via destination.server.

8.5 Diff Strategies — How Argo CD Detects Changes

Argo CD uses diff strategies to determine OutOfSync status. Understanding which strategy is active helps debug unexpected sync behavior.

StrategyHow It WorksWhen Used
Legacy (3-way)Compares live state, desired state, and last-applied-configuration annotationDefault
Server-Side DiffSends dry-run SSA to API server; Admission Controllers participate in diffEnable via controller.diff.server.side: true or per-app annotation ServerSideDiff=true

8.6 Tracking Strategies — Branch, Tag, or Commit

🌿
Branch

targetRevision: main — follows HEAD. Best for dev/staging with auto-sync.

🏷️
Tag

targetRevision: v2.1 — pinned to tag. Immutable, predictable. Best for production.

📌
Commit

targetRevision: abc123 — exact SHA. Maximum control for forensics.

CAPA Rule: Dev→branch, Staging→branch or tag, Production→tag or commit. Never use :latest for images.
