⏱️ Hands-On — 12 minutes
Scenario: Create an Argo CD Application from Scratch

Your team needs to deploy anihpj to a new production namespace. Complete these tasks:

  1. Create an AppProject named anihpj-prod that only allows the repo github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s and namespace anihpj-prod
  2. Create an Application that deploys from overlays/prod with auto-sync, pruning, and self-healing enabled
  3. What command shows the diff between Git and the cluster BEFORE syncing?
  4. After deploying, you notice a pod keeps crashing. The sync status shows "Healthy" but the health status shows "Degraded". Why?
📝 Click to reveal answers
# 1. AppProject:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  sourceRepos:
    - https://github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s
  destinations:
    - namespace: anihpj-prod
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc

# 2. Application:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: anihpj-prod
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

# 3. argocd app diff anihpj-prod — shows changes before sync!

# 4. "Synced" means the YAML was applied successfully.
#    "Degraded" means the running pods are unhealthy.
#    Check: kubectl logs <pod> -n anihpj-prod
#    Common cause: wrong image tag, missing ConfigMap, DB unreachable

🔄 Part 3: Argo Workflows Chapters 9-13

Chapter 9: Introduction to Argo Workflows

Argo Workflows is a container-native workflow engine on Kubernetes. Each step runs in its own container — it's like Docker Compose meets a DAG scheduler, all managed as a Kubernetes CRD. This chapter gets you from zero to your first running workflow.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🎯 CAPA 36%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand what Argo Workflows is and how it extends Kubernetes
  • ✅ Compare Kubernetes Jobs vs. Argo Workflows — when to use which
  • ✅ Grasp the architecture: Controller, Executor, Server
  • ✅ Install Argo Workflows on your cluster step by step
  • ✅ Run your first "Hello World" workflow from YAML to completion
📝
Workflow CRD

Orchestrates multiple pods as DAG/Steps

🏃
Entrypoint

Starting template — the "main" function

📦
Per-Step Pod

Each step = one K8s pod with its own container

🔄
@latest

Refers to most recent workflow — time saver!

🎓 CAPA Relevance — 36% of the Exam!

Argo Workflows is the largest CAPA domain at 36%. You must understand: Workflow fundamentals, generating/consuming artifacts, Workflow Templates, the Workflow Spec, DAG execution, and running data processing jobs. This chapter builds the foundation for all of it.

9.1 What is Argo Workflows?

Argo Workflows is an open-source container-native workflow engine for orchestrating parallel jobs on Kubernetes. Think of it as:

🐳

Container-Native

Each step IS a container. No VMs. No Jenkins plugins. Just Docker images orchestrated as a graph.

📊

DAG + Steps

Define complex pipelines as Directed Acyclic Graphs with dependencies, parallelism, and conditionals.

☸️

Kubernetes CRD

Workflow is a Kubernetes custom resource. kubectl get workflows — just like pods or deployments.

🧠 Beginner's Mental Model — "Cooking with Recipes"

Imagine you're cooking a complex meal. You have a recipe (Workflow YAML) that lists all the steps: chop vegetables → boil water → cook pasta (in parallel with) → make sauce → combine. Some steps MUST happen in order (boil water before cooking pasta), some can happen at the same time (make sauce while pasta cooks). Each step uses specific tools (container images like python:3.12 or docker:latest). Argo is the master chef that reads your recipe, starts each step at the right time, checks if each step succeeded, and cleans up when done. The kitchen is your Kubernetes cluster — and each cooking station is a Pod.

What Does a Workflow Look Like?
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ARGO WORKFLOW — A DAG of Containers                       │
│                                                            │
│              ┌───────────┐                                 │
│              │  Step A   │  Container: python:3.12        │
│              │ Run Tests │  Command: pytest jobpost/tests/ │
│              └─────┬─────┘                                 │
│                    │                                        │
│       ┌────────────┼────────────┐                          │
│       ▼            ▼            ▼                          │
│  ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐                      │
│  │ Step B  │ │ Step C  │ │ Step D  │  ALL run in parallel │
│  │ Lint    │ │ SAST    │ │ Build   │  (no deps between    │
│  │ Checks  │ │ Scan    │ │ CSS     │   them)              │
│  └────┬────┘ └────┬────┘ └────┬────┘                      │
│       └────────────┼────────────┘                          │
│                    ▼                                        │
│              ┌───────────┐                                 │
│              │  Step E   │  Container: docker:latest       │
│              │ Build     │  Build & push Docker image      │
│              │ & Push    │                                  │
│              └───────────┘                                 │
│                                                            │
│  Each box = its own Pod (its own container, logs, env)     │
│  Arrows = dependencies (Step E waits for B,C,D)           │
│  ENTRYPOINT = "Start here" — like main() in a program      │
│  TEMPLATES = The recipe steps — each defines a container   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Key Insight — "It's Just Containers"

There are NO special Argo binaries running your code. Each step runs a regular Docker container — the same containers you'd run with docker run. Argo simply manages the when, where, what order, and what to do if something fails. This means ANY tool that runs in a container can be a workflow step: curl, python, go, terraform, ansible, kubectl, helm — anything!

Use cases for Argo Workflows:

🔧CI/CD Pipelines: Clone → Test → Build → Push → Deploy (we'll build this for anihpj!)
📊Data Processing: Extract → Transform → Load (ETL) pipelines with artifact passing
🤖ML Pipelines: Train model → Evaluate → Deploy (each step a different container image)
🏗️Infra Automation: Provision → Configure → Validate — all as code, all on K8s

9.2 Why Not Just Use Kubernetes Jobs?

Kubernetes has a native Job resource — why do we need Argo Workflows? Because Jobs are linear, and real-world pipelines are graphs.

Kubernetes Job vs Argo Workflow — Visual Comparison
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  KUBERNETES JOB                    │  ARGO WORKFLOW               │
│  ─────────────                     │  ─────────────               │
│                                    │                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐           │       ┌──────────┐          │
│  │  Pod (1 container)  │           │       │  Clone   │          │
│  │  Runs ONCE           │           │       └────┬─────┘          │
│  │  Linear, no branches │           │            │                │
│  │  No DAG              │           │   ┌────────┼────────┐       │
│  │  No artifact passing │           │   ▼        ▼        ▼       │
│  │  Basic retry only    │           │ ┌────┐  ┌────┐  ┌────┐     │
│  └─────────────────────┘           │ │Test│  │Lint│  │Bld │     │
│                                    │ └──┬─┘  └──┬─┘  └──┬─┘     │
│  Good for:                         │   └───────┼───────┘          │
│  • Simple run-to-completion tasks  │           ▼                  │
│  • One-off batch processing        │       ┌──────┐              │
│  • Cron-triggered single tasks     │       │ Push │              │
│                                    │       └──────┘              │
│  anihpj example:                   │                              │
│  "Run python manage.py migrate"    │  anihpj example:             │
│  → Just a single Job               │  Clone → Test+Lint+Build    │
│                                    │  → Push → Update GitOps     │
│                                    │  → Full CI pipeline!        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
FeatureKubernetes JobArgo Workflow
StructureLinear (1 task)DAG / Steps / Graph
ParallelismFixed completionsDynamic fan-out/fan-in
Dependencies❌ None✅ depends: [...]
Conditionals❌ No✅ when: <expr>
Loops❌ No✅ withItems / withSequence / withParam
Artifact Passing❌ No✅ S3 / GCS / MinIO / Azure Blob
Retry StrategyBasic backoff✅ Exponential + custom policies
SchedulingCronJobCronWorkflow (richer)
Built-in UI❌ None✅ DAG visualizer & logs viewer
Use CaseSimple run-to-completionComplex pipelines (CI/CD, ML, ETL)
📌 Decision Rule

If you ask yourself "could this be more than one task?" → use Argo Workflows. If it's truly a single, linear operation → a K8s Job is fine. For the CAPA exam, expect to work with Workflows — that's the whole point of the certification!

9.3 Argo Workflows Architecture

Understanding the components helps you debug when things go wrong:

1
Workflow Controller — The brain. Watches for Workflow CRDs and orchestrates execution. Runs as a Deployment in the argo namespace.
2
Executor — Runs each step as its own Pod. The executor is a sidecar container injected into every workflow step pod. It reports status back to the controller.
3
Argo Server — REST API + Web UI. Serves the DAG visualizer at localhost:2746. Also handles archiving completed workflows.
4
Persistence (Postgres/MySQL) — Stores workflow state, logs, and archived records. The quick-start uses an in-cluster Postgres pod; production uses an external database.
Argo Workflows Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     ARGO WORKFLOWS ARCHITECTURE               │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────┐      watches       ┌────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Workflow    │◀──────────────────│ Workflow           │ │
│  │  Controller  │                    │ Controller          │ │
│  │  (Deployment) │                   │ (in argo ns)       │ │
│  └──────┬───────┘                    └────────┬───────────┘ │
│         │ creates                              │              │
│         ▼                                      │ reports      │
│  ┌──────────────┐                              ▼              │
│  │ Step Pod     │                    ┌────────────────────┐ │
│  │ ┌──────────┐ │                    │  Postgres / MySQL  │ │
│  │ │Container │ │                    │  (state + archive) │ │
│  │ │(your img)│ │                    └────────────────────┘ │
│  │ ├──────────┤ │                                           │
│  │ │Executor  │ │────── reports ──────▶ Controller          │
│  │ │(sidecar) │ │                                           │
│  │ └──────────┘ │    ┌────────────────────┐                 │
│  └──────────────┘    │  Argo Server       │                 │
│                      │  (API + UI :2746)  │                 │
│                      └────────────────────┘                 │
│                                                              │
│  1. You submit a Workflow YAML → Controller picks it up      │
│  2. Controller creates Pods for each step → each gets an     │
│     executor sidecar                                         │
│  3. Executor reports: Running → Succeeded/Failed → Controller │
│  4. Controller updates Workflow status → you see it via CLI  │
│  5. Workflow state stored in Postgres for archiving          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🤔 Decision Guide — Events vs CronWorkflow vs Direct Submit

A common beginner question: "I need something to happen automatically — should I use Argo Events, CronWorkflow, or just submit a workflow directly?"

ScenarioBest ToolWhy
"Run every night at 2 AM"CronWorkflowOne YAML, no Events infra needed
"Run when someone pushes to GitHub"Argo EventsExternal trigger — needs EventSource + Sensor
"Run when a file appears in S3"Argo EventsExternal trigger — S3 EventSource
"Run when a K8s resource changes"Argo EventsResource EventSource watches cluster
"Run this workflow once, right now"argo submitDirect — no scheduling needed
"Run every Monday AND on git push"Both!Calendar + GitHub EventSources → one Sensor
💡 "Events is Glue"

Argo Events doesn't replace CronWorkflows or direct submission — it complements them. Use CronWorkflow for simple schedules, argo submit for one-offs, and Argo Events when you need to react to external triggers. Events is the "when X happens → do Y" layer between the outside world and your workflows.

9.4 Installing Argo Workflows

1
Create namespace: kubectl create namespace argo
2
Apply install manifest: kubectl apply -n argo -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-workflows/stable/manifests/quick-start-minimal.yaml
3
Wait for pods: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n argo --timeout=300s
4
Install CLI: Download argo binary and put in /usr/local/bin
5
Access UI: kubectl -n argo port-forward svc/argo-server 2746:2746 → open https://localhost:2746
Terminal — Full Installation
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace argo

# Step 2: Install Argo Workflows (quick-start, minimal)
kubectl apply -n argo -f \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-workflows/stable/manifests/quick-start-minimal.yaml

# Step 3: Wait for all pods to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n argo --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -n argo
# Expected:
# NAME                                  READY  STATUS
# argo-server-...                       1/1    Running
# workflow-controller-...               1/1    Running
# postgres-...                          1/1    Running

# Step 4: Install Argo CLI
curl -sLO https://github.com/argoproj/argo-workflows/releases/latest/download/argo-linux-amd64.gz
gunzip argo-linux-amd64.gz
chmod +x argo-linux-amd64
sudo mv argo-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/argo

# Step 5: Access the Web UI
kubectl -n argo port-forward svc/argo-server 2746:2746
# Open https://localhost:2746
# Get auth token: argo auth token

# Step 6: Verify installation
argo version
# Expected: argo: v3.x.x  +  Workflow Controller: v3.x.x
💡 Artifact Repository Note

The quick-start manifest includes a built-in MinIO for artifact storage. For production, configure an external S3/GCS/Azure Blob by editing the workflow-controller-configmap in the argo namespace.

⚠️ Namespace Confusion Alert!

Argo Workflows uses namespace argo. Argo CD uses argocd. They are DIFFERENT tools in DIFFERENT namespaces. On the CAPA exam, always double-check you're targeting the right namespace: kubectl get pods -n argo for Workflows, kubectl get pods -n argocd for CD.

9.5 Your First Workflow — Hello anihpj!

Let's run a simple workflow that echoes a message. This is the "Hello World" of Argo Workflows — every concept builds from here.

hello-world.yaml — Your First Workflow
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Workflow
metadata:
  generateName: hello-anihpj-
  namespace: argo
spec:
  entrypoint: hello                  # Where to start
  templates:
  - name: hello                      # Template name = entrypoint
    container:
      image: alpine:latest
      command: [echo]
      args: ["Hello from anihpj jobpost! Argo Workflows is running! 🚀"]
Submit & Monitor
# Submit the workflow
argo submit hello-world.yaml -n argo
# Output: Name:                hello-anihpj-abc12
#         Namespace:           argo
#         Status:              Pending

# Watch it run in real-time
argo watch @latest -n argo
# Shows live status updates as the pod
# goes: Pending → Running → Succeeded

# Get the result
argo get @latest -n argo
# Shows: Status: Succeeded ✅

# View logs
argo logs @latest -n argo
# Output: Hello from anihpj jobpost!
#         Argo Workflows is running! 🚀
What Just Happened?
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. You submitted Workflow YAML   │
│           │                       │
│           ▼                       │
│  2. Controller detected new WF    │
│           │                       │
│           ▼                       │
│  3. Controller created a Pod:     │
│     ┌──────────────────┐         │
│     │ alpine:latest     │         │
│     │ echo "Hello..."   │         │
│     │ + executor sidecar│         │
│     └──────────────────┘         │
│           │                       │
│           ▼                       │
│  4. Container ran → exit 0        │
│           │                       │
│           ▼                       │
│  5. Executor reported: Succeeded  │
│           │                       │
│           ▼                       │
│  6. Workflow status = Succeeded ✅│
│     Pod cleaned up (unless        │
│     you set ttlStrategy)          │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
🎯 CAPA Exam Pattern: @latest

In the exam, use @latest to refer to the most recently submitted workflow. Saves you from copying the generated name (like hello-anihpj-abc12). Commands: argo logs @latest, argo get @latest, argo watch @latest.

💡 Key Takeaway

Every workflow has: (1) an entrypoint that says where to start, (2) templates that define what each step does, and (3) each template runs in its own container. This same pattern scales to 100-step DAGs!

⚠️ Common Beginner Gotchas — Read Before Your First Workflow!
  • Namespace matters: Workflows run in the argo namespace (NOT argocd!). Always add -n argo to your CLI commands. If your workflow is stuck "Pending" with no pods, you probably submitted to the wrong namespace.
  • generateName vs name: Use generateName: (not name:) in your Workflow YAML. generateName appends a random suffix so each run is unique. If you use name:, the second submission will fail with "already exists".
  • entrypoint must match a template: The spec.entrypoint value MUST exactly match a template's name field. "hello" ≠ "Hello" — template names are case-sensitive!
  • Pods disappear after completion: Unless you set ttlStrategy, completed workflow pods are cleaned up. If you need to debug, add ttlStrategy: {secondsAfterCompletion: 3600} to keep pods for 1 hour after finishing.
  • @latest only works for YOUR latest: @latest refers to the most recent workflow submitted from YOUR CLI session in the current namespace. It doesn't work across namespaces or users.
Workflow Lifecycle — The 6 States Every Workflow Goes Through
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WORKFLOW LIFECYCLE STATES                                 │
│                                                            │
│  ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐                │
│  │ Pending │───▶│ Running │───▶│Succeeded│ ✅ Done!       │
│  └─────────┘    └────┬────┘    └─────────┘                │
│                      │                                     │
│                      ├──────▶ ┌─────────┐                 │
│                      │        │  Failed  │ ❌ Error        │
│                      │        └─────────┘                 │
│                      │                                     │
│                      ├──────▶ ┌─────────┐                 │
│                      │        │  Error   │ ⚠️ System error │
│                      │        └─────────┘                 │
│                      │                                     │
│                      └──────▶ ┌──────────┐                │
│                               │Terminated │ 🛑 Killed     │
│                               └──────────┘                │
│                                                            │
│  Check status: argo get <workflow> -n argo               │
│  Phase column shows: Pending | Running | Succeeded |      │
│                      Failed | Error | Terminated           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How do you access the Argo Workflows UI?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl -n argo port-forward svc/argo-server 2746:2746 → open https://localhost:2746. Get auth token: argo auth token.

Explanation

The Argo CD API server serves on port 443 (HTTPS), not 80. The port-forward command is: kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443. Then access via https://localhost:8080. You'll get a certificate warning (it's self-signed) — accept it. For production, configure an Ingress or LoadBalancer Service with a proper TLS certificate. CAPA tip: The exam may require port-forward to access the UI — know the exact command and that the source port (8080) comes first, destination (443) second.

Chapter 10: Workflow Templates & Composition

Templates are the reusable building blocks of Argo Workflows. This chapter covers all 6 template types — Container, Script, Resource, DAG, Steps, and Suspend — plus WorkflowTemplates for sharing and reusing workflow definitions across your organization.

  • ✅ Differentiate Workflow vs WorkflowTemplate vs ClusterWorkflowTemplate

  • ✅ Build complex DAG pipelines with dependencies and parallelism

  • ✅ Pass artifacts (files, JSON, Docker images) between steps
TEMPLATE TYPES — DECISION TREE
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Which template type should I use?                       │
│                                                         │
│  Need to run a container? → Container / Script          │
│  Need inline code?       → Script (Argo wraps it)       │
│  Need to manage K8s CRs? → Resource                     │
│  Need complex pipeline?  → DAG (if many deps)           │
│                          → Steps (if linear with fanout)│
│  Need manual approval?   → Suspend                      │
│  Need to call REST API?  → HTTP                         │
│  Need cross-team reuse?  → templateRef                  │
│                                                         │
│  CAPA Focus: DAG vs Steps distinction is KEY             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

10.1 WorkflowTemplate vs Workflow

Think of it like a class vs an instance in programming:

ConceptCRD KindPurposeReusabilityScope
WorkflowWorkflowOne-time execution❌ Single useNamespace
WorkflowTemplateWorkflowTemplateReusable blueprint✅ Submit many timesNamespace
ClusterWorkflowTemplateClusterWorkflowTemplateReusable blueprint✅ Submit many timesCluster-wide!
Workflow vs WorkflowTemplate — The Relationship
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WorkflowTemplate (BLUEPRINT)                                │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ kind: WorkflowTemplate                                 │ │
│  │ metadata:                                              │ │
│  │   name: anihpj-ci-pipeline    ← Template name         │ │
│  │ spec:                                                  │ │
│  │   entrypoint: ci                                      │ │
│  │   templates:                                           │ │
│  │     - name: ci         ← Reusable!                    │ │
│  │       dag:                                             │ │
│  │         tasks:                                         │ │
│  │           - name: test                                 │ │
│  │           - name: build                                │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                         │                                    │
│                         │ argo submit --from wftmpl/NAME    │
│                         ▼                                    │
│  Workflow (INSTANCE)           Workflow (INSTANCE)           │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐         │
│  │ kind: Workflow        │  │ kind: Workflow        │        │
│  │ name: anihpj-ci-abc12 │  │ name: anihpj-ci-def34 │        │
│  │ # Uses same templates!│  │ # Uses same templates!│        │
│  │ # Different run!      │  │ # Different run!      │        │
│  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘         │
│                                                              │
│  anihpj USAGE:                                               │
│  • WorkflowTemplate = "anihpj-ci-pipeline" (define once)   │
│  • Workflow = each git push triggers a new run              │
│  • Every run has same steps, different code version         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Submit from WorkflowTemplate
# Create the template
argo template create anihpj-ci-pipeline.yaml -n argo

# List templates
argo template list -n argo

# Submit a workflow from the template
argo submit --from wftmpl/anihpj-ci-pipeline -n argo \
  --parameter image-tag=v2.1

# Submit with different parameters
argo submit --from wftmpl/anihpj-ci-pipeline -n argo \
  --parameter image-tag=v2.2
📌 templateRef vs Inline Templates — When to Use Which

A key CAPA concept: you can reference templates in two ways:

MethodSyntaxWhen to Use
Inlinetemplate: template-nameTemplates defined in the SAME Workflow/WorkflowTemplate. Simplest approach.
templateReftemplateRef:
  name: wftmpl-name
  template: tmpl-name		Templates from ANOTHER WorkflowTemplate. Enables composition and reuse across teams!

Example: Your CI pipeline uses templateRef to call a security scan template maintained by the security team — you don't need to copy their YAML, just reference it:

tasks:
- name: security-scan
  templateRef:
    name: security-scans      # ← Another WorkflowTemplate!
    template: trivy-scan      # ← Specific template within it
  arguments:
    parameters:
    - name: image
      value: "anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.tag}}"

10.2 Template Types Deep Dive

Argo Workflows provides 6 template types, each for a different purpose. You can mix and match them in the same workflow:

Template Type Decision Guide
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WHICH TEMPLATE TYPE SHOULD I USE?                            │
│                                                              │
│  ┌───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │ TEMPLATE TYPE          │ USE WHEN...                    ││
│  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ 🐳 Container           │ Run a container image with     ││
│  │                        │ args (like docker run)         ││
│  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ 📜 Script              │ Run inline code (Python/Bash/  ││
│  │                        │ Node) — source IN the YAML     ││
│  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ ☸️ Resource            │ Create/update/delete K8s       ││
│  │                        │ objects (ConfigMaps, etc.)     ││
│  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ 🔀 DAG                 │ Complex pipelines with         ││
│  │                        │ dependencies & parallelism     ││
│  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ 📋 Steps               │ Sequential + parallel steps    ││
│  │                        │ with fan-out (withItems)       ││
│  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤│
│  │ ⏸️ Suspend             │ Pause for manual approval      ││
│  │                        │ (prod deployment gates!)       ││
│  └───────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🐳 Container Template

Simplest type. Runs a container image with optional command/args. Equivalent to docker run but managed by Argo. Use for: running existing tools (curl, aws-cli, gcloud), build commands, any Docker image.

template:
  name: run-tests
  container:
    image: python:3.12
    command: [pytest]
    args: ["jobpost/tests/", "-v"]
📜 Script Template

Define source code directly in the YAML. Argo wraps it in a container automatically. Use for: quick scripts, data transforms, anything where the logic IS the workflow. Supports Python, Bash, Node.js, etc.

template:
  name: process-data
  script:
    image: python:3.12
    source: |
      import json
      data = {"jobs": 42}
      print(json.dumps(data))
☸️ Resource Template

Execute Kubernetes operations directly — create, update, patch, delete resources. Argo manages the kubectl equivalent. Use for: creating temporary ConfigMaps, spinning up test namespaces, deploying K8s objects as part of a pipeline.

template:
  name: create-config
  resource:
    action: create
    manifest: |
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: ConfigMap
      metadata:
        name: pipeline-status
      data:
        status: running
🔀 DAG Template

Define a Directed Acyclic Graph of tasks with dependencies. Each task is a template reference. Use for: CI/CD pipelines, any workflow where tasks depend on each other. This is the most tested template type on CAPA!

template:
  name: ci-pipeline
  dag:
    tasks:
    - name: test
      templateRef: {name: run-tests, template: pytest}
    - name: build
      dependencies: [test]
      templateRef: {name: build-image, template: docker}
📋 Steps Template

Sequential + parallel execution with fan-out via withItems. Each step is a template reference. Use for: processing items in parallel, ETL pipelines, batch operations.

template:
  name: process-envs
  steps:
  - - name: deploy-dev
      templateRef: {name: deploy, template: deploy}
  - - name: deploy-staging
      templateRef: {name: deploy, template: deploy}
      arguments: {parameters: [{name: env, value: staging}]}
⏸️ Suspend Template

Pauses the workflow until manually resumed. NO container runs — it simply waits. Use for: production deployment gates, manual QA approval, "are you sure?" checkpoints.

template:
  name: approve-deploy
  suspend: {}
# Resume with: argo resume
🔀 DAG vs Steps — When to Use Which (CAPA Critical!)

Both DAG and Steps orchestrate multiple templates, but they work differently. This is a frequently-tested CAPA distinction:

Aspect🔀 DAG📋 Steps
StructureFlat list of tasks with dependenciesNested list: outer=sequential, inner=parallel
ParallelismTasks without dependencies run in parallel automaticallySteps in the SAME inner list run in parallel
DependenciesExplicit: dependencies: [A, B]Implicit: group order IS the dependency
Best ForComplex pipelines, CI/CD, many independent tasksLinear workflows with occasional parallel fan-out
Mental Model"Graph" — tasks float freely; arrows connect them"Checklist" — groups execute top to bottom

Rule of thumb: If you have more than 5 tasks with complex dependency relationships → use DAG. If your workflow is mostly linear with occasional parallel steps → use Steps. For the CAPA exam, DAG is tested more heavily because it covers dependencies, parallelism, and task orchestration in one concept.

10.3 DAG Templates — CI/CD Pipeline for anihpj

DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is the most powerful template type. Tasks run in parallel when they have no dependencies, and sequentially when they do:

DAG Workflow — anihpj CI Pipeline
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DAG: anihpj CI Pipeline                                     │
│                                                              │
│                    ┌──────────┐                              │
│                    │  Clone   │  Step 1: Clone repo          │
│                    │  Repo    │                              │
│                    └────┬─────┘                              │
│                         │                                    │
│            ┌────────────┼────────────┐                       │
│            │            │            │                       │
│            ▼            ▼            ▼                       │
│      ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   Step 2:      │
│      │ Unit     │ │ Lint     │ │ SAST     │   Run in        │
│      │ Tests    │ │ Checks   │ │ Scan     │   PARALLEL!     │
│      └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘                 │
│           │            │            │                        │
│           └────────────┼────────────┘                        │
│                        │                                     │
│                        ▼                                     │
│                 ┌──────────┐         Step 3: Build Docker   │
│                 │ Build    │         image (waits for all   │
│                 │ Docker   │         3 parallel steps)      │
│                 │ Image    │                                 │
│                 └────┬─────┘                                 │
│                      │                                       │
│                      ▼                                       │
│                 ┌──────────┐         Step 4: Push to        │
│                 │ Push to  │         registry               │
│                 │ Registry │                                 │
│                 └────┬─────┘                                 │
│                      │                                       │
│                      ▼                                       │
│                 ┌──────────┐         Step 5: Update         │
│                 │ Update   │         GitOps repo (triggers  │
│                 │ GitOps   │         Argo CD sync!)         │
│                 └──────────┘                                 │
│                                                              │
│  ⏱️ Serial time = Sum of all steps                           │
│  ⏱️ DAG time = Clone + max(Test,Lint,SAST) + Build + ...    │
│    (Parallel steps save ~50% time!)                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
anihpj-ci-dag.yaml — DAG Workflow
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Workflow
metadata:
  generateName: anihpj-ci-
  namespace: argo
spec:
  entrypoint: ci-pipeline
  templates:
  - name: ci-pipeline
    dag:
      tasks:
      - name: clone
        template: git-clone

      - name: unit-tests
        dependencies: [clone]
        template: run-pytest

      - name: lint
        dependencies: [clone]
        template: run-flake8

      - name: sast-scan
        dependencies: [clone]
        template: run-bandit

      - name: build
        dependencies: [unit-tests, lint, sast-scan]
        template: docker-build

      - name: push
        dependencies: [build]
        template: docker-push

      - name: update-gitops
        dependencies: [push]
        template: update-manifest

  - name: git-clone
    container:
      image: alpine/git
      command: [git, clone, https://github.com/me/anihpj.git, /src]

  - name: run-pytest
    container:
      image: python:3.12
      command: [pytest]
      args: [/src/jobpost/tests/, -v]
      workingDir: /src

  - name: run-flake8
    container:
      image: alpine/flake8
      args: [/src]

  - name: run-bandit
    container:
      image: securesystemsengineering/bandit
      args: [-r, /src]

  - name: docker-build
    container:
      image: docker:latest
      command: [docker, build, -t, registry.example.com/anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.tag}}, /src]

  - name: docker-push
    container:
      image: docker:latest
      command: [docker, push, registry.example.com/anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.tag}}]

  - name: update-manifest
    container:
      image: alpine/git
      command: [/bin/sh, -c]
      args: ["cd /gitops && sed -i 's/newTag:.*/newTag: {{workflow.parameters.tag}}/' overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml && git commit -am 'Update to {{workflow.parameters.tag}}' && git push"]
🎯 CAPA DAG Rule

In a DAG: tasks run in parallel by default! The dependencies field is what makes them sequential. If task B has dependencies: [A], B waits for A. If no dependencies, tasks run simultaneously. This is frequently tested on CAPA!

10.4 Steps Templates — Sequential & Parallel

Steps templates use a nested list structure: outer list = sequential, inner list = parallel.

Steps Structure — Sequential vs Parallel
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEPS TEMPLATE — The "Double List" Pattern                  │
│                                                              │
│  steps:                                                      │
│  - - name: step-1a      ← First dash = GROUP 1 (sequential) │
│    - name: step-1b      ← Second dash = parallel within G1  │
│                                                              │
│  - - name: step-2a      ← GROUP 2 (runs AFTER Group 1 done) │
│    - name: step-2b                                          │
│    - name: step-2c      ← step-2a, 2b, 2c run in PARALLEL  │
│                                                              │
│  VISUAL:                                                     │
│  ════ Time ═══════════════════════════════════▶             │
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐                                    │
│  │ Step 1a │ │ Step 1b │   Group 1: runs in PARALLEL        │
│  └─────────┘ └─────────┘                                    │
│        │           │                                         │
│        └─────┬─────┘                                         │
│              ▼                                               │
│  ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐                       │
│  │ Step 2a │ │ Step 2b │ │ Step 2c │  Group 2: PARALLEL    │
│  └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘                       │
│                                                              │
│  KEY: [[a,b],[c,d,e]] = (a∥b) → (c∥d∥e)                    │
│        outer list = sequential, inner = parallel             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Steps with withItems — Deploy to Multiple Environments
template:
  name: deploy-envs
  steps:
  - - name: notify-start
      template: send-slack

  - - name: deploy
      template: deploy-to-env
      arguments:
        parameters:
        - name: env
          value: "{{item}}"
      withItems:
      - dev
      - staging
      - prod
    # deploy-dev, deploy-staging, deploy-prod run in PARALLEL!

  - - name: notify-done
      template: send-slack
    # Runs AFTER all 3 deploys finish

10.5 Artifacts — Passing Data Between Steps

Artifacts let you pass files, data, and even Docker images between workflow steps. Argo stores them in an artifact repository (S3, GCS, MinIO, Azure Blob) and makes them available to downstream steps:

How Artifacts Flow Between Steps
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ARTIFACT PASSING IN ARGO WORKFLOWS                          │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────┐                                            │
│  │  Step A      │  Output: /tmp/test-results.json           │
│  │  (run tests) │──▶ outputs.artifacts: results → MinIO     │
│  └──────────────┘                                            │
│          │                                                    │
│          │  Argo automatically uploads to artifact repo      │
│          ▼                                                    │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐                │
│  │  Artifact Repository (MinIO / S3 / GCS)  │                │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐  │                │
│  │  │ anihpj-ci-abc12/results            │  │                │
│  │  │ anihpj-ci-abc12/coverage-report    │  │                │
│  │  │ anihpj-ci-abc12/docker-image.tar   │  │                │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────┘  │                │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘                │
│          │                                                    │
│          │  Argo automatically downloads for Step B          │
│          ▼                                                    │
│  ┌──────────────┐                                            │
│  │  Step B      │  Input: /tmp/test-results.json            │
│  │  (analyze)   │  Reads results, generates report          │
│  └──────────────┘                                            │
│                                                              │
│  ARTIFACT TYPES:                                             │
│  • file — any file or directory                              │
│  • git — clone a repo as an artifact                        │
│  • http — download from URL                                  │
│  • raw — inline data passed directly                         │
│  • docker-image — pass Docker images between steps           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Artifact Example — Test Results to Report
templates:
- name: run-tests
  container:
    image: python:3.12
    command: [pytest, --json-report, --json-report-file=/tmp/results.json]
  outputs:
    artifacts:
    - name: test-results
      path: /tmp/results.json       # Upload to artifact repo

- name: analyze-results
  inputs:
    artifacts:
    - name: test-results
      path: /tmp/results.json       # Download from artifact repo
  container:
    image: python:3.12
    command: [python, analyze.py, /tmp/results.json]
✅ Common Artifact Storage Configurations
  • Quick-start (MinIO): Built-in, no config needed. Good for learning.
  • AWS S3: Edit workflow-controller-configmap, set s3.bucket, s3.region, s3.accessKeySecret
  • GCP GCS: Set gcs.bucket, gcs.serviceAccountKeySecret
  • Azure Blob: Set azure.accountName, azure.accountKeySecret

10.X Container Set & HTTP Templates — Advanced Types

Beyond the 6 core template types, Argo Workflows offers two additional template types for specialized use cases:

📦
Container Set

Runs MULTIPLE containers in a SINGLE pod, sharing network and volumes. Unlike DAG (separate pods per step), Container Set containers run together — great for sidecar patterns (e.g., app + log shipper). Use containerSet.containers array instead of single container field.

🌐
HTTP Template

Makes HTTP/REST API calls directly from a workflow step — no container needed! Define http.method, http.url, http.headers, http.body. Argo executes the request and captures the response. Use for: triggering external systems, health checks, Slack notifications, CI pipeline webhooks.

CAPA Distinction

Script template: runs code INSIDE a container (you write bash/python). HTTP template: sends HTTP request OUTSIDE any container (Argo's executor makes the call directly — faster, no image pull needed). Container Set: colocated containers in one pod (unlike DAG where each step is isolated).

📝 Chapter 10 — CAPA Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between Workflow, WorkflowTemplate, and ClusterWorkflowTemplate?
Show Answer
Answer

Workflow = one-time run. WorkflowTemplate = reusable (namespace-scoped). ClusterWorkflowTemplate = reusable (cluster-wide). Submit from template: argo submit --from wftmpl/NAME.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. Workflow = one-time run. WorkflowTemplate = reusable (namespace-scoped). ClusterWorkflowTemplate = reusable (cluster-wide). Submit from template: argo submit --from wftmpl/NAME. Key insight: The exam tests not just memorization of commands but understanding WHY Argo works this way — the architectural decisions behind the implementation. Practice this in a live cluster to build muscle memory for the hands-on exam tasks.

🔍 WORKFLOW ANATOMY
Entrypoint → Step A → Step B → Step C
                 │          │
                 └──▶ Step D ◀──┘
Each step = 1 K8s Pod | Artifacts via S3/MinIO
Q2
Which template type lets you write Python/Bash code directly in the YAML?
Show Answer
Answer

Script template. Define script.image and script.source. Argo wraps it in a container automatically.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. Script template. Define script.image and script.source. Argo wraps it in a container automatically. Key insight: The exam tests not just memorization of commands but understanding WHY Argo works this way — the architectural decisions behind the implementation. Practice this in a live cluster to build muscle memory for the hands-on exam tasks.

🔍 TEMPLATE TYPES
Container │ Script │ Resource │ Steps │ DAG
Suspend    │ HTTP   │ Plugin   │ templateRef
Each solves a different use case
Q3
In a DAG, how do you make task B run after task A?
Show Answer
Answer

Add dependencies: [A] to task B. Tasks without dependencies run in parallel. If B depends on A and C, use dependencies: [A, C].

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. Add dependencies: [A] to task B. Tasks without dependencies run in parallel. If B depends on A and C, use dependencies: [A, C]. Key insight: The exam tests not just memorization of commands but understanding WHY Argo works this way — the architectural decisions behind the implementation. Practice this in a live cluster to build muscle memory for the hands-on exam tasks.

🔍 GITOPS PRINCIPLES
┌──────────┐   watch   ┌──────────┐   sync   ┌──────────┐
│ Git Repo │─────────▶│ Argo CD  │─────────▶│ Cluster  │
│ (Truth)  │          │ (Agent)  │          │ (Actual) │
└──────────┘          └──────────┘          └──────────┘
     ▲                                           │
     └──────── git revert = rollback ────────────┘
Q4
What is the difference between DAG and Steps templates?
Show Answer
Answer

DAG uses explicit dependencies — tasks float freely. Steps uses a nested list — outer=sequential, inner=parallel. DAG is better for complex pipelines; Steps for linear with fan-out.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. DAG uses explicit dependencies — tasks float freely. Steps uses a nested list — outer=sequential, inner=parallel. DAG is better for complex pipelines; Steps for linear with fan-out. Key insight: The exam tests not just memorization of commands but understanding WHY Argo works this way — the architectural decisions behind the implementation. Practice this in a live cluster to build muscle memory for the hands-on exam tasks.

🔍 DAG vs STEPS
Steps: [A,B](∥) → [C](seq) → [D,E](∥)
DAG:   A ──┐       B ──┐
          ├──▶ C ──▶ D
       no dep          ┘
Q5
How do artifacts pass data between workflow steps?
Show Answer
Answer

Step A declares outputs.artifacts (Argo uploads to MinIO/S3). Step B declares inputs.artifacts with from referencing Step A. Argo downloads before Step B runs.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. Step A declares outputs.artifacts (Argo uploads to MinIO/S3). Step B declares inputs.artifacts with from referencing Step A. Argo downloads before Step B runs. Key insight: The exam tests not just memorization of commands but understanding WHY Argo works this way — the architectural decisions behind the implementation. Practice this in a live cluster to build muscle memory for the hands-on exam tasks.

🔍 ARTIFACT PASSING
Step A ──upload──▶ [MinIO/S3] ──download──▶ Step B
outputs.artifacts:              inputs.artifacts:
  - name: data                   - name: data
    path: /tmp/data.json           from: {{steps.A...}}

Resource template. Define resource.action (create/update/delete/patch) and resource.manifest (the YAML). Useful for dynamic test environments.

Q10
With withItems: [dev, staging, prod] in a Steps template, how do the items execute?
Show Answer
Answer

ALL items run in PARALLEL (if they're in the same inner list). Each item replaces {{item}} in parameters. For sequential execution with withItems, use separate step groups.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. ALL items run in PARALLEL (if they're in the same inner list). 11.1 Parameters & Inputs

Parameters make your workflows dynamic. Instead of hardcoding values, you pass them at submission time or between steps:

Parameters — Three Patterns
# PATTERN 1: Workflow-level parameters (passed at submit time)
spec:
  arguments:
    parameters:
    - name: image-tag
      value: "v2.1"
    - name: environment
      value: "staging"
# Submit: argo submit wf.yaml -p image-tag=v2.2 -p environment=prod

# PATTERN 2: Template-level inputs (consumed by a template)
templates:
- name: deploy
  inputs:
    parameters:
    - name: env
    - name: tag
  container:
    image: deploy-tool:latest
    command: [deploy]
    args: ["--env", "{{inputs.parameters.env}}", "--tag", "{{inputs.parameters.tag}}"]

# PATTERN 3: Pass parameter between steps (output→input)
- name: get-tag
  script:
    image: alpine:latest
    command: [sh, -c]
    args: ["echo 'v2.1' > /tmp/tag.txt"]
  outputs:
    parameters:
    - name: next-tag
      valueFrom:
        path: /tmp/tag.txt        # Read value from file

- name: deploy
  template: deploy-template
  arguments:
    parameters:
    - name: tag
      value: "{{steps.get-tag.outputs.parameters.next-tag}}"

💡 Memoization — Skip Already-Completed Steps

Memoization lets Argo Workflows skip steps that have already succeeded with the same inputs. This is a huge time-saver for CI/CD pipelines where 90% of steps haven't changed:

How Memoization Works
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WITHOUT MEMOIZATION             WITH MEMOIZATION             │
│  ─────────────────               ───────────────              │
│                                                              │
│  Run 1: All 7 steps run          Run 1: All 7 steps run       │
│  Run 2: All 7 steps run AGAIN    Run 2: Only changed steps   │
│  Run 3: All 7 steps run AGAIN    Run 3: Only changed steps   │
│                                                              │
│  ⏱️ Every run = full pipeline    ⏱️ Most runs = seconds      │
│  💰 Every run = full cost        💰 Most runs = minimal cost │
│                                                              │
│  MEMOIZATION HASH = template name + inputs + container       │
│  Same hash → SKIP (already done!)  Different hash → RUN      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Enabling Memoization
# Step 1: Configure the controller (ConfigMap)
# kubectl edit configmap workflow-controller-configmap -n argo
data:
  config: |
    memoization:
      enabled: true
      cacheSizeGB: 1
      # Requires a persistent cache (PVC or DB)

# Step 2: Enable per-template
- name: run-tests
  memoize:
    key: "{{inputs.parameters.git-commit}}"
    maxAge: "24h"     # Cache valid for 24 hours
  container:
    image: python:3.12
    command: [pytest]
🎯 CAPA Memoization Hint

Memoization requires a cache database (Postgres/MySQL). The quick-start manifest does NOT include it — you need the full install. On the exam, if you see "step was skipped" in workflow output, memoization is likely enabled!

11.2 Conditionals & Loops

Argo Workflows supports conditionals (when) and three types of loops. These are key CAPA topics:

🔀 when — Conditional Execution

Skip a step based on a boolean expression. Uses the same syntax as K8s label selectors and Go templates.

tasks:
- name: deploy-prod
  template: deploy
  when: "{{inputs.parameters.env}} == prod"
  # Only runs when env parameter equals "prod"

- name: notify-failure
  template: send-alert
  when: "{{status}} == Failed"
  # Only runs if previous step failed
🔢 withSequence — Numeric Loop

Run a step N times with a counter. Like a for i in range(start, end) loop.

- name: run-batch
  template: process-chunk
  withSequence:
    start: "1"
    end: "10"
  # Runs process-chunk 10 times, with {{item}} = 1,2,3,...,10
📋 withItems — List Iteration

Iterate over a static list. Each item spawns a parallel instance.

- name: deploy-envs
  template: deploy
  arguments:
    parameters:
    - name: env
      value: "{{item}}"
  withItems:
  - dev
  - staging
  - prod
  # Runs deploy 3 times in parallel: dev, staging, prod
🔄 withParam — Dynamic Expansion

Iterate over a dynamic JSON array produced by a previous step. Most powerful loop type!

# Step 1: Generate list
- name: find-images
  script:
    image: python:3.12
    source: |
      import json
      images = [{"name": "anihpj:v1"}, {"name": "anihpj:v2"}]
      print(json.dumps(images))
  outputs:
    parameters:
    - name: image-list
      valueFrom:
        path: /tmp/images.json

# Step 2: Scan each image
- name: scan-images
  template: security-scan
  arguments:
    parameters:
    - name: image
      value: "{{item.name}}"
  withParam: "{{steps.find-images.outputs.parameters.image-list}}"
  # Dynamically runs scan for each image from Step 1!

11.3 Retry, Timeout, & Error Handling

Production workflows need robust error handling. Argo provides multiple mechanisms:

MechanismWhat It DoesExample
retryStrategyRetry failed steps with backoffretryStrategy: {limit: 3, retryPolicy: Always}
activeDeadlineSecondsMax total time for workflowactiveDeadlineSeconds: 3600 (1 hour)
timeoutMax time per steptimeout: "300s"
onExitCleanup handler — runs even on failureonExit: cleanup-notify
exitHandlerAlways-run final stepSend notification regardless of outcome
Complete Error Handling Example
spec:
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600     # Kill after 1 hour total
  onExit: notify-team             # Always run this on exit
  templates:
  - name: ci-pipeline
    dag:
      tasks:
      - name: run-tests
        template: pytest
        retryStrategy:
          limit: 3
          retryPolicy: Always
          backoff:
            duration: "10s"       # Wait 10s between retries
            factor: 2             # Exponential: 10s, 20s, 40s
        timeout: "600s"           # Max 10 min for tests

  - name: notify-team
    container:
      image: curlimages/curl
      command: [curl, -X, POST, https://hooks.slack.com/..., -d, "Workflow {{workflow.name}} completed with status {{workflow.status}}"]
⚠️ CAPA Trap

The onExit handler runs even if the workflow is terminated or fails. Use it for cleanup: delete temp resources, send notifications, etc. The exit handler CANNOT change the workflow's final status — it can only do side-effect operations.

11.4 Volume Claims & Persistent Storage

Share data between workflow steps using PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs). Argo can create a temporary PVC that lives only for the duration of the workflow:

Shared PVC Between Steps
spec:
  volumeClaimTemplates:           # Auto-creates PVC for this workflow
  - metadata:
      name: shared-data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi

  templates:
  - name: generate-data
    container:
      image: alpine:latest
      command: [sh, -c]
      args: ["echo 'important data' > /shared/output.txt"]
      volumeMounts:
      - name: shared-data
        mountPath: /shared

  - name: consume-data
    container:
      image: alpine:latest
      command: [cat, /shared/output.txt]
      volumeMounts:
      - name: shared-data
        mountPath: /shared
    # Reads the file written by generate-data!
💡 When to Use PVC vs Artifacts

PVC: Large files, frequent read/write, binary data. Artifacts: Small files, pass-once pattern, works across clusters. For anihpj: use PVC for shared build cache, artifacts for test results.

11.5 CronWorkflows — Scheduled Workflows

CronWorkflows are like Kubernetes CronJobs but for Argo Workflows. Schedule any workflow to run on a cron schedule:

CronWorkflow — Nightly DB Backup for anihpj
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: CronWorkflow
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-backup
  namespace: argo
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"            # Every day at 2 AM
  timezone: "America/New_York"
  concurrencyPolicy: Replace       # Replace if previous still running
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 300
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 7    # Keep last 7 successful runs
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3        # Keep last 3 failed runs
  workflowSpec:
    entrypoint: backup
    templates:
    - name: backup
      container:
        image: python:3.12
        command: [python, manage.py, dumpdata, --output, /backups/backup-{{workflow.creationTimestamp.Y}}_{{workflow.creationTimestamp.m}}_{{workflow.creationTimestamp.d}}.json]
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-credentials
              key: url
        volumeMounts:
        - name: backups
          mountPath: /backups
concurrencyPolicyBehavior
AllowMultiple instances can run simultaneously (default)
ForbidSkip this run if previous is still running
ReplaceKill previous run and start new one

11.6 Resource Templates — K8s Operations from Workflows

Resource templates let you create, update, or delete Kubernetes resources directly from a workflow step. This is powerful for setting up test environments dynamically:

Resource Template — Dynamic Test Namespace
templates:
- name: create-test-ns
  resource:
    action: create
    manifest: |
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Namespace
      metadata:
        name: test-{{workflow.name}}

- name: run-tests-in-ns
  resource:
    action: create
    manifest: |
      apiVersion: batch/v1
      kind: Job
      metadata:
        name: integration-tests
        namespace: test-{{workflow.name}}
      spec:
        template:
          spec:
            containers:
            - name: test
              image: python:3.12
              command: [pytest, /tests/]
            restartPolicy: Never

- name: cleanup-test-ns
  resource:
    action: delete
    flags: ["namespace", "test-{{workflow.name}}"]
    # Cleans up after tests complete!

🧹 Workflow Cleanup: ttlStrategy & podGC

By default, completed workflow pods stick around forever, consuming cluster resources. Two mechanisms control cleanup:

MechanismWhat It ControlsExample
ttlStrategyAuto-delete the entire Workflow CRD + pods after N secondsttlStrategy: {secondsAfterCompletion: 3600} (delete 1hr after finishing)
podGC.strategyWhen to delete individual step podspodGC: {strategy: OnPodCompletion} (delete pod as soon as step finishes)
Cleanup Configuration
spec:
  # Delete the entire workflow 1 hour after it finishes
  ttlStrategy:
    secondsAfterCompletion: 3600
    secondsAfterSuccess: 7200     # Keep successful longer for audit
    secondsAfterFailure: 86400    # Keep failures 24h for debugging

  # Or: delete pods as each step completes
  podGC:
    strategy: OnPodCompletion     # Options: OnPodCompletion, OnWorkflowCompletion, OnWorkflowSuccess
⚠️ CAPA Note: Cleanup is NOT automatic!

Without ttlStrategy or podGC, workflow pods stay forever. On the exam, you may be asked to configure cleanup. Remember: ttlStrategy deletes the CRD object, podGC deletes just the pods. Use both for a clean cluster!

11.X Enhanced Depends Logic — Advanced DAG Control

Beyond simple dependencies: [A, B] (wait for ALL), Argo Workflows supports enhanced depends logic for complex orchestration patterns. This is tested on CAPA for scenario-based pipeline questions.

ENHANCED DEPENDS LOGIC
Standard:  dependencies: [A, B]         → A AND B must succeed
Enhanced:  depends: "A"                → Same as standard
           depends: "A || B"           → A OR B (any one succeeds)
           depends: "(A && B) || C"    → (A AND B) OR C
           depends: "A.Succeeded"      → Only if A succeeded (not skipped)
           depends: "A.AnyCondition"   → Any final state (success/fail/skip)
Operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT), () for grouping
Conditions: .Succeeded, .Failed, .Errored, .Skipped, .Daemoned, .AnyCondition

CAPA Pattern: "Run notification IF step A fails OR step B fails"
→ depends: "A.Failed || B.Failed"

11.Y Synchronization — Concurrency Control

Argo Workflows provides synchronization primitives to prevent race conditions when multiple workflows access shared resources:

🔒
Mutex

Only ONE workflow holds the lock at a time. Use for exclusive DB access: synchronization.mutex.name: db-migration — only one migration runs at a time.

🚦
Semaphore

Limit to N concurrent workflows. Use for API rate limiting: semaphore.configMapKeyRef.name: api-limit — max 5 workflows calling external API.

📊
Parallelism

Limit steps within ONE workflow: parallelism: 10 — max 10 steps run simultaneously, rest queue up.

12.1 Database Migration Workflow for anihpj

Running Django migrations is risky. This workflow takes a pre-migration backup, runs the migration, verifies, and notifies — all with rollback capability:

anihpj DB Migration Workflow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DB MIGRATION WORKFLOW for anihpj                            │
│                                                              │
│  ┌────────────────┐                                          │
│  │ 1. Backup DB   │  python manage.py dumpdata → /backups/  │
│  │    (pre-mig)   │                                          │
│  └───────┬────────┘                                          │
│          │                                                    │
│          ▼                                                    │
│  ┌────────────────┐                                          │
│  │ 2. Run         │  python manage.py migrate               │
│  │    Migrations  │                                          │
│  └───────┬────────┘                                          │
│          │                                                    │
│     ┌────┴────┐                                              │
│     │ Success? │                                              │
│     └────┬────┘                                              │
│          │                                                    │
│     ┌────┼────────────────┐                                  │
│     ▼    │                 ▼                                  │
│  ✅ YES  │              ❌ NO                                 │
│     │    │                 │                                  │
│     ▼    │                 ▼                                  │
│  ┌──────────┐        ┌──────────┐                            │
│  │3. Verify │        │3. Restore│  python manage.py         │
│  │   DB     │        │   Backup │  loaddata backup.json     │
│  └────┬─────┘        └──────────┘                            │
│       │                                                       │
│       ▼                                                       │
│  ┌──────────┐                                                │
│  │4. Notify │  Slack/email: "Migration succeeded"           │
│  │   Team   │                                                │
│  └──────────┘                                                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
anihpj-migration-wf.yaml (simplified)
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: WorkflowTemplate
metadata:
  name: anihpj-migration
  namespace: argo
spec:
  entrypoint: migrate
  templates:
  - name: migrate
    steps:
    - - name: backup
        template: dump-db
    - - name: run-migrate
        template: django-migrate
    - - name: verify
        template: verify-db
        when: "{{steps.run-migrate.status}} == Succeeded"
    - - name: notify
        template: send-notification

  - name: dump-db
    container:
      image: registry.example.com/anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.tag}}
      command: [python, manage.py, dumpdata, -o, /backups/pre-migrate.json]
      env:
      - name: DATABASE_URL
        valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db-creds, key: url}}

  - name: django-migrate
    container:
      image: registry.example.com/anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.tag}}
      command: [python, manage.py, migrate, --noinput]
    retryStrategy:
      limit: 2
      retryPolicy: OnFailure

  - name: verify-db
    container:
      image: registry.example.com/anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.tag}}
      command: [python, manage.py, check, --deploy]

  - name: send-notification
    container:
      image: curlimages/curl
      command: [curl, -X, POST, "{{workflow.parameters.slack-webhook}}"]

12.2 CI/CD Pipeline with Workflows

This is the complete CI pipeline from Chapter 10, now as a reusable WorkflowTemplate for anihpj. On every git push, this pipeline clones, tests (in parallel), builds, pushes, and updates the GitOps repo:

1
Git Push
2
Clone Repo
3
Test + Lint + SAST
4
Build Image
5
Push Registry
6
Update GitOps Repo
7
Argo CD Syncs!
Complete CI/CD WorkflowTemplate for anihpj
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: WorkflowTemplate
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ci-cd
  namespace: argo
spec:
  entrypoint: ci-cd-pipeline
  arguments:
    parameters:
    - name: repo-url
      value: "https://github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj.git"
    - name: git-ref
      value: "main"
    - name: image-tag
      value: "latest"
    - name: gitops-repo
      value: "https://github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj-k8s.git"

  templates:
  - name: ci-cd-pipeline
    dag:
      tasks:
      - name: clone
        template: git-clone

      - name: unit-tests
        dependencies: [clone]
        template: run-pytest

      - name: lint
        dependencies: [clone]
        template: run-flake8

      - name: sast-scan
        dependencies: [clone]
        template: run-bandit

      - name: build
        dependencies: [unit-tests, lint, sast-scan]
        template: docker-build

      - name: push
        dependencies: [build]
        template: docker-push

      - name: update-gitops
        dependencies: [push]
        template: update-manifest

  - name: git-clone
    container:
      image: alpine/git
      command: [git, clone, "{{workflow.parameters.repo-url}}", /src]
      args: ["--branch", "{{workflow.parameters.git-ref}}"]

  - name: run-pytest
    container:
      image: python:3.12
      command: [pytest]
      args: [/src/jobpost/tests/, -v, --junitxml=/tmp/results.xml]
      workingDir: /src
    outputs:
      artifacts:
      - name: test-results
        path: /tmp/results.xml

  - name: run-flake8
    container:
      image: alpine/flake8
      args: [/src]

  - name: run-bandit
    container:
      image: securesystemsengineering/bandit
      args: [-r, /src, -f, json, -o, /tmp/bandit-report.json]
    outputs:
      artifacts:
      - name: sast-report
        path: /tmp/bandit-report.json

  - name: docker-build
    container:
      image: docker:dind
      command: [docker, build]
      args: [-t, "registry.example.com/anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.image-tag}}", /src]
      env:
      - name: DOCKER_HOST
        value: tcp://localhost:2375

  - name: docker-push
    container:
      image: docker:dind
      command: [docker, push]
      args: ["registry.example.com/anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.image-tag}}"]

  - name: update-manifest
    container:
      image: alpine/git
      command: [/bin/sh, -c]
      args:
      - |
        git clone {{workflow.parameters.gitops-repo}} /gitops
        cd /gitops
        sed -i 's/newTag:.*/newTag: {{workflow.parameters.image-tag}}/' overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
        git config user.email "argo@anihpj.dev"
        git config user.name "Argo CI"
        git commit -am "[CI] Update anihpj to {{workflow.parameters.image-tag}}"
        git push origin main
💡 Integration Pattern — The Argo Holy Grail

This CI workflow updates the GitOps repo's Kustomize overlay with the new image tag. Argo CD detects the Git change and auto-syncs to the cluster. This is the full Argo CI/CD pattern: Argo Workflows (CI) → GitOps Repo → Argo CD (CD). We'll cover the end-to-end integration with Argo Events triggering in Part 6 (Chapter 20).

GitHub/GitLab Integration: Use a webhook (covered in Chapter 18) to trigger this workflow automatically on every push. The webhook payload provides repo-url, git-ref, and image-tag parameters dynamically.

12.3 Data Processing Pipeline — ETL for JobPost Data

Extract job postings from the Django DB, transform to CSV, and load to an analytics database — all as an Argo Workflow using artifact passing between steps:

ETL Pipeline for jobpost Data
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ETL WORKFLOW: jobpost Analytics Pipeline                     │
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐    │
│  │ 1. EXTRACT  │────▶│ 2. TRANSFORM│────▶│  3. LOAD    │    │
│  │             │     │             │     │             │    │
│  │ python      │     │ python      │     │ python      │    │
│  │ manage.py   │     │ transform.py│     │ load_to_db  │    │
│  │ dumpdata    │     │             │     │             │    │
│  │ → jobs.json │     │ → jobs.csv  │     │ → analytics │    │
│  └─────────────┘     └─────────────┘     └─────────────┘    │
│       │                    │                    │            │
│       │ artifact:          │ artifact:          │            │
│       │ jobs.json          │ jobs.csv           │            │
│       └─── S3/MinIO ───────┴─── S3/MinIO ───────┘            │
│                                                              │
│  Each step gets the previous step's output as input artifact │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Complete ETL WorkflowTemplate for jobpost Analytics
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: WorkflowTemplate
metadata:
  name: jobpost-etl-pipeline
  namespace: argo
spec:
  entrypoint: etl
  arguments:
    parameters:
    - name: date-range
      value: "last-30-days"

  templates:
  - name: etl
    steps:
    - - name: extract
        template: extract-jobs
    - - name: transform
        template: transform-to-csv
        arguments:
          artifacts:
          - name: raw-data
            from: "{{steps.extract.outputs.artifacts.jobs-json}}"
    - - name: load
        template: load-to-analytics
        arguments:
          artifacts:
          - name: processed-data
            from: "{{steps.transform.outputs.artifacts.jobs-csv}}"
          parameters:
          - name: date-range
            value: "{{workflow.parameters.date-range}}"

  - name: extract-jobs
    container:
      image: registry.example.com/anihpj:latest
      command: [python, manage.py, dumpdata, jobpost, --indent=2]
      env:
      - name: DATABASE_URL
        valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db-readonly-creds, key: url}}
    outputs:
      artifacts:
      - name: jobs-json
        path: /tmp/jobs-dump.json
        archive:
          none: {}        # Store as raw JSON (not tar.gz)

  - name: transform-to-csv
    inputs:
      artifacts:
      - name: raw-data
        path: /tmp/jobs-dump.json
    container:
      image: python:3.12
      command: [python]
      source: |
        import json, csv, sys

        # Read extracted JSON
        with open('/tmp/jobs-dump.json') as f:
            data = json.load(f)

        # Transform JobPost entries to CSV
        with open('/tmp/jobs.csv', 'w', newline='') as csvfile:
            writer = csv.writer(csvfile)
            writer.writerow(['id', 'title', 'company', 'location', 'skills', 'created'])
            for item in data:
                if item['model'] == 'jobpost.jobpost':
                    fields = item['fields']
                    writer.writerow([
                        item['pk'],
                        fields.get('title', ''),
                        fields.get('author', ''),
                        fields.get('location', ''),
                        ','.join(str(s) for s in fields.get('skills', [])),
                        fields.get('created_at', '')
                    ])
        print(f"Transformed {len(data)} records to CSV")
    outputs:
      artifacts:
      - name: jobs-csv
        path: /tmp/jobs.csv

  - name: load-to-analytics
    inputs:
      artifacts:
      - name: processed-data
        path: /tmp/jobs.csv
    container:
      image: python:3.12
      command: [python]
      source: |
        import csv, sqlite3, sys

        # Load CSV into analytics SQLite DB
        conn = sqlite3.connect('/data/analytics.db')
        cursor = conn.cursor()
        cursor.execute('''CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS job_analytics
            (id INTEGER, title TEXT, company TEXT,
             location TEXT, skills TEXT, created TEXT)''')

        with open('/tmp/jobs.csv') as f:
            reader = csv.DictReader(f)
            for row in reader:
                cursor.execute(
                    'INSERT OR REPLACE INTO job_analytics VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?)',
                    [row['id'], row['title'], row['company'],
                     row['location'], row['skills'], row['created']]
                )
        conn.commit()
        print(f"Loaded {cursor.rowcount} rows to analytics DB")

# Submit: argo submit --from wftmpl/jobpost-etl-pipeline -p date-range=last-7-days
🎯 CAPA Artifact Pattern

Notice how each step: (1) declares outputs.artifacts for what it produces, (2) the downstream step declares inputs.artifacts for what it consumes, and (3) the from field references the upstream step by name. This artifact chain is a frequently tested CAPA pattern!

Weekly DB Optimize0 3 * * 0 (3 AM Sunday)VACUUM/optimize tables, rebuild indexes

What steps should a production DB migration workflow include?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Pre-migration backup (dump data), 2) Run migration, 3) Verify (check DB health), 4) Notify team. Use retryStrategy on the migration step and onExit for notification.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. 1) Pre-migration backup (dump data), 2) Run migration, 3) Verify (check DB health), 4) Notify team. Q6
What's the difference between CronWorkflow and Calendar EventSource for scheduling?
Show Answer
Answer

CronWorkflow = simpler, one YAML. Calendar EventSource = more powerful, integrates with Argo Events, can trigger multiple workflows from one schedule. Both support cron expressions.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. CronWorkflow = simpler, one YAML. Calendar EventSource = more powerful, integrates with Argo Events, can trigger multiple workflows from one schedule. Both support cron expressions. Key insight: The exam tests not just memorization of commands but understanding WHY Argo works this way — the architectural decisions behind the implementation. Practice this in a live cluster to build muscle memory for the hands-on exam tasks.

🔍 CRONWORKFLOW
schedule: '0 2 * * *' (daily 2 AM)
concurrencyPolicy:
  Forbid  = skip if prev running
  Replace = kill old, start new
  Allow   = run in parallel
Q7
What concurrencyPolicy should you use for a nightly backup CronWorkflow?
Show Answer
Answer

Forbid — if the backup runs long, skip the next scheduled run rather than running two backups simultaneously. Or Replace if you want the latest to always run.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 13
  • Retry vs Resubmit: argo retry retries from the FAILED step (preserving successful steps). argo resubmit restarts the ENTIRE workflow from scratch. Know the difference — the exam will test it.
  • TTL cleanup: Without ttlStrategy, completed workflow pods accumulate forever. Set secondsAfterCompletion: 3600 to auto-clean after 1 hour. On a busy cluster, this prevents resource exhaustion.
  • Pending pods: If a workflow step is stuck "Pending", check in order: node resources, taints/tolerations, PVC binding, image pull errors, namespace resource quotas.

13.3 Debugging Failed Workflows

When a workflow fails, here's your systematic debugging approach:

1
Get status overview: argo get <wf> -n argo — Which step failed? What's the error message?
2
Check logs: argo logs <wf> -c <step-name> -n argo — What did the container output?
3
Describe the pod: kubectl describe pod <wf-pod> -n argo — Check Events for image pull, OOM, scheduling issues
4
Check controller logs: kubectl logs deploy/workflow-controller -n argo — Controller-level issues
5
Retry: argo retry <wf> -n argo — Retry from the failed step (fix first!)
SymptomLikely CauseFix
ImagePullBackOffWrong image name/tag or registry authCheck image name, add imagePullSecrets
OOMKilledContainer used too much memoryAdd resources.limits.memory to template
CrashLoopBackOffContainer exits with errorCheck argo logs for application error
Artifact 404Artifact repo misconfiguredVerify workflow-controller-configmap S3/MinIO settings
Workflow stuck PendingResource quota or schedulingkubectl describe pod → check Events
Permission deniedRBAC issue in workflowCheck ServiceAccount has needed roles

How do you view real-time logs of a specific workflow step?
