🎯 CAPA Practice Drill — Part 3 (15 min)

⏱️ Time Target: 15 minutes | 📋 5 Hands-On Tasks
Scenario: anihpj CI Pipeline Troubleshooting

Your team has an Argo Workflows CI pipeline for anihpj. The Senior DevOps engineer is out sick, and you've been asked to fix several issues.

  1. Create a WorkflowTemplate named anihpj-ci with a DAG that has: clone → unit-tests (dependency: clone) → build (dependency: unit-tests). Use container images of your choice.
  2. Submit a workflow from the template with parameter image-tag=v3.0.
  3. Check the logs of the unit-tests step. It failed with "module not found: pytest". Fix the image and resubmit.
  4. Add a retry strategy to the unit-tests: retry up to 3 times with 10-second backoff.
  5. Schedule this workflow as a CronWorkflow to run every day at 8 AM. Keep the last 5 successful runs.
💡 Hint: For task 1, use dag: with tasks: and dependencies:. For task 2, argo submit --from wftmpl/anihpj-ci -p image-tag=v3.0. For task 3, check if the image has pytest installed — use python:3.12 which includes it. For task 4, add retryStrategy: {limit: 3, backoff: {duration: "10s"}}. For task 5, use kind: CronWorkflow with schedule: "0 8 * * *" and successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 5.
🔍 Click to Reveal Step-by-Step Solution
# TASK 1: Create WorkflowTemplate with DAG
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: WorkflowTemplate
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ci
  namespace: argo
spec:
  entrypoint: ci
  templates:
  - name: ci
    dag:
      tasks:
      - name: clone
        template: git-clone
      - name: unit-tests
        dependencies: [clone]
        template: run-tests
      - name: build
        dependencies: [unit-tests]
        template: docker-build

  - name: git-clone
    container:
      image: alpine/git
      command: [git, clone, https://github.com/me/anihpj.git, /src]

  - name: run-tests
    retryStrategy:
      limit: 3
      backoff:
        duration: "10s"
    container:
      image: python:3.12
      command: [pytest]
      args: [/src/jobpost/tests/, -v]

  - name: docker-build
    container:
      image: docker:latest
      command: [docker, build, -t, anihpj:{{workflow.parameters.image-tag}}, /src]
EOF

# Verify: argo template get anihpj-ci -n argo

# TASK 2: Submit workflow from template
argo submit --from wftmpl/anihpj-ci -n argo -p image-tag=v3.0

# TASK 3: Check logs and fix
argo logs @latest -c unit-tests -n argo
# Error: "module not found: pytest"
# Fix: Change image from alpine to python:3.12 (has pytest)
# kubectl edit workflowtemplate anihpj-ci -n argo  # Fix the image
argo submit --from wftmpl/anihpj-ci -n argo -p image-tag=v3.0

# TASK 4: Retry strategy (added in TASK 1's run-tests template above)
# Already included: retryStrategy: {limit: 3, backoff: {duration: "10s"}}

# TASK 5: Schedule as CronWorkflow
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: CronWorkflow
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ci-daily
  namespace: argo
spec:
  schedule: "0 8 * * *"
  timezone: "America/New_York"
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 5
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  workflowSpec:
    workflowTemplateRef:
      name: anihpj-ci
EOF

# Verify: argo cron list -n argo
✅ Verify Your Work
  • argo template get anihpj-ci -n argo — Template exists with correct DAG
  • argo list -n argo — Your workflow ran to completion
  • argo logs <wf> -c unit-tests -n argo — Tests pass after fix
  • argo cron list -n argo — CronWorkflow is scheduled

🚀 Part 4: Argo Rollouts Chapters 14-16

Chapter 14: Introduction to Progressive Delivery

Standard Kubernetes Deployments are all-or-nothing — when you update an image, ALL users see the new version instantly. If it's broken, everyone suffers. Progressive delivery fixes this by gradually shifting traffic to the new version while monitoring for problems.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🎯 CAPA 18%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the risks of standard Kubernetes Deployments
  • ✅ Grasp the concept of progressive delivery and traffic shifting
  • ✅ Master blue-green deployments: instant cutover and instant rollback
  • ✅ Master canary deployments: gradual percentage-based rollout
  • ✅ Compare Argo Rollouts vs standard Deployments
CANARY vs BLUE-GREEN — VISUAL COMPARISON
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CANARY (Gradual):        BLUE-GREEN (Instant):          │
│                                                         │
│  Step 1:  10% v2  90% v1  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │
│  Step 2:  25% v2  75% v1  │ Blue v1  │ │Green v2  │   │
│  Step 3:  50% v2  50% v1  │  ACTIVE  │ │  IDLE    │   │
│  Step 4: 100% v2          └──────────┘ └──────────┘   │
│                           ↓ PROMOTE ↓                   │
│  Best for: API/web apps   ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │
│  Rollback: Stop at any %  │ Blue v1  │ │Green v2  │   │
│  Analysis: At each step   │  IDLE    │ │  ACTIVE  │   │
│                           └──────────┘ └──────────┘   │
│                           Best for: Stateful apps       │
│                           Rollback: Switch Service back │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.1 The Problem with Standard Kubernetes Deployments

Kubernetes Deployments are great for basic rollout, but they have a critical flaw: no traffic control during the rollout. When you update the image, the Deployment controller replaces pods as fast as it can. All users are immediately exposed to the new version.

😰 WITHOUT Progressive Delivery — The anihpj Nightmare
  • Friday 4:55 PM — Deploy new jobpost search feature to production
  • 4:56 PM — Bug: Search returns 500 errors for ALL queries
  • 4:57 PM — ALL users see broken search (100% traffic to v2)
  • 5:00 PM — On-call engineer paged, spends weekend debugging
  • Result: 45 min downtime, weekend incident, unhappy team
😌 WITH Progressive Delivery (Argo Rollouts) — The anihpj Success Story
  • Friday 4:55 PM — Deploy new jobpost search via canary at 10% traffic
  • 4:56 PM — Bug detected: error rate spikes to 8% on canary pods
  • 4:56 PM — Argo auto-rollback: canary scaled to 0, 100% traffic back to v1
  • 4:57 PM — Only 10% of users saw a brief glitch. 90% never noticed.
  • Result: Zero downtime, zero pages, team enjoys weekend!
Standard Deployment Rollout — All or Nothing
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STANDARD DEPLOYMENT ROLLOUT                                 │
│                                                              │
│  BEFORE UPDATE:                    DURING UPDATE:            │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐           ┌─────────────────────┐  │
│  │ anihpj v1           │           │ anihpj v1 │ v2      │  │
│  │ ████████████████████│ 100%      │ █████████ │ ░░░░░░░░│  │
│  │ All users see v1    │           │ Some see v1, some v2 │  │
│  └─────────────────────┘           │ NO CONTROL over who! │  │
│                                    └─────────────────────┘  │
│  PROBLEMS:                                                   │
│  ❌ If v2 has a bug → ALL transitioning users affected      │
│  ❌ No way to test with 5% of users first                   │
│  ❌ Rollback is slow: kubectl rollout undo (recreates pods) │
│  ❌ No metric-based decision making                         │
│                                                              │
│  anihpj SCENARIO:                                            │
│  Friday 4:55 PM — Deploy new jobpost search feature         │
│  Bug: Search returns 500 errors for all queries             │
│  Result: ALL users see broken search → weekend incident!    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ The Friday Deploy Nightmare

This is how production incidents happen. A bad deploy at 5 PM Friday affects 100% of users instantly. The on-call engineer spends their weekend debugging. Progressive delivery would have caught the error at 10% traffic and auto-rolled back — zero user impact.

14.2 What is Progressive Delivery?

Progressive delivery is the practice of gradually exposing new versions to subsets of users, monitoring key metrics at each step, and automatically rolling back if something goes wrong. Think of it as "drive a mile, check the engine, drive another mile" instead of "floor it and hope".

🧠 Beginner's Mental Model — "The Restaurant Soft Opening"

Imagine you're renovating a restaurant. Instead of closing the old kitchen and opening the new one to ALL customers at once (risky!), you do a soft opening: invite 10% of your regulars to try the new menu while the old kitchen still serves the other 90%. If the 10% love it — expand to 25%, then 50%, then fully switch. If they complain about cold food — you immediately switch everyone back to the old kitchen. No one else even noticed. Blue-Green is like having two complete kitchens and switching which door customers use. Canary is like slowly redirecting a percentage of customers to the new kitchen. Argo Rollouts is the restaurant manager who orchestrates all of this automatically.

Progressive Delivery — Gradual Traffic Shift
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PROGRESSIVE DELIVERY — The Safe Way to Deploy               │
│                                                              │
│  TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────▶       │
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │ STEP 1: 10% v2   │ STEP 2: 25% v2   │ STEP 3: 50% v2   ││
│  │ ██░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ │ █████░░░░░░░░░░░ │ ██████████░░░░░░░ ││
│  │ v2 ░░░░░░v1░░░░░│  v2  ░░░░v1░░░░░│   v2   ░░v1░░░░░ ││
│  │ ⏱️ Wait 30s      │ ⏱️ Wait 2 min    │ ⏱️ Wait 5 min    ││
│  │ ✅ Error < 1%?   │ ✅ Latency OK?   │ ✅ All metrics?   ││
│  │ ✅ Latency OK?   │ ✅ CPU normal?   │                  ││
│  │ → Continue       │ → Continue       │ → Continue       ││
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │ STEP 4: 100% v2  │ AT ANY STEP:                         ││
│  │ ████████████████ │ ❌ Error > 5% → AUTO-ROLLBACK!      ││
│  │  v2 (all users)  │ ↩️ All traffic back to v1 instantly ││
│  │ ✅ Fully deployed │ 0% user impact from bad deploy      ││
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
│                                                              │
│  anihpj BENEFIT:                                             │
│  New jobpost search bug → caught at 10% step → auto-rollback│
│  → Only 10% of users saw a brief error → no incident!       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.3 Blue-Green Deployments

Blue-Green uses two complete environments: Blue (current/stable) and Green (new version). Traffic switches from Blue to Green in one atomic operation — like flipping a switch. The magic: if something goes wrong, flip the switch back — instant rollback.

Blue-Green Deployment — Instant Cutover
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BLUE-GREEN DEPLOYMENT                                       │
│                                                              │
│  BEFORE CUTOVER:                    AFTER CUTOVER:           │
│  ┌─────────────────┐               ┌─────────────────┐      │
│  │ 🔵 BLUE (v1)    │◀── traffic   │ 🔵 BLUE (v1)    │      │
│  │ 3 pods running  │               │ 3 pods (idle)   │      │
│  │ activeService    │               └─────────────────┘      │
│  └─────────────────┘                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────┐               ┌─────────────────┐      │
│  │ 🟢 GREEN (v2)   │               │ 🟢 GREEN (v2)   │◀──  │
│  │ 3 pods running  │  idle         │ 3 pods running  │traffic│
│  │ previewService   │               │ activeService   │      │
│  └─────────────────┘               └─────────────────┘      │
│                                                              │
│  ⏱️ Cutover: ~1 second (Argo swaps Service selector label) │
│  ↩️ Rollback: Swap label back → instant (still ~1 sec)    │
│                                                              │
│  KEY: Both versions run simultaneously — you just switch    │
│  which one the Service points to.                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔵 activeService

The Service that receives production traffic. Initially points to Blue (v1). After promotion, it points to Green (v2). This is the "traffic switch" — changing the selector label from version: blue to version: green.

🟢 previewService

An optional Service for testing Green BEFORE cutting over. Your QA team can hit anihpj-preview.example.com to verify Green works, while real users still use Blue via the activeService.

🤖 autoPromotion

When autoPromotionEnabled: true, Argo automatically promotes Green to active as soon as all Green pods are healthy. When false, you must manually run kubectl argo rollouts promote <rollout>. For production anihpj, set to false — always have a human approve!

↩️ Instant Rollback

The killer feature of blue-green: since Blue pods are STILL RUNNING (just idle), rolling back is instant. Argo just swaps the selector label back. No pod restarts, no image pulls, no waiting. Compare this to kubectl rollout undo which has to recreate old pods from scratch.

14.4 Canary Deployments

Canary deployments gradually shift a percentage of traffic to the new version. Unlike blue-green (all-or-nothing switch), canary lets you send 10% of users to v2, check metrics, then 25%, then 50%, then 100%. This is like sending a canary into a coal mine — if the canary stops singing (errors spike), you know there's danger.

Canary Deployment Stages
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CANARY DEPLOYMENT — Gradual Traffic Shift                    │
│                                                              │
│  TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────▶       │
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐                 │
│  │ STEP 1: 10% v2  │    │ STEP 2: 25% v2  │                 │
│  │ ██░░░░░░░░░░░░░ │    │ █████░░░░░░░░░░ │                 │
│  │ v2 ░░░░░░v1░░░ │    │  v2  ░░░░v1░░░ │                 │
│  │ ⏱️ pause: 30s   │    │ ⏱️ pause: 2min  │                 │
│  └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘                 │
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐                 │
│  │ STEP 3: 50% v2  │    │ STEP 4: 100% v2 │                 │
│  │ ██████████░░░░░ │    │ ███████████████ │                 │
│  │   v2   ░░v1░░░ │    │   v2 (all)      │                 │
│  │ ⏱️ pause: 5min  │    │ ✅ Fully rolled │                 │
│  └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘                 │
│                                                              │
│  AT ANY STEP: Error rate > 5% → ❌ AUTO-ROLLBACK to v1     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚖️ Weight Steps (setWeight)

Each setWeight defines what percentage of traffic goes to the canary (new version). The remaining traffic stays on the stable (old) version. setWeight: 10 = 10% canary, 90% stable. You can set any weight: 5, 20, 33, etc.

⏸️ Pause Durations

After each weight step, you can pause for a duration (e.g., pause: {duration: 2m}) or indefinitely (pause: {} — requires manual promotion). Pauses give your metrics time to accumulate meaningful data before deciding to continue.

📊 Metric Analysis

Instead of (or in addition to) time-based pauses, you can run an analysis step that queries Prometheus/Datadog/NewRelic for error rates, latency, CPU, etc. The analysis runs for a configured duration and returns pass/fail. This is the production-grade approach — don't guess, measure!

🛑 Auto-Rollback

If any analysis step fails (e.g., error rate exceeds threshold), Argo Rollouts automatically scales down the canary pods and shifts 100% traffic back to the stable version. No human intervention needed. The rollout is marked as "Degraded" and you can investigate later.

14.5 Argo Rollouts vs Standard Deployments

FeatureK8s DeploymentArgo Rollout
Rollout StrategyRollingUpdate or RecreateBlue-Green + Canary
Traffic Control❌ No control✅ Percentage-based
Rollback SpeedSlow (recreate pods)Instant (swap selector)
Pre-Production Testing❌ None✅ previewService + analysis
Metric-Driven❌ No✅ Prometheus/DataDog/etc.
Auto-Rollback❌ Manual only✅ Automatic on metric failure
Pause/Resume❌ No✅ Manual or time-based
Drop-in ReplacementN/A✅ Same pod spec, just change kind
kubectl Support✅ Native✅ kubectl plugin
💡 The "One Field" Difference

A Rollout is literally a Deployment with one extra field: strategy. The replicas, selector, and template are identical. You can convert any Deployment to a Rollout by changing kind: Deployment → kind: Rollout and adding strategy: {canary: ...} or strategy: {blueGreen: ...}. That's it!

🔵🟢 Blue-Green vs 🐤 Canary — Decision Guide

Both are progressive delivery strategies, but they solve different problems:

Decision Factor🔵🟢 Blue-Green🐤 Canary
Cutover SpeedInstant (~1 second)Gradual (minutes to hours)
Rollback SpeedInstant (swap label back)Gradual (shift weight back)
Resource Cost2× resources (both environments)Just + canary pods
Risk LevelMedium (all-or-nothing switch)Low (gradual exposure)
Testing DepthFull environment (previewService)Partial exposure only
Best ForMajor releases, DB migrations, infra changesFeature rollouts, UI changes, incremental updates
anihpj ExampleDjango 4→5 upgrade, Postgres migrationNew jobpost search, UI redesign
💡 Rule of Thumb

If a rollback would require database migration reversal → use Blue-Green (test Green fully before switching). If the change is stateless and reversible → use Canary (cheaper resources, gradual confidence). For CAPA: know both strategies cold — they're 18% of the exam!

📝 Chapter 14 — CAPA Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between Blue-Green and Canary deployment?
Show Answer
Answer

Blue-Green swaps ALL traffic at once between two environments. Canary shifts a PERCENTAGE gradually (5%→25%→50%→100%). Canary is lower risk — you can rollback at any percentage before full promotion.

Explanation

Blue-Green provisions a COMPLETE duplicate environment (the "Green" side). When you're satisfied, you flip a switch — all traffic moves at once. The rollback is instant (flip back), but the resource cost is 2x (you run both environments). Best for: Stateful applications, database schema changes, or when you need to test the full environment before ANY user sees it.

Canary shifts traffic INCREMENTALLY. You start with 5% of users on v2, monitor for 10 minutes, then 25%, then 50%, then 100%. At any step, if metrics fail, traffic reverts to v1. Resource cost is lower (only 5-25% extra pods during canary). Best for: Stateless web apps, APIs, when you want gradual risk reduction. CAPA will test your ability to CHOOSE between these based on a scenario.

🔍 BLUE-GREEN vs CANARY — SIDE BY SIDE
BLUE-GREEN: [Blue 100%]──SWITCH──▶[Green 100%]  (all at once)
CANARY:     [v1 95%|v2 5%]→[v1 75%|v2 25%]→[v1 50%|v2 50%]→[v2 100%]  (gradual)
Key: Blue-Green = instant but 2x resources. Canary = gradual, lower risk.
Q2
In a Rollout's canary strategy, what triggers an automatic rollback?
Show Answer
Answer

Analysis template failure — e.g., error rate > 1% or latency > 500ms for 5 consecutive minutes. The Rollout auto-aborts and reverts to the stable version.

Explanation

The AnalysisTemplate (or ClusterAnalysisTemplate) defines metric probes that run DURING each canary step. Each probe queries a metric provider and compares against success/failure thresholds. All probes must pass for the step to succeed. If ANY probe fails for failureLimit consecutive measurements, the AnalysisRun is marked Failed → the Rollout auto-aborts and reverts to stable. This is what makes Argo Rollouts "progressive delivery" rather than just "slower deployment" — it's METRICS-DRIVEN, not just time-driven.

Common CAPA scenario: "The canary is stuck at 10% — what's wrong?" Answer: Check the AnalysisRun status. If metrics are failing, the canary won't progress. Use kubectl get analysisrun and kubectl describe analysisrun to diagnose.

🔍 ANALYSIS-DRIVEN ROLLBACK
Canary 10% → AnalysisRun starts → Prometheus: error_rate > 1%?
                                     │
                              ┌──────┴──────┐
                              ▼              ▼
                           PASS            FAIL (3x consecutive)
                           continue        Rollout auto-aborts
                           to 25%          Traffic → 100% stable
                                           Canary pods → scaled down
Q3
What is an AnalysisTemplate and what metrics can it check?
Show Answer
Answer

A reusable metric probe definition. Checks: Prometheus queries, Datadog metrics, New Relic APM, Wavefront, Job status, web HTTP results. If ANY metric fails, the canary aborts.

Explanation

An AnalysisTemplate is a reusable CRD (namespace-scoped) or ClusterAnalysisTemplate (cluster-wide). It defines a list of metrics, each with a provider (Prometheus, Datadog, NewRelic, Wavefront, Web, Job, CloudWatch, Graphite, InfluxDB, SkyWalking) and success/failure conditions. Key fields: interval (how often to query — e.g., 30s), count (number of measurements — e.g., 10), failureLimit (consecutive failures to abort — e.g., 3), successCondition (expression — e.g., "result < 1"). The AnalysisRun CR is the INSTANCE created when a canary step references an AnalysisTemplate — think of it as Template:AnalysisRun :: WorkflowTemplate:Workflow.

🔍 ANALYSIS TEMPLATE — METRIC PROVIDERS
AnalysisTemplate "canary-check":
├── Metric 1: Prometheus  → error_rate < 1% for 5min
├── Metric 2: Datadog     → p95_latency < 500ms
├── Metric 3: Web/HTTP    → GET /health returns 200
├── Metric 4: K8s Job     → migration-test completed
└── All must PASS → canary promotes | Any FAIL → auto rollback
Q4
How does a Rollout differ from a standard K8s Deployment?
Show Answer
Answer

Rollout adds: canary/blue-green strategies, step-based traffic control, automatic rollback via analysis, pause/resume promotion. Under the hood it creates/manages a Deployment (stable) and ReplicaSets.

Explanation

A standard K8s Deployment has ONE strategy: RollingUpdate (replace pods gradually with maxSurge/maxUnavailable). There's no canary, no blue-green, no analysis, no pause/resume, and no automatic rollback based on metrics — if a bad version rolls out, you must manually kubectl rollout undo.

A Rollout REPLACES the Deployment entirely. The Rollout controller creates and manages ReplicaSets just like a Deployment, but adds the strategy field. Under the hood: the Rollout controller creates a "stable" ReplicaSet and, during updates, a "canary" or "preview" ReplicaSet. It manages two Services (stable + canary/preview). When the canary succeeds, the canary RS becomes the new stable RS. Key CAPA distinction: you convert from Deployment → Rollout, not use both simultaneously — they would fight for control of the same pods.

🔍 DEPLOYMENT vs ROLLOUT — SIDE BY SIDE
DEPLOYMENT:                ROLLOUT:
spec:                      spec:
  replicas: 3                replicas: 3
  selector: ...              selector: ...
  template: ...              template: ...
  strategy:                  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: {}          canary:           ← THE DIFFERENCE
                                 steps: [...]
            Replace Deployment YAML with Rollout YAML
            (same apiVersion except argoproj.io/v1alpha1)
Q5
What are canary "steps" in Argo Rollouts?
Show Answer
Answer

Gradual weight increases: setWeight: 20 then pause: {duration: "5m"}, then setWeight: 50, etc. Each step increases canary traffic percentage. Pause duration lets metrics stabilize before next step.

Explanation

Canary steps are the heart of progressive delivery. Each step is EITHER a setWeight (traffic percentage for canary pods) or a pause (wait for a duration). You can also add an analysis step to run metric probes. The steps array is ORDERED — they execute top to bottom.

CAPA Math: With replicas: 10 and setWeight: 20, you get 2 canary pods (20% × 10 = 2) and 8 stable pods. Argo ROUNDS DOWN fractional pods. Without a traffic manager: traffic is split by pod count ratio (Service randomly picks pods — roughly 20% hit canary). With a traffic manager (Istio/NGINX): traffic is split at the ingress/mesh level for precise percentages. The exam focuses on the pod-count-ratio model (simpler, no extra setup).

🔍 CANARY STEP SEQUENCE
Step 1: setWeight: 10  →  1 canary pod,  9 stable (10% traffic)
Step 2: pause: 2m      →  WAIT  (metrics stabilize)
Step 3: setWeight: 50  →  5 canary,      5 stable (50% traffic)
Step 4: pause: 10m     →  WAIT  (longer observation)
Step 5: (no step)      →  Implicit 100% — canary becomes new stable
Replicas=10 → each 10% = 1 pod (10×0.10). 25%→2 pods (round down)
Q6
What does argo rollouts promote do?
Show Answer
Answer

Skips remaining pause durations and immediately promotes to the next step. Use --full to skip ALL remaining steps and go straight to 100% stable.

Explanation

argo rollouts promote is the manual override for pause durations. During a canary, when a pause: {duration: "1h"} step is active, the Rollout WAITS. If you're confident the canary is healthy and don't want to wait the full hour, you run promote to skip the remaining pause and advance to the next step immediately.

promote advances ONE step. promote --full skips ALL remaining pause steps and promotes directly to 100% (the canary becomes the new stable ReplicaSet). Use promote when: (a) your monitoring shows green across the board, (b) you need to accelerate a critical hotfix deployment, (c) you're in a maintenance window that's closing. CAPA will test: "How do you skip a pause?" → argo rollouts promote <name>.

🔍 PROMOTE vs PROMOTE --FULL
Canary: [10%]──pause──▶[50%]──pause──▶[100%]
           │               │
    promote skips      promote skips
    THIS pause         THIS pause

promote --full: skips ALL pauses → straight to 100%
Equivalent to: "I'm confident, deploy fully NOW"
Q7
What's the purpose of a prePromotionAnalysis?
Show Answer
Answer

Runs analysis BEFORE any traffic shifts to canary. If it fails, the rollout never starts. Use for smoke tests: "does the new version even boot?"

Explanation

prePromotionAnalysis is a SAFETY NET that runs BEFORE any user traffic reaches the canary. Think of it as a "smoke test" for your deployment. Common use cases:

(1) Boot check: "Do the canary pods start and pass readiness probes?" — A web metric hitting /health on the canary pod. (2) DB connectivity: "Can the new version connect to the database?" — A K8s Job running a quick query. (3) Dependency check: "Is Redis/Elasticsearch reachable from the new pods?" — A script run as a Job.

prePromotionAnalysis vs regular analysis: pre runs BEFORE traffic shifts (gatekeeper). Regular analysis runs DURING traffic shifts (observer). If prePromotionAnalysis fails, the canary pods are NEVER exposed to users — the rollout is cancelled before it starts. This is the safest deployment pattern and highly recommended for production.

🔍 PRE vs REGULAR ANALYSIS
prePromotionAnalysis:
  Canary pods created → Run smoke tests → PASS? → Traffic starts
                                            FAIL? → Rollout cancelled

Regular analysis (during canary steps):
  Traffic flowing → Run metrics → PASS? → Continue to next step
                                  FAIL? → Auto-rollback to stable

prePromotion = "Does it boot?" | Regular = "Is it healthy under load?"
Q8
How do you watch a rollout's progress in real-time?
Show Answer
Answer

argo rollouts get rollout <name> --watch -n <ns>. Shows canary weight, step progress, analysis status. Also: kubectl argo rollouts dashboard for web UI.

Explanation

CLI: argo rollouts get rollout <name> --watch -n <ns> shows a real-time status dashboard with: canary weight percentage, current step index, pause duration remaining, stable/canary ReplicaSet names and pod counts, and analysis run status. This is your go-to command during deployments.

Dashboard (Web UI): kubectl argo rollouts dashboard starts a local web server (default port 3100). The dashboard shows: visual canary progress bar, traffic split pie chart, ReplicaSet pod visualization, and analysis run results. It's excellent for demonstrating deployments but for CAPA, focus on the CLI — that's what the exam terminal provides.

Additional monitoring: kubectl get replicasets -l app=jobpost shows both stable and canary RS. kubectl describe rollout <name> shows the full status including conditions and events.

🔍 MONITORING COMMANDS
argo rollouts get rollout jobpost --watch -n anihpj
  Status:  ●●●○○○○○○○  Progressing  (Canary 30%)
  Step:    2/4  (pause: 3m remaining)
  Stable:  jobpost-abc123  (7 pods)
  Canary:  jobpost-def456  (3 pods)
  Analysis: canary-check → Running (2/10 measurements)
Q9
What's the difference between Experiment and Rollout?
Show Answer
Answer

Experiment runs ANALYSIS ONLY — no user traffic. Rollout manages actual deployment + traffic + analysis. Experiment compares two versions side-by-side; Rollout gradually replaces one with another.

Explanation

An Experiment is a standalone CRD for A/B testing and analysis WITHOUT affecting production traffic. It creates two or more "template" ReplicaSets, runs them side-by-side for a specified duration, collects metrics via AnalysisTemplate, and reports results. No traffic routing, no Service manipulation. Use when: you want to compare v1 vs v2 performance under identical synthetic load before deciding which to deploy.

A Rollout is the FULL progressive delivery controller — it manages production traffic, ReplicaSet lifecycle, Service updates, and analysis. It gradually replaces the old version with the new one. Use when: you're actually deploying to production.

CAPA distinction: Experiment = "Let's TEST v2 against v1 in a sandbox." Rollout = "Let's DEPLOY v2 to replace v1 in production." Experiments are optional and less commonly tested; Rollouts are core CAPA material.

🔍 EXPERIMENT vs ROLLOUT
EXPERIMENT:                    ROLLOUT:
[v1 pods] [v2 pods]            Production Users
    │          │                     │
    └────┬─────┘              ┌──────┴──────┐
         ▼                    ▼              ▼
    Analysis Only        Stable(v1)90%  Canary(v2)10%
    No user traffic          │              │
    "Just testing"           └─── ANALYSIS ──┘
                                 (real traffic)
Q10
What happens when you run argo rollouts abort during a canary?
Show Answer
Answer

Immediately reverts ALL traffic to the stable version and scales down the canary pods. Equivalent to undoing everything the canary has done.

Explanation

argo rollouts abort is the EMERGENCY STOP button. When you run it during an active canary:

1. Traffic reversion: The stable Service immediately points back to the stable ReplicaSet (100% traffic to v1). Any canary Service traffic weighting is reset.

2. Canary cleanup: The canary ReplicaSet is scaled down to zero pods.

3. Status update: The Rollout's status changes to "Degraded" with a message indicating it was aborted.

When to use: Metrics are failing (error rate spike), you see application errors in logs, a critical bug is discovered mid-deployment, or the AnalysisTemplate isn't configured but you know something is wrong. Abort vs Undo: Abort stops an IN-PROGRESS canary. Undo reverts an ALREADY-PROMOTED rollout to the previous version. Abort during canary; Undo after full promotion.

🔍 ABORT vs UNDO — WHEN TO USE
ABORT (during canary):          UNDO (after promotion):
Canary 10% active               v2 fully deployed (100%)
    │                                │
    ▼                                ▼
abort → 100% traffic to v1     undo → reverts to v1
canary pods → scaled to 0      creates new RS with v1 spec

Key: Abort = "STOP!" during deployment | Undo = "Go back" after deployment

Chapter 15: Argo Rollouts — Installation & Core Concepts

Argo Rollouts is a Kubernetes controller and CRD that replaces the standard Deployment resource with progressive delivery capabilities. This chapter covers installation, the Rollout CRD anatomy, and how to convert existing Deployments.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🎯 CAPA 18%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the Argo Rollouts controller and how it extends Kubernetes
  • ✅ Install Argo Rollouts and the kubectl plugin
  • ✅ Master every field of the Rollout CRD
  • ✅ Convert existing Deployments to Rollouts with one command
ROLLOUT CONTROLLER — WHAT IT MANAGES
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Rollout Controller                      │
│                         │                                │
│         ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐               │
│         ▼               ▼               ▼               │
│  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐        │
│  │ Stable RS  │  │ Canary RS  │  │ Analysis   │        │
│  │ (v1, 9pods)│  │ (v2, 1pod) │  │ Prometheus │        │
│  └─────┬──────┘  └─────┬──────┘  └─────┬──────┘        │
│        │               │               │                │
│  ┌─────┴──────┐  ┌─────┴──────┐        │                │
│  │Stable Svc  │  │Canary Svc  │        │                │
│  │(90% traff) │  │(10% traff) │        │                │

│        │               │               │                │

│                ▼                       ▼                │
│          Traffic Split          Metric Validation       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 15
  • Service selector must match pod labels: The Rollout's pod template labels MUST match the Service selector. If they don't, traffic won't reach pods. The Rollout controller manages this automatically — don't manually edit the Service.
  • Blue-Green activeService: This Service ALWAYS points to the live version. The Rollout swaps which ReplicaSet it points to during promotion. The previewService lets you test before switching.
  • Missing AnalysisTemplate: If you reference an AnalysisTemplate in canary steps that doesn't exist, the canary gets stuck waiting forever. Verify the template name and namespace match exactly.

15.1 What is Argo Rollouts?

Argo Rollouts is a drop-in replacement for Kubernetes Deployments. It consists of:

🎮

Rollout Controller

A Kubernetes controller that watches Rollout CRDs and manages the progressive delivery process — creating ReplicaSets, scaling pods, and updating Services.

📋

Rollout CRD

A new Kubernetes resource kind that looks exactly like a Deployment but adds strategy: {blueGreen|canary}. Same pod template, same selector, same replicas.

🔌

kubectl Plugin

Extends kubectl with rollout-specific commands: kubectl argo rollouts get/list/promote/abort/undo. Plus a rich dashboard UI.

How Argo Rollouts Fits in the Argo Ecosystem
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ARGO ROLLOUTS — The Delivery Controller                     │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐              │
│  │ Argo     │───▶│ Argo     │───▶│ Argo     │              │
│  │ Workflows│    │ CD       │    │ Rollouts │              │
│  │ (CI)     │    │ (GitOps) │    │ (Deploy) │              │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘              │
│       │               │               │                      │
│       ▼               ▼               ▼                      │
│  Build & Push    Sync from     Progressive Delivery          │
│  Docker Image    Git to K8s    Blue-Green / Canary           │
│                                                              │
│  anihpj FLOW:                                                │
│  Code Push → Workflows CI → New Image → CD Syncs →          │
│  Rollouts deploys (canary 10%→100%) with metrics!           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

15.2 Installing Argo Rollouts

1
Create namespace: kubectl create namespace argo-rollouts
2
Apply install manifest: kubectl apply -n argo-rollouts -f https://github.com/argoproj/argo-rollouts/releases/latest/download/install.yaml
3
Install kubectl plugin: brew install argo-rollouts (macOS) or download binary
4
Verify: kubectl get pods -n argo-rollouts and kubectl argo rollouts version
Terminal — Full Installation
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace argo-rollouts

# Step 2: Install controller
kubectl apply -n argo-rollouts -f \
  https://github.com/argoproj/argo-rollouts/releases/latest/download/install.yaml

# Step 3: Wait for controller
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n argo-rollouts --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -n argo-rollouts
# Expected:
# NAME                              READY  STATUS
# argo-rollouts-...                 1/1    Running

# Step 4: Install kubectl plugin (macOS)
brew install argo-rollouts

# Linux:
curl -LO https://github.com/argoproj/argo-rollouts/releases/latest/download/kubectl-argo-rollouts-linux-amd64
chmod +x kubectl-argo-rollouts-linux-amd64
sudo mv kubectl-argo-rollouts-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/kubectl-argo-rollouts

# Step 5: Verify
kubectl argo rollouts version
# Expected: kubectl-argo-rollouts: v1.x.x
⚠️ Namespace Alert!

Argo Rollouts uses argo-rollouts. Argo Workflows uses argo. Argo CD uses argocd. Three different namespaces for three different tools. On CAPA: kubectl get pods -n argo-rollouts to verify rollouts are running!

🧠 Deep Dive: What the Install Manifest Actually Creates

The install.yaml creates more than just a Deployment — it sets up the complete Argo Rollouts machinery:

  • CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs): Registers Rollout, AnalysisRun, AnalysisTemplate, ClusterAnalysisTemplate, and Experiment with the K8s API. Without these, kubectl apply -f rollout.yaml would fail with "no matches for kind Rollout."
  • ServiceAccount + ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding: Gives the controller permissions to manage ReplicaSets, Services, and watch AnalysisRuns across all namespaces.
  • Deployment: Runs the controller itself — a single replica by default (scale for HA).
  • Service: Exposes controller metrics on port 8090 for Prometheus scraping.
  • MutatingWebhook: Automatically injects the argo-rollouts sidecar into Rollout pods for metric collection during analysis.

15.3 The Rollout CRD — Deep Dive

The Rollout CRD looks almost identical to a Deployment — same replicas, selector, and template. The magic is in the strategy field:

🔍 Anatomy of an Argo Rollout

📋 Kind/VersionapiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1, kind: Rollout — This is the only difference from a Deployment (apps/v1 → argoproj.io/v1alpha1, Deployment → Rollout).
🔢 Replicasreplicas: 5 — Same as Deployment. Total number of pods across both stable and canary.
🏷️ Selectorselector.matchLabels.app: anihpj — Same as Deployment. Identifies which pods belong to this Rollout.
📦 Templatetemplate.spec.containers[0].image: anihpj:v2 — Same as Deployment. The pod specification.
🎯 StrategyTHE ARGO MAGIC! strategy.canary.steps or strategy.blueGreen. This field doesn't exist in standard Deployments — it's what enables progressive delivery.
Complete Rollout YAML — Canary Strategy for anihpj
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: anihpj-rollout
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.example.com/anihpj:v2.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi}
          limits: {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 10
      - pause: {duration: 30s}
      - setWeight: 25
      - pause: {duration: 2m}
      - setWeight: 50
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 100
Blue-Green Strategy Variant
  strategy:
    blueGreen:
      activeService: anihpj-active      # Service receiving prod traffic
      previewService: anihpj-preview    # Service for testing Green
      autoPromotionEnabled: false       # Require manual approval
      prePromotionAnalysis:             # Run before switching traffic
        templates:
        - templateName: smoke-test
      postPromotionAnalysis:            # Run after switching
        templates:
        - templateName: health-check

15.4 Converting Deployments to Rollouts

Argo provides a one-command conversion that transforms any existing Deployment into a Rollout:

Convert Deployment to Rollout
# Convert existing Deployment to Rollout
kubectl argo rollouts convert deploy/anihpj -n anihpj-prod

# This command:
# 1. Reads the existing Deployment
# 2. Changes kind: Deployment → kind: Rollout
# 3. Changes apiVersion: apps/v1 → argoproj.io/v1alpha1
# 4. Adds a default canary strategy
# 5. Applies the new Rollout
# 6. Scales down the old Deployment to 0

# Verify the conversion:
kubectl get rollouts -n anihpj-prod
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj -n anihpj-prod

# If you need to revert:
kubectl argo rollouts undo rollout/anihpj -n anihpj-prod
⚠️ What Changes and What Doesn't
  • Changes: kind, apiVersion, adds strategy field
  • Stays the same: replicas, selector, template, metadata, all pod specs
  • IMPORTANT: The old Deployment is NOT deleted — it's scaled to 0 replicas. You can always switch back.
  • Service compatibility: Existing Services continue to work because the pod labels don't change.
⚠️ Common Rollout Gotchas — Read Before Production!
  • activeService MUST exist before blue-green: Argo doesn't create Services for you. Create anihpj-active and anihpj-preview Services BEFORE deploying the Rollout, or it will error.
  • setWeight needs enough replicas: With 2 replicas and setWeight: 10, you get 0 canary pods (2 × 10% = 0.2 → rounds to 0). Always have enough replicas for meaningful canary steps.
  • canaryService + stableService are optional: If you don't specify them, Argo modifies the existing Service's selector. If you DO specify them, Argo creates/manages those specific Services.
  • AnalysisTemplate can time out: If Prometheus is unreachable, the analysis runs indefinitely. Set up proper monitoring before relying on metric analysis.
  • Rollouts don't work with HPA by default: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler may conflict with the Rollout controller over replica counts. Use Argo's built-in scaling instead.

15.X Traffic Management — Controlling the Flow

Argo Rollouts integrates with ingress controllers and service meshes to control traffic splitting during canary deployments. The Rollout doesn't directly route traffic — it tells the ingress/mesh how to split it.

ProviderTypeTraffic ControlCAPA Note
NGINXIngressCanary-by-header or canary-by-weight annotationsMost common
AWS ALBIngressWeighted target groups via ALB Ingress ControllerEKS users
IstioService MeshVirtualService + DestinationRule weight splittingAdvanced
SMIService MeshTrafficSplit CRD (vendor-neutral API)Standard
TraefikIngressTraefikService weighted round-robinAlternative
Without Traffic Manager (default behavior)

If no traffic manager is configured, Argo Rollouts uses pod count ratio for canary: with 10 replicas and setWeight: 20, it creates 2 canary pods and 8 stable pods. Traffic is split by the Service's random pod selection — roughly 20% goes to canary. This is the simplest setup and what CAPA focuses on.

15.Y HPA Support — Autoscaling with Rollouts

Argo Rollouts works with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA). When HPA scales pods, the Rollout controller respects those changes. Key considerations:

  • HPA targets the Rollout, not individual ReplicaSets — the HPA references the Rollout's scaleTargetRef.
  • During canary: HPA scales TOTAL pods (stable + canary). The canary percentage determines the split of the HPA-scaled count.
  • CAPA gotcha: If HPA scales to 20 pods during a 10% canary, you get 2 canary pods and 18 stable pods — NOT 10% of the original count. HPA overrides replicas.
  • VPA support: Vertical Pod Autoscaler also supported for resource optimization during rollouts.

Q2
What are the four required fields in every Rollout spec?

Q4
How does the Rollout controller know which Service to update?
Show Answer
Answer

The spec.selector.matchLabels must match the Service's selector AND the pod template labels. The controller manages TWO ReplicaSets (stable + canary) and updates the Service endpoints.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. The spec.selector.matchLabels must match the Service's selector AND the pod template labels. The controller manages TWO ReplicaSets (stable + canary) and updates the Service endpoints. Q5
What's the difference between a Service pointing to stable vs canary?
Show Answer
Answer

The Rollout creates a stable Service pointing to the stable ReplicaSet. During canary, the canary Service splits traffic based on weight. At full promotion, the stable Service updates to the new version.

Explanation

A Service provides a STABLE network identity for a set of pods. Pods come and go (IPs change), but the Service IP stays constant. The Service uses label selectors to find pods: if a pod has app: jobpost and the Service selector is app: jobpost, traffic flows to that pod. Argo Rollouts needs TWO Services: an activeService (always points to the live version) and a previewService (points to the new version during Blue-Green before traffic switches). This two-Service pattern is Argo Rollouts-specific.

🔍 CANARY DEPLOYMENT
Stable v1 (90%) ──▶ Users
Canary v2 (10%) ──▶ Users
Steps: 10%→pause→50%→pause→100%
Analysis at each step: Fail → Auto Rollback

Answer

Set strategy.blueGreen: {activeService: svc-name, previewService: svc-preview, autoPromotionEnabled: true/false}. The previewService lets you test the new version before switching active.

Can a Rollout reference pods from multiple clusters?

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 16
  • Rollout vs Argo CD sync order: Argo CD should sync the Rollout CRD, THEN the Rollout controller starts the canary/blue-green. These are sequential — if Argo CD syncs and the controller hasn't started, the Rollout appears stuck.
  • :latest tag danger: Never use :latest tag in a Rollout. The controller needs SPECIFIC tags to differentiate stable from canary ReplicaSets. :latest = ambiguous version tracking.
  • Undo after promotion: argo rollouts undo works even after full promotion. It reverts to the PREVIOUS ReplicaSet spec, not the original one.

16.1 Blue-Green Deployment for anihpj

For major anihpj releases (e.g., Django 4→5 upgrade, database schema changes), blue-green provides the safest deployment with instant rollback. The key insight: both versions run simultaneously, so rolling back is as fast as changing a label:

Rollback Speed — Why Blue-Green Wins for Critical Deployments
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ROLLBACK SPEED COMPARISON                                   │
│                                                              │
│  STANDARD DEPLOYMENT ROLLBACK:                               │
│  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                │
│  │ Detect   │──▶│ kubectl  │──▶│ Recreate │   ⏱️ 2-5 min   │
│  │ Problem  │   │ rollout  │   │ Old Pods │                │
│  │          │   │ undo     │   │          │                │
│  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘                │
│                                                              │
│  ARGO BLUE-GREEN ROLLBACK:                                   │
│  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                                │
│  │ Detect   │──▶│ Swap     │   ⏱️ ~1 second!               │
│  │ Problem  │   │ Selector │                                │
│  │          │   │ Label    │   Old pods STILL RUNNING!      │
│  └──────────┘   └──────────┘                                │
│                                                              │
│  ARGO CANARY ROLLBACK:                                       │
│  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                │
│  │ Detect   │──▶│ Scale    │──▶│ Shift    │   ⏱️ 30s-1min  │
│  │ Problem  │   │ Canary→0 │   │ Weight→0 │                │
│  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘                │
│                                                              │
│  anihpj RECOMMENDATION:                                      │
│  • DB migrations → Blue-Green (instant rollback if needed)  │
│  • New features → Canary (gradual, lower resource cost)     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
anihpj Blue-Green — Step by Step
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  anihpj BLUE-GREEN WORKFLOW                                  │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Deploy Green:                                      │   │
│  │    kubectl apply -f anihpj-rollout.yaml              │   │
│  │    (Green pods start alongside Blue)                  │   │
│  │                                                       │   │
│  │ 2. Verify Green:                                      │   │
│  │    curl http://anihpj-preview.example.com/health     │   │
│  │    → Smoke tests pass ✅                              │   │
│  │                                                       │   │
│  │ 3. Promote:                                           │   │
│  │    kubectl argo rollouts promote anihpj-rollout       │   │
│  │    → Traffic switches Blue→Green (~1 second)         │   │
│  │                                                       │   │
│  │ 4. Monitor:                                           │   │
│  │    kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj --watch   │   │
│  │    → Check: Healthy, no errors                        │   │
│  │                                                       │   │
│  │ 5. Rollback (if needed):                              │   │
│  │    kubectl argo rollouts undo anihpj-rollout          │   │
│  │    → Traffic switches Green→Blue (~1 second)         │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
anihpj Blue-Green Rollout
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: anihpj-bluegreen
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.example.com/anihpj:v2.0
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
  strategy:
    blueGreen:
      activeService: anihpj-active
      previewService: anihpj-preview
      autoPromotionEnabled: false
      prePromotionAnalysis:
        templates:
        - templateName: smoke-test-anihpj
      postPromotionAnalysis:
        templates:
        - templateName: health-check-anihpj

16.2 Canary Deployment for anihpj

For incremental feature rollouts (new jobpost search, UI redesign), canary lets you expose the change gradually:

anihpj Canary Rollout — Feature Gradual Release
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: anihpj-canary
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  replicas: 10                    # 10 total pods (stable + canary)
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.example.com/anihpj:v2.1-new-search
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: anihpj-canary       # Optional: dedicated canary Service
      stableService: anihpj-stable       # Optional: dedicated stable Service
      steps:
      - setWeight: 10                    # 10% = 1 pod canary, 9 pods stable
      - pause: {duration: 1m}            # Let metrics accumulate
      - setWeight: 25                    # 25% = ~3 pods canary
      - pause: {duration: 5m}            # Longer observation
      - setWeight: 50                    # 50% = 5 pods canary
      - pause: {duration: 10m}           # Extended monitoring
      - setWeight: 100                   # Full rollout!
🎯 CAPA Canary Math

With replicas: 10 and setWeight: 10, you get 1 canary pod (10% × 10 replicas = 1). Argo rounds down fractional pods. At 25%, you get 2 canary pods (25% × 10 = 2.5 → 2). The remaining pods serve the stable version. This calculation is tested on CAPA!

16.3 Metric-Driven Promotion with Analysis

Instead of blind time-based pauses, use metric analysis to let data decide whether to continue or roll back:

Metric-Driven Canary — Auto-Promote or Auto-Rollback
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  METRIC-DRIVEN CANARY for anihpj                             │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐              │
│  │ Canary   │───▶│ Analysis │───▶│ Decide   │              │
│  │ 10% v2   │    │ Run      │    │          │              │
│  └──────────┘    └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘              │
│                       │               │                      │
│             ┌─────────┴─────────┐     │                      │
│             │                   │     │                      │
│             ▼                   ▼     ▼                      │
│       ┌──────────┐       ┌──────────┐                       │
│       │ ✅ PASS  │       │ ❌ FAIL  │                       │
│       │ Continue │       │ Rollback │                       │
│       │ to 25%   │       │ to v1    │                       │
│       └──────────┘       └──────────┘                       │
│                                                              │
│  AnalysisTemplate checks every 30s for 5 minutes:           │
│  ✅ error_rate < 1%    → GREEN (continue)                   │
│  ❌ error_rate >= 5%   → RED (auto-rollback)               │
│  ⚠️ 1% ≤ error < 5%   → AMBER (keep checking)             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 AnalysisTemplate

A cluster-scoped resource that defines WHAT metrics to check, HOW often, and for HOW long. Reusable across multiple Rollouts. Contains: metric name, provider (Prometheus/Datadog/NewRelic), query, success/failure conditions.

📊 Prometheus Query

The provider.prometheus.query fetches real-time metrics from your Prometheus server. For anihpj, you'd query: error rate by version, p95 latency, CPU usage per pod, and DB query duration. The query result is compared against successCondition and failureCondition.

✅ Auto-Promote

When ALL metrics in the AnalysisTemplate pass their successCondition, Argo automatically advances to the next canary step. No human needed. This is the dream: code goes to production automatically, guarded by metrics.

🛑 Auto-Rollback

When ANY metric triggers failureCondition, Argo immediately scales down canary pods and shifts 100% traffic back to stable. The rollout enters "Degraded" state. You get alerted via notifications (Chapter 6).

AnalysisTemplate for anihpj Error Rate
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: error-rate-check
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  metrics:
  - name: error-rate
    interval: 30s                   # Check every 30 seconds
    count: 10                       # Run 10 times = 5 minutes total
    successCondition: result < 0.01 # Less than 1% errors = SUCCESS
    failureCondition: result >= 0.05 # 5% or more errors = FAILURE
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: |
          sum(rate(http_errors_total{
            app="anihpj",
            version="{{args.version}}"
          }[1m])) /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{
            app="anihpj",
            version="{{args.version}}"
          }[1m]))

  - name: p95-latency
    interval: 30s
    count: 10
    successCondition: result < 0.5  # Less than 500ms p95
    failureCondition: result >= 2.0 # More than 2 seconds p95
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{
              app="anihpj",
              version="{{args.version}}"
            }[1m])) by (le))

16.4 Traffic Routing with Service Meshes

For precise traffic splitting (not just pod count), Argo Rollouts integrates with service meshes and ingress controllers:

ProviderTraffic Split MechanismBest For
IstioVirtualService + DestinationRule — splits at the sidecar proxy levelZero-trust, mTLS, complex routing rules
LinkerdSMI TrafficSplit — lightweight, fast proxySimple, low-overhead traffic splitting
NGINX IngressCanary annotations on Ingress — nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true" + canary-weight: "10"Simple setup, no service mesh needed
AWS ALBALB Ingress Controller with forward actions and weighted target groupsAWS-native, EKS environments
SMITrafficSplit CRD — vendor-neutral API standardPortability across service meshes
💡 For anihpj (Beginner-Friendly)

Start with NGINX Ingress — no service mesh needed, simple annotations. The Rollout YAML adds trafficRouting.nginx configuration. As you grow, migrate to Istio or Linkerd for richer observability.

16.5 Monitoring Rollouts

Argo Rollouts provides a rich dashboard and CLI tools for monitoring deployments in real time:

Monitoring Commands
# Watch rollout progress in real time (like argo watch for workflows)
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj --watch -n anihpj-prod

# See detailed status
kubectl argo rollouts status anihpj -n anihpj-prod

# View rollout history
kubectl argo rollouts history anihpj -n anihpj-prod

# Launch the web dashboard (local browser)
kubectl argo rollouts dashboard
# Opens http://localhost:3100 — shows ALL rollouts visually!

# Promote a paused canary/blue-green
kubectl argo rollouts promote anihpj -n anihpj-prod

# Abort a rollout (immediate rollback)
kubectl argo rollouts abort anihpj -n anihpj-prod

# Roll back to previous version
kubectl argo rollouts undo anihpj -n anihpj-prod

# Restart all pods (same version, fresh pods)
kubectl argo rollouts restart anihpj -n anihpj-prod

How do you integrate Argo CD with Argo Rollouts for anihpj?

Answer

Define the Rollout YAML in the GitOps repo. Argo CD syncs the Rollout resource. The Rollout controller then performs the progressive delivery. Argo CD sees the Rollout as "Progressing" until fully promoted.

🎯 CAPA Practice Drill — Part 4 (15 min)

⏱️ Time Target: 15 minutes | 📋 5 Hands-On Tasks
Scenario: anihpj Canary Deployment

You need to deploy a new jobpost search feature (v2.1) to production using canary deployment. The rollout should start at 10%, pause for 1 minute, go to 25%, pause for 5 minutes, then go to 100%.

  1. Create a Rollout named anihpj-canary with 5 replicas, the anihpj:v2.1 image, and the canary steps described above.
  2. Deploy it and watch the rollout progress. Check how many canary pods are running at 10% weight.
  3. During the 25% pause, promote the rollout manually to skip the remaining pause.
  4. The rollout succeeded but the next day users report issues. Roll back to the previous version.
  5. Create an AnalysisTemplate for error rate checking that queries Prometheus every 30s for 3 minutes, succeeds if error rate < 1%, fails if ≥ 5%.
💡 Hint: Use setWeight and pause in the steps array. For task 3, use kubectl argo rollouts promote. For task 4, use kubectl argo rollouts undo. For task 5, use successCondition and failureCondition in the AnalysisTemplate metrics.
🔍 Click to Reveal Step-by-Step Solution
# TASK 1: Create canary Rollout
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: anihpj-canary
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.example.com/anihpj:v2.1
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 10
      - pause: {duration: 1m}
      - setWeight: 25
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 100
EOF

# TASK 2: Watch progress
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj-canary -n anihpj-prod --watch
# At 10% weight with 5 replicas: 5 × 10% = 0.5 → 1 canary pod (rounds up)

# TASK 3: Promote manually during 25% pause
kubectl argo rollouts promote anihpj-canary -n anihpj-prod
# This skips the remaining pause duration and moves to the next step

# TASK 4: Rollback
kubectl argo rollouts undo anihpj-canary -n anihpj-prod
# Reverts to the previous ReplicaSet (v2.0)

# TASK 5: Create AnalysisTemplate
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: error-rate-check
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  metrics:
  - name: error-rate
    interval: 30s
    count: 6              # 6 × 30s = 3 minutes
    successCondition: result < 0.01
    failureCondition: result >= 0.05
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: |
          sum(rate(http_errors_total{app="anihpj"}[1m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="anihpj"}[1m]))
EOF
✅ Verify Your Work
  • kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj-canary -n anihpj-prod — Shows Healthy status
  • kubectl get analysisruns -n anihpj-prod — Shows analysis completed
  • kubectl get replicasets -n anihpj-prod | grep anihpj — Shows both old and new ReplicaSets
  • kubectl argo rollouts dashboard — Open browser to see visual status

Chapter 17: Introduction to Event-Driven Automation

Argo Events is the trigger system for the Argo ecosystem. It listens for events from 20+ sources — GitHub pushes, S3 uploads, Kafka messages, cron schedules — and automatically triggers Argo Workflows in response. If Argo CD is "Git state → cluster" and Workflows is "YAML → pods", then Events is "something happened → do something".

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 17
  • EventBus is required: Argo Events won't work without an EventBus. If events aren't flowing, check kubectl get eventbus -n argo-events first. The EventBus runs NATS — if it's not Ready, nothing works.
  • Sensor RBAC: The Sensor's ServiceAccount needs permissions to create the resources it triggers (Workflows, HTTP calls). Missing RBAC = silent trigger failure with no obvious error.
  • Event deduplication: Sensors track processed event IDs. If the same event is re-delivered (NATS retry), the Sensor ignores it — preventing duplicate workflow triggers.

17.1 What is Argo Events?

Argo Events is an event-driven workflow automation framework for Kubernetes. It connects external event sources (GitHub, S3, Kafka, webhooks, calendars) to Argo Workflows. Think of it as the "glue" that makes things happen automatically:

Argo Events — The Trigger System
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ARGO EVENTS — "Something Happened → Do Something"           │
│                                                              │
│  EXTERNAL WORLD                     KUBERNETES CLUSTER        │
│  ──────────────                     ──────────────────        │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────┐                      ┌──────────────────────┐  │
│  │ 👨‍💻 GitHub│── push event ──────▶│ 🔔 Argo Events       │  │
│  │   Push   │                      │  Listens → Filters → │  │
│  └──────────┘                      │  Triggers Workflow   │  │
│                                    └──────────┬───────────┘  │
│  ┌──────────┐                                 │              │
│  │ ☁️ S3    │── file uploaded ───▶            ▼              │
│  │  Bucket  │                      ┌──────────────────────┐  │
│  └──────────┘                      │ 🔄 Argo Workflows    │  │
│                                    │  CI/CD, ETL, Backup  │  │
│  ┌──────────┐                      └──────────────────────┘  │
│  │ 🕐 Cron  │── 2 AM trigger ────▶                            │
│  │ Schedule │                                                │
│  └──────────┘                                                │
│                                                              │
│  KEY INSIGHT: Events decouples "what happened" from         │
│  "what to do about it". Change the trigger without           │
│  changing the workflow, and vice versa.                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧠 Beginner's Mental Model — "The Smart Doorbell"

Imagine your house has a doorbell. When someone presses it (EventSource), a signal travels through the wiring (EventBus) to a smart hub that checks who it is (Sensor with filters). If it's the delivery person, the hub unlocks the door (Trigger → Argo Workflow). If it's a stranger, it ignores them. Argo Events is that smart doorbell system for your cluster — it listens for specific things and only acts when conditions are right.

👂

20+ Event Sources

Webhooks, GitHub, S3, Kafka, SQS, NATS, Calendar, Slack, Stripe, and more. If it can send an event, Argo can listen.

🔗

Decoupled Architecture

EventSource (listen) → EventBus (transport) → Sensor (filter+trigger). Change any part independently.

🎯

Smart Filtering

Not all events are equal. Filter by data fields, context, or time. Only trigger on matching events.

17.2 Argo Events Architecture

The architecture has four components that form a pipeline: EventSource → EventBus → Sensor → Trigger:

1
EventSource — Listens for events from external systems. Defines WHAT to listen to (GitHub webhook, S3 bucket, Kafka topic). Each EventSource CRD creates a pod that maintains the connection.
2
EventBus — Internal event transport layer. Uses NATS (lightweight, high-performance messaging). All EventSources publish events here; all Sensors subscribe from here.
3
Sensor — The brain. Defines WHICH events to react to (dependencies), HOW to filter them (data/context filters), and WHAT to do (triggers). A Sensor can listen to multiple EventSources.
4
Trigger — The action. Most commonly submits an Argo Workflow, but can also call HTTP endpoints, send Slack messages, invoke AWS Lambda, publish to Kafka, and more.
Argo Events — Full Architecture

🧠 Deep Dive: Why NATS for the EventBus?

NATS was chosen as the EventBus backend because it's: (1) Extremely lightweight — a single binary, ~20MB memory footprint, perfect for running alongside Argo components. (2) At-most-once delivery — events are fire-and-forget, not persisted (unlike Kafka). This is ideal because Argo Events doesn't need message persistence — if an event is lost, the external system (GitHub, S3) will resend it. (3) Subject-based routing — NATS subjects map directly to EventSource/Sensor names, making routing trivial. (4) High throughput — NATS can handle millions of messages per second on modest hardware.

Each namespace with Argo Events needs its own EventBus. The EventBus creates a NATS Deployment + Service. Sensors subscribe to subjects matching their EventSource dependencies; EventSources publish to subjects when events arrive.

17.3 Installing Argo Events

1
Create namespace: kubectl create namespace argo-events
2
Install controller + CRDs: kubectl apply -n argo-events -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-events/stable/manifests/install.yaml
3
Install EventBus (NATS): Apply an EventBus CRD — this creates the NATS pod
4
Verify: kubectl get pods -n argo-events — eventbus, controller, and eventsource/sensor pods
Terminal — Full Installation
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace argo-events

# Step 2: Install Argo Events (controller + CRDs)
kubectl apply -n argo-events -f \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-events/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Step 3: Create EventBus (NATS — required!)
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -n argo-events -f -
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: EventBus
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  nats:
    native:
      replicas: 1
EOF

# Step 4: Verify installation
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n argo-events --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -n argo-events
# Expected:
# NAME                                  READY  STATUS
# eventbus-default-...                  1/1    Running
# eventsource-controller-...            1/1    Running
# sensor-controller-...                 1/1    Running
⚠️ EventBus is REQUIRED!

Without an EventBus, EventSources can't deliver events and Sensors can't receive them. The EventBus is the internal messaging backbone. Always create it immediately after installing Argo Events. On CAPA: if events aren't flowing, check kubectl get eventbus -n argo-events!

⚠️ Namespace Alert #4!

Argo Events uses argo-events. Argo CD = argocd. Argo Workflows = argo. Argo Rollouts = argo-rollouts. Four tools, four namespaces. Know them for CAPA!

What is a Sensor's dependency group?
Show Answer
Answer

Events that must ALL arrive before the trigger fires (logical AND). Example: "webhook event AND S3 file uploaded" — both must occur. Use multiple dependency groups for OR logic.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. Events that must ALL arrive before the trigger fires (logical AND). Group 2 (OR):  [Webhook]

Q6
What's the difference between an AND dependency group and multiple groups?
Show Answer
Answer

One group with multiple deps = ALL must fire (AND). Multiple dependency groups = ANY group firing triggers the sensor (OR). Groups execute in parallel.

Explanation

Chapter 18: EventSources & Sensors

EventSources and Sensors are the two most important CRDs in Argo Events. EventSources listen — they connect to external systems. Sensors decide and act — they filter events and trigger workflows. This chapter covers all 20+ EventSource types, building your first webhook listener, and mastering Sensor configuration.

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 18
  • Calendar vs CronWorkflow: Calendar EventSource is MORE flexible (one schedule triggers multiple workflows via Sensor). But CronWorkflow is SIMPLER (single YAML). Use Calendar when you need to trigger multiple things from one schedule.
  • Webhook path collisions: Each webhook EventSource needs a unique endpoint path. Two EventSources on the same path will conflict.
  • GitHub webhook auto-registration: If the GitHub token has insufficient permissions, the EventSource deploys successfully but webhooks aren't created. Check Sensor logs for clues.

18.2 Creating Your First EventSource — Webhook

A webhook EventSource creates an HTTP endpoint that external services can POST events to. This is the most versatile type — any system that can make HTTP requests can trigger your workflows:

Webhook EventSource for anihpj CI
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: EventSource
metadata:
  name: anihpj-webhook
  namespace: argo-events
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  webhook:
    github-push:              # Event name (used by Sensor)
      port: "12000"           # Listening port
      endpoint: "/push"       # URL path → POST /push
      method: POST
    github-pr:                # Second event on same EventSource!
      port: "12000"
      endpoint: "/pr"
      method: POST

# After creating, expose with port-forward or Ingress:
# kubectl -n argo-events port-forward svc/anihpj-webhook-eventsource-svc 12000:12000
# Test: curl -X POST http://localhost:12000/push -d '{"ref":"refs/heads/main"}'
💡 Production Exposure

For production, expose the EventSource service via Ingress with TLS. The webhook URL would be https://events.anihpj.dev/push. Configure this URL in your GitHub repo Settings → Webhooks. GitHub will POST to this URL on every push event.

18.3 Sensor Deep Dive

The Sensor is where the intelligence lives. It defines which events to react to, how to filter them, and what to do:

🔍 Anatomy of a Sensor

📡 DependenciesWhich events? References EventSource + event name. Example: eventSourceName: anihpj-webhook, eventName: github-push. A Sensor can depend on MULTIPLE events — workflow triggers only when ALL or ANY dependencies are met.
🔍 FiltersWhich of those events? Data filters (check event payload fields) and context filters (check metadata like event time). Example: only trigger if body.ref == "refs/heads/main" — ignore pushes to other branches.
⚡ TriggersWhat to do? The action: submit an Argo Workflow, call an HTTP endpoint, send a Slack message, invoke AWS Lambda, publish to Kafka. Most common: Argo Workflow trigger — submits a workflow with parameters from the event.
🔗 Trigger TypesArgo Workflow (most common), HTTP, Kafka, AWS Lambda, Slack, NATS, OpenWhisk, Azure Event Hubs, Log, and custom triggers. For CAPA: know Argo Workflow and HTTP triggers.
Sensor — Filter GitHub Push + Trigger CI Workflow
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Sensor
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ci-sensor
  namespace: argo-events
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  dependencies:
  - name: github-push-dep
    eventSourceName: anihpj-webhook
    eventName: github-push
    filters:
      data:
      - path: body.ref              # Check the payload
        type: string
        comparator: "="
        value:
        - "refs/heads/main"         # ONLY main branch pushes!
  triggers:
  - template:
      name: ci-trigger
      conditions: "github-push-dep" # Trigger when this dependency matches
      argoWorkflow:
        operation: submit
        source:
          resource:
            apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
            kind: Workflow
            metadata:
              generateName: anihpj-ci-
              namespace: argo
            spec:
              entrypoint: ci-pipeline
              arguments:
                parameters:
                - name: git-commit
                  value: "placeholder"  # Will be overridden by parameterization
              templates:
              - name: ci-pipeline
                container:
                  image: alpine
                  command: [echo, "CI running for commit {{workflow.parameters.git-commit}}"]
        parameters:
        - src:
            dependencyName: github-push-dep
            dataKey: body.head_commit.id   # Extract commit SHA from event!
          dest: spec.arguments.parameters.0.value

18.4 Parameterization — Passing Event Data to Workflows

The most powerful feature of Sensors is parameterization — extracting data from the event payload and injecting it into the triggered workflow. This is how a GitHub push event's commit SHA becomes a workflow parameter:

Event Data → Workflow Parameters
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PARAMETERIZATION FLOW                                       │
│                                                              │
│  GitHub Push Event (JSON payload):                           │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ {                                                      │ │
│  │   "ref": "refs/heads/main",                            │ │
│  │   "head_commit": {                                     │ │
│  │     "id": "abc123def456",        ◀── We want this!     │ │
│  │     "message": "Fix jobpost search",                   │ │
│  │     "author": {"name": "Alice"}                        │ │
│  │   },                                                   │ │
│  │   "repository": {                                      │ │
│  │     "full_name": "team-anihpj/anihpj"                  │ │
│  │   }                                                    │ │
│  │ }                                                      │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                         │                                    │
│                         │ Sensor extracts via parameters:    │
│                         ▼                                    │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ parameters:                                            │ │
│  │   - src:                                               │ │
│  │       dependencyName: github-push-dep                  │ │
│  │       dataKey: body.head_commit.id  ◀── JSON path!     │ │
│  │     dest: spec.arguments.parameters.0.value            │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                         │                                    │
│                         ▼                                    │
│  Workflow receives: git-commit = "abc123def456"             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Multi-Parameter Extraction from Event
parameters:
# Extract commit SHA → workflow parameter "git-commit"
- src:
    dependencyName: github-push-dep
    dataKey: body.head_commit.id
  dest: spec.arguments.parameters.0.value

# Extract repository name → workflow parameter "repo"
- src:
    dependencyName: github-push-dep
    dataKey: body.repository.full_name
  dest: spec.arguments.parameters.1.value

# Extract author → workflow parameter "author"
- src:
    dependencyName: github-push-dep
    dataKey: body.head_commit.author.name
  dest: spec.arguments.parameters.2.value

# Template in the trigger:
# value: "placeholder" gets replaced with actual event data!
⚠️ Common Events Gotchas — Save Yourself Hours!
  • EventBus MUST exist: Without an EventBus CRD, EventSources can't deliver events and Sensors can't receive them. Always create it first: kubectl get eventbus -n argo-events.
  • Sensor conditions syntax: The conditions field in triggers uses the dependency NAME, not the event name. If your dependency is name: push-dep, your condition is conditions: push-dep.
  • parameterization dest path: The dest path navigates the trigger's YAML structure. spec.arguments.parameters.0.value targets the first parameter's value. Wrong path = silently broken parameterization.
  • Webhook needs exposure: EventSource pods are ClusterIP by default — not reachable from outside. Use Ingress or a LoadBalancer Service for GitHub/S3 to reach your webhook.
  • NATS is internal only: The EventBus NATS pod is NOT exposed externally. It's an internal pub/sub bus. External systems talk to EventSources, EventSources publish to NATS, Sensors subscribe from NATS.

18.X Trigger Types & Event Filters — The Full Picture

Sensors can trigger 12+ different action types beyond just Argo Workflows. They also support sophisticated event filtering before triggering:

⚙️
Argo Workflow

Submit Workflow/WorkflowTemplate. Most common trigger. Pass event data as parameters.

☸️
K8s Objects

Create/Update/Delete any K8s resource: ConfigMap, Deployment, Job, etc.

🌐
HTTP Request

Call any REST API. Use for webhooks, external service integration, Slack messages.

λ
AWS Lambda

Invoke Lambda functions directly from events. Serverless integration.

📨
Kafka/NATS

Publish messages to Kafka topics or NATS subjects.

💬
Slack

Post messages to Slack channels directly from Sensor triggers.

Event Filters (5 types): Expr Filter — boolean expression on event data (body.ref == "main"). Data Filter — path+comparator matching (path: body.action, comparator: "=", value: "opened"). Script Filter — Lua script for complex logic. Context Filter — filter by event context (source, type, subject). Time Filter — only trigger during specific time windows (cron syntax). Expr and Data filters are the most commonly used on CAPA.

How does a Sensor handle event deduplication?
