Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 19
  • Infinite CI loops: If the CI workflow commits back to the same Git repo, the commit triggers another CI run. Add an event filter to ignore commits from the CI bot user.
  • Parameter extraction path: Event data is nested JSON. dataKey: body.ref extracts ref from the body object. Wrong path = empty parameter = failed workflow.
  • Sensor trigger ordering: Multiple triggers in a Sensor execute SEQUENTIALLY by default. For parallel execution, use separate Sensors or the trigger policy field.

19.1 Auto-Deploy on Git Push — The Holy Grail

This is the pattern that ties everything together: push code → auto-deploy. When a developer pushes to the main branch, Argo Events triggers the CI workflow, which builds and pushes the image, updates the GitOps repo, and Argo CD deploys it:

✅ The Dream: Push-to-Deploy in Action
  • 10:00 AM — Alice pushes "Fix jobpost search pagination" to main branch
  • 10:00:05 — GitHub webhook fires → Argo Events Sensor receives push event
  • 10:00:06 — Sensor filters: branch == "main" ✅ → triggers CI Workflow
  • 10:02:00 — Workflow: Clone → Unit tests pass ✅ → Lint passes ✅
  • 10:05:00 — Workflow: Build Docker image → Push to registry
  • 10:05:30 — Workflow: Update GitOps repo with new image tag
  • 10:06:00 — Argo CD detects Git change → syncs to staging
  • 10:06:30 — Argo Rollouts: canary 10% → metrics OK → 100% deployed
  • 10:12:00 — Users see the fix. Alice didn't touch a server or run a command.
  • Total time: 12 minutes. Human involvement: ZERO.

Complete Push-to-Deploy YAMLs (EventSource + Sensor)
# ─── EventSource ───
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: EventSource
metadata:
  name: anihpj-github
  namespace: argo-events
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  github:                          # Native GitHub integration!
    push-event:
      owner: team-anihpj
      repository: anihpj
      events:
      - push                        # Listen for push events
      webhook:
        url: /github-webhook
        port: "12000"
      apiToken:
        name: github-token          # K8s Secret with GitHub token
        key: token
      webhookSecret:
        name: github-webhook-secret # Verify webhook signature
        key: secret
---
# ─── Sensor ───
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Sensor
metadata:
  name: anihpj-push-sensor
  namespace: argo-events
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  dependencies:
  - name: push-dep
    eventSourceName: anihpj-github
    eventName: push-event
    filters:
      data:
      - path: body.ref
        type: string
        comparator: "="
        value:
        - "refs/heads/main"         # Only main branch
  triggers:
  - template:
      name: ci-trigger
      conditions: push-dep
      argoWorkflow:
        operation: submit
        source:
          resource:
            apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
            kind: Workflow
            metadata:
              generateName: anihpj-ci-
              namespace: argo
            spec:
              entrypoint: ci
              templates:
              - name: ci
                container:
                  image: alpine
                  command: [echo, "Deploying commit {{workflow.parameters.commit}}"]
        parameters:
        - src:
            dependencyName: push-dep
            dataKey: body.head_commit.id
          dest: spec.arguments.parameters.0.value

When a business user uploads a CSV of job postings to an S3 bucket, Argo Events detects it and automatically triggers an ETL pipeline:

S3 EventSource for CSV Uploads
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: EventSource
metadata:
  name: anihpj-s3
  namespace: argo-events
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  s3:
    csv-upload:
      bucket:
        name: anihpj-data           # S3 bucket name
        key: jobs-import/           # Only watch this prefix
      events:
      - s3:ObjectCreated:*          # Trigger on new objects
      filter:
        prefix: "jobs-import/"
        suffix: ".csv"              # Only .csv files!
      region: us-east-1
      accessKey:
        name: aws-credentials       # K8s Secret
        key: accessKey
      secretKey:
        name: aws-credentials
        key: secretKey

19.3 Scheduled Maintenance with Calendar Events

The Calendar EventSource provides cron-like scheduling as an alternative to CronWorkflows. It's useful when you want to centralize all event handling through Argo Events rather than using separate CronWorkflow CRDs:

Calendar EventSource — Nightly Maintenance
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: EventSource
metadata:
  name: anihpj-schedules
  namespace: argo-events
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  calendar:
    nightly-backup:
      schedule: "0 2 * * *"          # Every day at 2 AM
      timezone: "America/New_York"
      interval: 24h
    weekly-report:
      schedule: "0 8 * * 1"          # Every Monday at 8 AM
      timezone: "America/New_York"
      interval: 168h                 # 7 days
    monthly-scan:
      schedule: "0 4 1 * *"          # 1st of month at 4 AM
      timezone: "America/New_York"
      interval: 720h                 # 30 days

# Each calendar event triggers a different Sensor + Workflow combo
💡 Calendar vs CronWorkflow

Use CronWorkflow when your schedule directly corresponds to one workflow. Use Calendar EventSource when you want to centralize scheduling in Argo Events, chain multiple actions from one schedule, or apply Sensor filtering to scheduled events. Both are valid — CAPA tests both concepts.

19.4 Kubernetes Resource Watch Automation

The Resource EventSource watches Kubernetes resources for create/update/delete events. This enables self-healing and auto-reaction patterns — when something changes in the cluster, automatically respond:

Resource EventSource — Watch JobPost Changes
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: EventSource
metadata:
  name: anihpj-resource-watch
  namespace: argo-events
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  resource:
    new-jobpost:
      namespace: anihpj-prod
      group: ""                     # Core API group
      version: v1
      resource: configmaps          # Watch ConfigMaps (or custom CRDs)
      filter:
        labels:
        - key: app
          operation: "=="
          value: anihpj
      eventTypes:
      - ADDED
      - MODIFIED

# Example use: When a ConfigMap with app=anihpj changes,
# trigger a workflow to validate the configuration and
# restart affected pods automatically.

Q8
What K8s RBAC does the Sensor pod need?
Show Answer
Answer

A ServiceAccount with Role to create and get Workflows in the target namespace. The Sensor's service account must be bound to this Role via RoleBinding.

Explanation

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) in Kubernetes has 4 components: Role/ClusterRole (defines permissions — 'CAN get pods'), RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding (assigns role to users/groups — 'Alice GETS pod-reader role'), Subject (User, Group, or ServiceAccount), and Verbs (get, list, create, update, delete, watch). Argo uses ServiceAccounts: the Application Controller, Repo Server, and API Server each have ServiceAccounts with specific permissions. On CAPA, you need to know which ServiceAccount needs which permissions.

🔍 RBAC CHAIN
Subject ──▶ Role ──▶ RoleBinding
(User/SA)   (verbs)  (assignment)
'Alice CAN get pods in namespace anihpj'

🎯 CAPA Practice Drill — Part 5 (15 min)

⏱️ Time Target: 15 minutes | 📋 5 Hands-On Tasks
Scenario: anihpj Event-Driven CI

You need to set up event-driven automation so that every push to GitHub's main branch automatically triggers the anihpj CI pipeline.

  1. Create a webhook EventSource named anihpj-webhook in namespace argo-events that listens on port 12000 at /push.
  2. Create a Sensor that depends on this EventSource and filters for pushes to the main branch only (check body.ref == "refs/heads/main").
  3. Add an Argo Workflow trigger to the Sensor that submits a simple workflow (any entrypoint).
  4. Parameterize the trigger to extract the commit SHA (body.head_commit.id) and pass it as a workflow parameter named commit.
  5. Test the webhook with curl: curl -X POST -d '{"ref":"refs/heads/main","head_commit":{"id":"abc123"}}' http://localhost:12000/push
💡 Hint: EventSource uses webhook: with port and endpoint. Sensor uses filters.data with path: body.ref. Parameterization uses src.dependencyName + dataKey and dest: spec.arguments.parameters.0.value.
🔍 Click to Reveal Step-by-Step Solution
# TASK 1: Create webhook EventSource
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -n argo-events -f -
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: EventSource
metadata:
  name: anihpj-webhook
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  webhook:
    push:
      port: "12000"
      endpoint: "/push"
      method: POST
EOF

# TASK 2: Create Sensor with filter
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -n argo-events -f -
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Sensor
metadata:
  name: anihpj-sensor
spec:
  eventBusName: default
  dependencies:
  - name: push-dep
    eventSourceName: anihpj-webhook
    eventName: push
    filters:
      data:
      - path: body.ref
        type: string
        comparator: "="
        value: ["refs/heads/main"]
  triggers:
  - template:
      name: ci-trigger
      conditions: push-dep
      argoWorkflow:
        operation: submit
        source:
          resource:
            apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
            kind: Workflow
            metadata:
              generateName: ci-
              namespace: argo
            spec:
              entrypoint: ci
              arguments:
                parameters:
                - name: commit
                  value: "placeholder"
              templates:
              - name: ci
                container:
                  image: alpine
                  command: [echo, "CI {{workflow.parameters.commit}}"]
        # TASK 4: Parameterization
        parameters:
        - src:
            dependencyName: push-dep
            dataKey: body.head_commit.id
          dest: spec.arguments.parameters.0.value
EOF

# TASK 5: Test
kubectl -n argo-events port-forward svc/anihpj-webhook-eventsource-svc 12000:12000 &
curl -X POST http://localhost:12000/push \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"ref":"refs/heads/main","head_commit":{"id":"abc123"}}'

# Verify:
argo list -n argo  # Should show ci- workflow submitted!
✅ Verify Your Work
  • kubectl get eventsource -n argo-events — anihpj-webhook exists
  • kubectl get sensor -n argo-events — anihpj-sensor exists
  • kubectl describe sensor anihpj-sensor -n argo-events — Shows dependency + filter config
  • argo list -n argo — Workflow was submitted after curl test

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 20
  • Tight coupling fallacy: Each Argo component is independent. If one fails (e.g., Events), others may continue unaware (Argo CD still syncs). Always add monitoring at each stage — a broken pipeline link doesn't always produce obvious errors.
  • Multiple sources of truth: The GitOps repo must be the ONE place where desired state is defined. If you update both the GitOps repo AND the cluster directly, Argo CD will detect drift and may revert your manual changes.
  • Cross-cutting secrets: All 4 Argo projects need secrets (registry creds, Git tokens, DB passwords). Centralize with External Secrets Operator or Vault — don't duplicate secrets across components.

✅ The Dream Pipeline — anihpj in Production
  • 10:00:00 — Alice merges PR "Fix jobpost pagination" to main
  • 10:00:05 — GitHub webhook fires → Argo Events receives push
  • 10:00:06 — Sensor filters main branch → triggers CI Workflow
  • 10:02:00 — Workflow: Clone → Unit+Lint+SAST (parallel) all pass
  • 10:05:00 — Build Docker image → Push to registry
  • 10:05:30 — Update GitOps repo with new image tag
  • 10:06:00 — Argo CD detects Git change → syncs staging
  • 10:08:00 — Staging tests pass → promote to prod
  • 10:08:30 — Argo Rollouts: canary 10% → metrics OK
  • 10:12:00 — Canary 25% → 50% → 100% deployed!
  • Alice never touched a server. Zero human steps. 12 minutes end-to-end.
🧠 Deep Dive: Why Four Separate Projects?

A common question: "Why does Argo have four separate projects instead of one unified tool?" The answer is the Unix philosophy: each tool does one thing well, and they compose together. This has several advantages:

  • Independent adoption: You can use Argo CD without Argo Workflows, or vice versa. Teams adopt what they need, when they need it.
  • Independent release cycles: Argo CD can release security patches without affecting Argo Workflows deployments. Each project moves at its own pace.
  • Focused expertise: The Argo CD team focuses on GitOps UX. The Workflows team focuses on pipeline orchestration. The Rollouts team focuses on deployment strategies. Each team's deep expertise produces better tools.
  • Failure isolation: If the Workflows controller crashes, Argo CD continues syncing. If the Events EventBus has issues, Rollouts still promote. No single point of failure brings down the entire pipeline.

The tradeoff is integration complexity — you need to wire them together. But the CAPA exam tests exactly this: understanding how each project fits into the larger GitOps pipeline.

20.2 Setting Up the Pipeline — Step by Step

Here's the complete setup order for anihpj, from infrastructure to first auto-deploy:

1
Install all 4 Argo controllers: CD in argocd, Workflows in argo, Rollouts in argo-rollouts, Events + EventBus in argo-events.
2
Create CI WorkflowTemplate: DAG pipeline from Chapter 10 — clone → test+lint+sast → build → push → update GitOps.
3
Create webhook EventSource + Sensor: From Chapter 18/19 — GitHub push → filter main → trigger CI → parameterize SHA.
4
Create Rollout + AnalysisTemplate: From Chapter 16 — canary 10→25→50→100 with Prometheus error-rate check.
5
Create Argo CD Application: Point to GitOps overlays/prod. Auto-sync with prune + selfHeal.
6
Test end-to-end: Push to GitHub → watch Events → watch Workflows → watch CD sync → watch Rollouts canary.
💡 Prerequisites Checklist

Before starting: (1) GitHub repo with anihpj code, (2) GitOps repo with Kustomize overlays, (3) Container registry, (4) Prometheus for metrics (optional), (5) Ingress for webhook exposure.

20.3 Pipeline Optimization — 5 Techniques

Speed matters. Here are 5 techniques to make your anihpj pipeline fast:

CI/CD Pipeline Optimization Techniques
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PIPELINE OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES                             │
│                                                              │
│  1. PARALLELIZE TESTS (DAG)                                  │
│     Clone (1m) → Unit(2m)∥Lint(1m)∥SAST(3m)∥Integration(5m) │
│     Total: 1 + max(2,1,3,5) = 6 min (NOT 1+2+1+3+5=12!)    │
│                                                              │
│  2. DOCKER LAYER CACHING                                     │
│     COPY requirements.txt .  ← Cache if unchanged           │
│     RUN pip install ...       ← Only runs if reqs change    │
│     COPY . .                  ← Only runs if code changes   │
│                                                              │
│  3. REGISTRY PROXIMITY                                       │
│     Pull from local registry (not Docker Hub)               │
│     python:3.12-slim vs python:3.12 = 10x size difference!  │
│                                                              │
│  4. SMART RETRY STRATEGIES                                   │
│     Don't retry on permanent failures (bad code)            │
│     Retry on transient failures (network, registry)         │
│     Limit retries to 3 with exponential backoff              │
│                                                              │
│  5. PERSISTENT VOLUME FOR DEPENDENCIES                       │
│     Mount PVC at /root/.cache/pip                           │
│     pip packages cached across workflows!                   │
│     Reduces pip install from 2 min → 10 seconds             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 21: Argo CD + Workflows + Events + Rollouts — Integration Patterns

Now that you understand each tool individually, this chapter shows the proven patterns for making them work together. These are the battle-tested recipes used by Intuit, NVIDIA, Adobe, and Capital One in production.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🎯 CAPA Integration

  • ✅ Understand component chaining — which tool feeds into which
  • ✅ Design a multi-environment promotion strategy (dev→staging→prod)

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 21
  • Image Updater overrides Git: If Image Updater writes to Git directly, it bypasses your PR/code review process. Configure it to create PRs instead of direct commits for production environments.
  • Helm vs Kustomize for GitOps: Helm templates are harder to read in Git (Go templates, not final YAML). Kustomize overlays are pure YAML — easier for GitOps diffing. CAPA favors Kustomize for GitOps scenarios.
  • Progressive sync vs progressive delivery: Argo CD's sync waves control deployment ORDER. Argo Rollouts control traffic SPLITTING. They solve different problems — don't confuse them.

21.1 Common Integration Patterns

There are 4 proven patterns for combining Argo tools. Each solves a different class of problem:

Pattern 1: Push-to-Deploy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PATTERN 1: PUSH-TO-DEPLOY                                   │
│                                                              │
│  Push Code → Events → Workflows → Argo CD                    │
│                                                              │
│  1. Dev pushes to GitHub                                     │
│  2. Webhook EventSource receives push event                  │
│  3. Sensor triggers CI Workflow                              │
│  4. Workflow: Clone → Test → Build → Push → Update GitOps    │
│  5. Argo CD detects GitOps change → auto-syncs               │
│  6. App deployed!                                            │
│                                                              │
│  anihpj: Every push to main auto-deploys to dev              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Pattern 2: Manifest Generation
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PATTERN 2: MANIFEST GENERATION                              │
│                                                              │
│  Workflow → Generate K8s YAML → Argo CD deploys              │
│                                                              │
│  1. Workflow renders K8s manifests from templates            │
│  2. Output YAML is committed to GitOps repo                  │
│  3. Argo CD syncs the generated manifests                    │
│                                                              │
│  anihpj: CI Workflow generates env-specific YAML             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Pattern 3: CD + Rollouts (Progressive Delivery)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PATTERN 3: CD + ROLLOUTS (Progressive Delivery)             │
│                                                              │
│  Argo CD → Rollout CRD → Canary/BlueGreen                    │
│                                                              │
│  1. Argo CD deploys a Rollout (NOT a Deployment)             │
│  2. Rollout controller manages progressive delivery          │
│  3. AnalysisTemplate checks metrics before each step         │
│  4. Auto-promote or auto-rollback based on metrics           │
│                                                              │
│  anihpj: CD deploys Rollout, Rollout does canary 10→100%     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Pattern 4: Cluster Watchdog
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PATTERN 4: CLUSTER WATCHDOG                                 │
│                                                              │
│  Resource EventSource → Workflow (remediation)               │
│                                                              │
│  1. EventSource watches for specific K8s resource changes    │
│  2. Sensor triggers Workflow when anomaly detected           │
│  3. Workflow performs automated remediation                  │
│                                                              │
│  anihpj: Watch JobPost CRDs → auto-validate new posts        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  COMPONENT CHAINING — How Argo Tools Feed Each Other         │

│  Events                                                      │

Q8
What is Progressive Sync in Argo CD?
Show Answer
Answer

Sync resources in a specific order and wait for healthy status before continuing. Example: sync ConfigMap first → wait healthy → sync Deployment → wait healthy. Use sync waves (annotations) to control order.

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. Sync resources in a specific order and wait for healthy status before continuing. Q9
How do you handle schema migrations safely with Rollouts?
Show Answer
Answer

Run migration as a separate Workflow BEFORE the Rollout canary starts. Use an initContainer or a pre-sync hook. The Rollout should wait until migration completes. Ensure migration is backward-compatible with the OLD version.

Explanation

This concept is tested on CAPA because it demonstrates understanding of Argo's operational model. Run migration as a separate Workflow BEFORE the Rollout canary starts. Use an initContainer or a pre-sync hook. The Rollout should wait until migration completes. Ensure migration is backward-compatible with the OLD version. Key insight: The exam tests not just memorization of commands but understanding WHY Argo works this way — the architectural decisions behind the implementation. Practice this in a live cluster to build muscle memory for the hands-on exam tasks.

🔍 DB MIGRATION
1. Backup (pg_dump → S3)
2. Migrate (manage.py migrate)
3. Verify (check migration table)
4. THEN deploy new app
⚠️ Migration must be BACKWARD compatible

Common CAPA Mistakes — Chapter 22
  • Disabling admin without SSO: If you set admin.enabled: false in argocd-cm without configuring SSO first, you'll lock yourself out of Argo CD completely. Always verify SSO login works before disabling local admin.
  • No resource limits: Argo CD components without CPU/memory limits can OOMKill during large syncs. Repo Server: 512Mi-1Gi. Application Controller: 1-2Gi. Redis: 256Mi-512Mi.
  • Skipping minor versions during upgrade: Going from 2.8 to 2.11 can break CRD compatibility. Always upgrade ONE minor version at a time and test in staging first.

22.3 Security Best Practices — Top 10

🔐 TOP 10 ARGO SECURITY PRACTICES
  1. Change default passwords immediately: The default admin password is in a well-known Secret — change it before exposing anything externally.
  2. Use SSO/OIDC, not local users: Integrate with Okta, Azure AD, Google, GitHub. Configure argocd-cm → oidc.config.
  3. Disable admin after SSO: Set admin.enabled: "false" in argocd-cm once SSO is working.
  4. Restrict AppProject destinations: NEVER use namespace: "*". Always specify exact namespaces and clusters per project.
  5. Never store plaintext secrets in Git: Use Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or HashiCorp Vault. Plaintext secrets in repos = security incident.
  6. Apply Network Policies: Restrict Argo CD egress to only trusted Git repos. Restrict ingress from trusted sources only.
  7. Enable audit logging: Track who deployed what and when. Critical for SOC2, PCI, and HIPAA compliance.
  8. Update Argo regularly: Subscribe to GitHub security advisories. Run argocd version to check.
  9. Use private repos + deploy keys: argocd repo add url --ssh-private-key-path key. Rotate keys regularly.
  10. Set resource limits on all Argo pods: Prevent DoS — especially workflow pods which can consume unlimited resources without limits.

22.4 Troubleshooting Common Issues

When things go wrong, here's your systematic reference across all 4 Argo tools:

ToolSymptomLikely CauseFix
CDSync stuck "Unknown"Repo unreachable / auth failedCheck repo URL + credentials
OutOfSync, nothing changedController lag / cache issueargocd app sync --force
Healthy but resources missingWrong server URL or namespaceVerify destination server+ns
WFPod pending indefinitelyResource quota or node taintkubectl describe pod → Events
Artifact "not found"Artifact repo misconfiguredVerify MinIO/S3 in configmap
DAG tasks never startDependency not resolvableVerify dependencies in DAG spec
RolloutsTraffic not shiftingService selector mismatchVerify activeService + labels
AnalysisRun stuckPrometheus unreachableCheck analysis provider config
EventsWebhook returns 500NATS down / EventBus not readykubectl logs -n argo-events
Sensor not firingEventSource not publishingCheck EventSource + Sensor logs
⚠️ Top Production Deployment Gotchas
  • Don't use the built-in MinIO for production artifacts: The quick-start MinIO is for development only. Use S3/GCS/Azure Blob with bucket versioning and backups.
  • Don't run Argo CD as admin after SSO setup: Once you configure OIDC/SSO, disable the admin account. The admin password is in a well-known Kubernetes Secret.
  • Don't skip resource limits on workflow pods: A workflow step without resource limits can consume an entire node's memory. Always set resources.limits on every template.
  • Don't expose the EventBus port: NATS is internal-only. If you expose it, anyone can publish events to your cluster. Use NetworkPolicy to restrict access.
  • Don't forget to backup Argo CD's database: If you lose the argocd DB, you lose all Application configurations, sync history, and RBAC settings. Backup regularly.

22.5 Beyond CAPA — Production Scaling & High Availability

These are real-world operational insights from the official Argo CD HA documentation. Not directly tested on CAPA, but essential knowledge for anyone running Argo in production.

PRODUCTION SCALING — COMPONENT TUNING
COMPONENT              KEY TUNING PARAMETERS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
argocd-repo-server     --parallelismlimit (concurrent manifests)
                       --repo-cache-expiration (default 24h)
                       TMPDIR → use persistent volume
                       ARGOCD_EXEC_TIMEOUT (default 90s)

argocd-application-    --status-processors (default 20)
controller             --operation-processors (default 10)
                       --repo-server-timeout-seconds
                       --sharding-method (legacy|round-robin|consistent-hashing)
                       ARGOCD_CONTROLLER_REPLICAS (shard count)

argocd-server          ARGOCD_API_SERVER_REPLICAS
                       ARGOCD_GRPC_MAX_SIZE_MB (default 200)

For 1000+ apps: status-processors=50, operation-processors=25
For multi-cluster: shard with consistent-hashing method
Monorepo (50+ apps): use manifest-paths annotation + qualified refs
🧠 Production Scaling Rules of Thumb

Repo Server: Mount a persistent volume at /tmp to avoid disk pressure. Set --repo-cache-expiration 1h for low-volume environments instead of default 24h. Use refs/heads/main (fully qualified) instead of main on monorepos to avoid slow reference resolution.

Application Controller: For every 100 apps, add ~5 status-processors. Use consistent-hashing sharding to minimize cluster reshuffling when shards change. Set timeout.reconciliation in argocd-cm to control Git poll interval (default 3m). Add jitter to spread reconciliation load.

Server: Stateless — just add replicas. Increase ARGOCD_GRPC_MAX_SIZE_MB if managing 3000+ applications (default 200MB response limit).

⚠️ Security Beyond CAPA — Hardening for Production

JWT Tokens: Admin tokens expire after 24 hours (CVE-2021-26921). SSO/Dex tokens also expire after 24h. Project-scoped automation tokens have configurable expiration. All revoked by deletion.

Git Repo Security: Attackers with write access to a trusted Git repo can: (1) deploy malicious images, (2) use Kustomize remote bases or Helm chart dependencies to reference untrusted repos, (3) inject commands through config management tools. Mitigation: restrict write access, audit Git history, disable unused tools.

Cluster RBAC: Argo CD defaults to cluster-admin. For production: limit the ClusterRole to only the namespaces/resources Argo CD manages. Use resource.exclusions in argocd-cm to deny access to sensitive resource types.

Auditing: Argo CD emits Kubernetes Events for all Application activity: who created/synced/deleted, when, and the result. Persist these with Event Exporter or Event Router for long-term audit trails. Git history + K8s Events = complete compliance audit.

22.6 Beyond CAPA — Performance Optimization

⏩
Shallow Clone

For repos with large history: depth: "1" in repo secret or argocd repo add --depth 1. Only clones the required commit, not full history. Dramatically speeds up initial clone for large repos.

📋
Manifest Paths Annotation

argocd.argoproj.io/manifest-generate-paths: .;../shared — tells Argo CD which paths to check for changes. If no files in those paths changed, skip reconciliation entirely. Critical for monorepos.

🚦
Rate Limiting

Prevent reconciliation storms: WORKQUEUE_BUCKET_SIZE (burst, default 500), WORKQUEUE_BUCKET_QPS (per-second limit). Per-item exponential backoff with cooldown period prevents single app from dominating the queue.

📝 Chapter 22 — CAPA Practice Questions

Q1
What RBAC principle should Argo CD use for production?
Show Answer
Answer

Least privilege. ServiceAccounts scoped to specific namespaces. RBAC policies restricting who can sync/delete applications. Use SSO (OIDC) with group-based access (admins, developers, viewers).

Explanation

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) in Kubernetes has 4 components: Role/ClusterRole (defines permissions — 'CAN get pods'), RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding (assigns role to users/groups — 'Alice GETS pod-reader role'), Subject (User, Group, or ServiceAccount), and Verbs (get, list, create, update, delete, watch). Argo uses ServiceAccounts: the Application Controller, Repo Server, and API Server each have ServiceAccounts with specific permissions. On CAPA, you need to know which ServiceAccount needs which permissions.

🔍 RBAC CHAIN
Subject ──▶ Role ──▶ RoleBinding
(User/SA)   (verbs)  (assignment)
'Alice CAN get pods in namespace anihpj'

Chapter 23: CAPA Exam Overview & Strategy

The Certified Argo Project Associate (CAPA) exam tests your ability to use all four Argo tools in real-world scenarios. This chapter gives you the exam format, proven strategies, terminal setup, and a 4-week study plan to ensure you pass.

🧠 CAPA Quick Facts — Memorize These!
  • All Argo CRDs use: apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 — NOT v1 or v1beta1
  • 4 Namespaces: CD=argocd | WF=argo | Rollouts=argo-rollouts | Events=argo-events
  • DAG syntax: dependencies: [taskA, taskB] — tasks without deps run in parallel
  • Blue-green requires: activeService + previewService — must exist BEFORE Rollout
  • EventBus is REQUIRED: No EventBus = events don't flow. Always check kubectl get eventbus
  • Pass: 75% (~45/60) | Time: 90 min | Format: MCQ + hands-on CLI

23.2 Exam-Day Strategy

1
First 5 min — Setup: Set all aliases (see 23.4), bookmark key docs pages, verify cluster context with kubectl cluster-info. Don't skip this — it saves 10+ minutes during the exam.
2
90s per question: If you're stuck after 2 minutes, FLAG it and move on. Return to flagged questions at the end. Easy questions first = more confidence.
3
Verify every CLI answer: After running a command, always verify: argo get / argocd app get / kubectl describe. Partial credit is rare — be thorough.
4
Last 10 min — Review flagged: Revisit all flagged questions. Check for silly mistakes (wrong namespace, typos). If unsure, eliminate obviously wrong answers and guess.
📋 Day-Before-Exam Checklist

  • ✅ Pre-create aliases file: save terminal setup from 23.4 as ~/.capa-aliases.sh
  • ✅ Bookmark: Argo CD declarative setup, Workflows examples, Rollouts spec, Events EventSource types
  • ✅ Run Lab 5 (Full Simulation) at least once — time yourself honestly
  • ✅ Review the Top 10 Mistakes (23.3) — most exam failures come from these
  • ✅ Get good sleep! Don't cram. 90 minutes goes fast. Have water ready.

23.3 Top 10 CAPA Exam Mistakes to Avoid

❌ TOP 10 EXAM MISTAKES
  1. Forgetting to check namespace: Argo CD = argocd, Workflows = argo, Rollouts = argo-rollouts, Events = argo-events. Always verify with -n.
  2. Writing YAML from scratch: Use kubectl create --dry-run=client -o yaml or argocd app create --dry-run to generate skeletons.
  3. Confusing Workflow and WorkflowTemplate: Workflow = one-time run, WorkflowTemplate = reusable. Submit from WFTmpl with argo submit --from wftmpl/NAME.
  4. Ignoring sync waves: If resources must deploy in order, use argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave annotation. Lower numbers sync first.
  5. Not setting resource limits on workflow pods: OOM kills are the #1 workflow failure cause. Always set resources.limits.
  6. Rollout without activeService: Blue-green requires activeService and previewService to exist BEFORE the Rollout is created.
  7. EventSource webhook not receiving: Check EventBus is running: kubectl get eventbus -n argo-events. No EventBus = no events.
  8. Not bookmarking docs: Before the exam, bookmark: Argo CD declarative setup, Workflows examples, Rollouts spec, Events EventSource types.
  9. Using wrong API version: All Argo CRDs use argoproj.io/v1alpha1 — NOT v1 or v1beta1.
  10. Skipping verification after each task: Always run argo get, argocd app get, or kubectl describe to confirm success before moving on.

Chapter 24: CAPA Practice Questions — All Domains

60 practice questions distributed by official exam weights. Each question includes the answer and a detailed explanation. These simulate the real CAPA exam format — multiple choice and hands-on CLI scenarios.

🔴 Exam Prep⏱️ ~3 hours60 Questions

24.1 Argo Workflows Questions (22 Questions — 36%)

Sample Questions (Full 22 in exam simulation)

Q1: You need to run a CI pipeline where unit tests and lint checks run in parallel after cloning, then a build step runs after both complete. Which template type should you use?

A: DAG. DAG templates allow you to define tasks with dependencies — tasks without dependencies run in parallel. Set unit-tests and lint to both depend on clone, and build to depend on both unit-tests and lint.

Q2: How do you submit a workflow from a WorkflowTemplate named anihpj-ci with parameter image-tag=v2.0?

A: argo submit --from wftmpl/anihpj-ci -p image-tag=v2.0 -n argo. The --from flag references the WorkflowTemplate by name, and -p passes parameters.

Q3: What does argo logs @latest -c step-name do?

A: Shows logs from the container named step-name in the most recently submitted workflow. @latest is a shortcut for the latest workflow in the current namespace.

Q4: How do you configure a CronWorkflow to run every 6 hours and keep the last 3 successful runs?

A: schedule: "0 */6 * * *" and successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3.

Q5: What's the difference between retryStrategy and onExit?

A: retryStrategy retries a failed step up to N times with backoff. onExit runs a cleanup handler regardless of success/failure — it's for side effects like notifications or resource cleanup.

24.2 Argo CD Questions (20 Questions — 34%)

Sample Questions (Full 20 in exam simulation)

Q1: What namespace must Argo CD Application resources be created in?

A: argocd. Argo CD only watches for Application CRDs in its own namespace. Applications created in other namespaces are ignored.

Q2: How do you configure auto-sync with pruning and self-healing?

A: syncPolicy: {automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}}. Prune deletes resources not in Git; selfHeal auto-corrects drift.

Q3: Which generator creates one Application per folder in a Git repository?

A: Git Generator. It scans the specified path and creates an Application for each subdirectory found. Perfect for monorepo patterns.

Q4: How do you verify an Application is synced and healthy?

A: argocd app get <app> — check that Status shows "Healthy" and "Synced". The UI also shows green hearts (healthy) and green checkmarks (synced).

Q5: What does the CreateNamespace=true sync option do?

A: Argo CD automatically creates the destination namespace if it doesn't exist. Without this option, sync fails if the namespace is missing.

Q6: How do you roll back an Argo CD application?

A: argocd app rollback <app> <REVISION>. Find the revision with argocd app history <app>.

Q7: What's the difference between prune and selfHeal?

A: prune deletes resources not in Git. selfHeal auto-corrects resources modified outside Git (drift detection).

24.3 Argo Rollouts Questions (11 Questions — 18%)

Sample Questions (Full 11 in exam simulation)

Q1: What's the key difference between blue-green and canary deployments?

A: Blue-green switches ALL traffic at once (instant cutover). Canary gradually shifts a percentage of traffic (10% → 25% → 50% → 100%). Blue-green needs 2× resources; canary uses less.

Q2: With 5 replicas and setWeight: 20, how many canary pods run?

A: 1 canary pod (5 × 20% = 1.0). Argo rounds fractional pods. At 25% with 10 replicas: 10 × 25% = 2.5 → 2 canary pods.

Q3: What command promotes a paused canary rollout to the next step?

A: kubectl argo rollouts promote <rollout>. This skips the remaining pause duration and advances to the next setWeight step.

24.4 Argo Events Questions (7 Questions — 12%)

Sample Questions (Full 7 in exam simulation)

Q1: What are the four components of the Argo Events architecture?

A: EventSource (listens) → EventBus/NATS (transports) → Sensor (filters + decides) → Trigger (acts, usually submits Workflow).

Q2: Which EventSource type would you use to trigger a workflow when a file is uploaded to S3?

A: S3 EventSource. Configure the bucket name, events (s3:ObjectCreated:*), and optional prefix/suffix filters.

Q3: How does parameterization pass event data to a workflow?

A: In the Sensor trigger, use parameters with src.dependencyName + dataKey (JSON path in event payload) and dest (path in workflow spec). Example: dataKey: body.head_commit.id extracts the commit SHA from a GitHub push event.

Chapter 25: Hands-On Labs — CAPA Exam Simulation

Five hands-on labs that simulate the actual CAPA exam tasks. Each lab has step-by-step instructions with verification points. Lab 5 is a full 60-minute timed simulation — take it 2 days before your exam.

🔴 Exam Prep⏱️ ~4 hours5 Labs

25.1 Lab 1: Install and Configure Argo CD

Goal: Install Argo CD on a fresh cluster, create an Application for anihpj, and configure auto-sync.

  1. kubectl create namespace argocd
  2. Install Argo CD: kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
  3. Wait for pods: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n argocd --timeout=300s
  4. Get admin password: kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d
  5. Create Application YAML pointing to your GitOps repo at overlays/dev with syncPolicy.automated.prune: true and selfHeal: true
  6. Apply and verify: argocd app get anihpj-dev
✅ Verification
  • argocd app list — anihpj-dev shows Healthy and Synced
  • kubectl get pods -n anihpj-dev — anihpj pods running

25.2 Lab 2: Argo Workflows CI Pipeline

Goal: Create a WorkflowTemplate with a DAG CI pipeline: clone → test (parallel with lint) → build → push.

  1. Create WorkflowTemplate with entrypoint ci-pipeline
  2. DAG tasks: clone → unit-tests (depends: clone) + lint (depends: clone) → build (depends: unit-tests, lint) → push (depends: build)
  3. Submit: argo submit --from wftmpl/ci-pipeline -n argo -p image-tag=v1.0
  4. Watch: argo watch @latest -n argo
  5. Check logs: argo logs @latest -n argo
✅ Verification
  • argo get @latest -n argo — Status: Succeeded
  • Unit-tests and lint ran in parallel (check timestamps)

25.3 Lab 3: Canary Deployment with Rollouts

Goal: Convert anihpj Deployment to Rollout with canary strategy.

  1. Create a Rollout with canary steps: 10% (pause 30s) → 25% (pause 2m) → 50% (pause 5m) → 100%
  2. Apply and watch: kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj --watch
  3. During pause, promote: kubectl argo rollouts promote anihpj
  4. Check canary pod count at each step
✅ Verification
  • Rollout reaches Healthy with 100% weight
  • kubectl get replicasets — Both old and new ReplicaSets exist

25.4 Lab 4: Event-Driven Automation

Goal: Create webhook EventSource + Sensor that triggers CI workflow on push to main.

  1. Create webhook EventSource on port 12000 at /push
  2. Create Sensor with filter: body.ref == "refs/heads/main"
  3. Add Argo Workflow trigger with parameterization (extract body.head_commit.id)
  4. Test: curl -X POST localhost:12000/push -d '{"ref":"refs/heads/main","head_commit":{"id":"abc123"}}'
✅ Verification
  • argo list -n argo — New workflow submitted after curl
  • argo get <wf> -n argo — Shows commit parameter = "abc123"

25.5 Lab 5: Full CAPA Simulation (60 min)

Goal: Complete 10 tasks across all 4 domains within 60 minutes. This is the closest thing to the real exam.

⏱️ Full Simulation — 10 Tasks
  1. [CD] Install Argo CD and create an Application for anihpj-dev
  2. [CD] Configure auto-sync with pruning and self-healing
  3. [CD] Create an AppProject that restricts deployments to anihpj-* namespaces only
  4. [WF] Create a WorkflowTemplate with DAG: clone → test → build
  5. [WF] Add a retry strategy: 3 retries with 10s backoff on the test step
  6. [WF] Submit the workflow with parameter image-tag=v3.0
  7. [Rollouts] Create a canary Rollout: 10% (pause 1m) → 100%
  8. [Rollouts] Promote the canary after 30 seconds (skip remaining pause)
  9. [Events] Create a webhook EventSource and Sensor
  10. [Events] Configure parameterization to extract body.ref from the webhook payload
💡 Scoring Rubric

Each task is worth 10 points. Pass threshold: 75/100. Grade yourself honestly. If you score below 75, identify weak domains and re-do those chapters + labs before your exam date.

📎 Appendix F: anihpj Complete Manifests Reference

All YAML files needed to deploy the anihpj/jobpost Django application using every Argo tool. Use as your CAPA exam reference!

F.1 Dockerfile — Multi-Stage Build

Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
RUN useradd -m -u 1000 django && chown -R django:django /app
USER django
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]

F.2 K8s Base Manifests

Core resources: deployment.yaml (anihpj:v1.0, port 8000, liveness/readiness probes, resource limits), service.yaml (ClusterIP port 80→8000, selector app=anihpj), configmap.yaml (DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE, DB_HOST, DEBUG), secret.yaml (DB_PASSWORD, SECRET_KEY as base64), namespace.yaml (anihpj-dev, anihpj-staging, anihpj-prod).

F.3 Kustomize Layout (Base + Overlays)

base/ → common resources shared across all environments. overlays/dev/ → 1 replica, debug=True. overlays/staging/ → 2 replicas, debug=False. overlays/prod/ → 5 replicas, resource limits CPU:500m-2000m, Mem:512Mi-2Gi, configmap-patch per environment.

F.4 Argo CD Application YAMLs

Three files: anihpj-dev.yaml (path overlays/dev, ns anihpj-dev), anihpj-staging.yaml (path overlays/staging), anihpj-prod.yaml (path overlays/prod). All with syncPolicy.automated.prune:true and selfHeal:true.

F.5 Argo CD ApplicationSet

One file generates 3 Applications using a List Generator: [dev, staging, prod]. Template sets source.path: overlays/{{env}} and destination.namespace: anihpj-{{env}}. Matrix option: env × region = 6+ Applications.

F.6 CI WorkflowTemplate

DAG pipeline: clone anihpj → parallel(unit tests, lint, SAST) → docker build -t registry.io/anihpj:{{version}} → docker push → update GitOps repo (commit new image tag). Artifacts: test-results.json, lint-report.txt.

F.7 DB Migration CronWorkflow

schedule: "0 2 * * *" (2 AM nightly). Steps: pg_dump backup → python manage.py migrate → python manage.py check --deploy → Slack notification. concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, historyLimit: 7.

F.8 Canary Rollout + AnalysisTemplate

Rollout: replicas: 5, canary steps: 10%(30s)→25%(2m)→50%(5m)→100%. AnalysisTemplate queries Prometheus: sum(rate(http_errors{app="anihpj"}[1m])) < 0.01. activeService: anihpj-active, previewService: anihpj-preview.

F.9 Webhook EventSource + Sensor

EventSource: GitHub webhook, port 12000, POST /push. Sensor: filter on push to main, extract commit SHA, trigger CI WorkflowTemplate. Parameters: repo_url=github.com/team-anihpj/anihpj, commit_sha={{sha}}.

F.10 App-of-Apps Bootstrap

Single Application with source.path: argo-apps/ that syncs all F.4-F.9 files. ONE kubectl apply → entire anihpj infrastructure running on Argo CD + Workflows + Events! This is the "one-click deploy" pattern for the complete anihpj platform.

📎 Appendix I: Argo Glossary Reference

TermDefinition
ApplicationArgo CD CRD linking a Git repository to a K8s cluster for GitOps deployment
AppProjectGroups Applications and enforces RBAC restrictions (sources, destinations)
ApplicationSetTemplate that automatically generates multiple Applications from generators
SyncProcess of making cluster state match the desired state defined in Git
DriftWhen actual cluster state differs from desired Git state
PruneAutomatically delete cluster resources that no longer exist in Git
Self-HealAutomatically correct drift by reverting changes made outside Git
WorkflowDAG or Steps-based container execution orchestrated as a K8s CRD
WorkflowTemplateReusable workflow blueprint — submit multiple times with different parameters
DAGDirected Acyclic Graph — tasks with dependencies, parallel execution
ArtifactFile or data passed between workflow steps via S3/MinIO/GCS
CronWorkflowScheduled workflow using cron expression syntax
RolloutArgo's replacement for K8s Deployment — adds blue-green and canary strategies
Blue-GreenInstant cutover deployment using two complete environments
CanaryGradual traffic shift deployment (10%→25%→50%→100%)
AnalysisTemplateDefines metric-based criteria for promoting or rolling back a canary
EventSourceCRD that listens for external events (webhook, S3, Kafka, GitHub, etc.)
SensorCRD that filters events and triggers actions (usually submits a Workflow)
EventBusInternal NATS streaming transport connecting EventSources to Sensors
GitOpsGit as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications
KustomizeK8s-native YAML patching tool using base + overlay model
HelmPackage manager for K8s using Go template charts and values files
CRDCustom Resource Definition — extends the K8s API with new resource types

💡 Kustomize vs Helm — Quick Decision

Kustomize: Simpler, built into kubectl, base+overlay patching. Best for anihpj and CAPA learning. Helm: More powerful templating, package distribution, versioned releases. Best for distributing charts to others. CAPA tests both — know the Argo CD source configuration for each.
